Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 1:

﴿O Prophet, fear Allah, and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾

The opening of the surah with the address to the Prophet ﷺ, calling him by his prophetic description, indicates that what matters most in this surah's discourse concerns the circumstances of the Prophet ﷺ.

He is addressed in it five times, at the openings of different topics of legislation, some of which are specific to him and some of which concern others but have a connection to him.

The first address introduces the principal topic: defining the duties of his mission toward his Lord.

The second address introduces the topic of honouring his wives and bringing them closer to his station.

The third address introduces the explanation of defining the shifting affairs of his mission in dealing with the community.

The fourth address opens the topic of the rulings on his marriages and his conduct with his wives.

The fifth address concerns his conveying the etiquette of women, from among the people of his household and from among the believing women.

So this first address is the opening of the principal purpose for the rest of the purposes, which is defining the duties of his mission in carrying out the will of his Lord, exalted is He, in the most perfect manner, without the enemies of the religion spoiling his works. It is similar to the address in His saying: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67], and His saying: ﴿O Messenger, let not those who race to disbelief grieve you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41], and the verses.

The address of the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, by the description of prophethood rather than his proper name is an honouring of him through the excellence of this description, so that his station is elevated above being addressed in the manner others are addressed. For this reason, in the Qur'an he is addressed only as (﴿O Prophet﴾) or (﴿O Messenger﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41]). By contrast, when he is referred to in narration, he is sometimes described by this attribute, as in His saying: (﴿The day Allah will not disgrace the Prophet﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8]), (﴿And the Messenger said, "My Lord..."﴾ [al-Furqan: 30]), (﴿Say, "The spoils are for Allah and the Messenger"﴾ [al-Anfal: 1]), (﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6]), and he is sometimes referred to by his proper name, as in His saying: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any man among you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 40].

Sometimes his proper name is necessarily used so that the attribute of messengership may be mentioned after it, as in His exalted saying: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Fath: 29] and His saying: ﴿Muhammad is but a messenger﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 144]. These are situations in which the aim is to teach people that the bearer of that name is the Messenger of Allah, or to instruct them to call him by that name and to address him with it, for knowing his names is part of faith, so that he is not confused with others. For this reason, "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: I have five names: I am Muhammad, I am Ahmad, I am al-Mahi (the Eraser) through whom Allah erases disbelief, I am al-Hashir (the Gatherer) at whose feet people will be gathered, and I am al-'Aqib (the Successor), as a teaching for the community."

Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi reduced the names of the Prophet ﷺ to sixty-seven, and al-Suyuti extended them to three hundred. Ibn al-'Arabi also reported that some Sufis said: the names of the Prophet are a thousand names, as will come at His saying, exalted is He: (﴿O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [al-Ahzab: 45]).

The command to the Prophet to fear Allah is a preparation for the prohibition against following the disbelievers and the hypocrites, so that from the two clauses there results a restriction of his piety to attachment to Allah alone, to the exclusion of others. For the meaning of "do not obey" is synonymous with the meaning of "do not fear the disbelievers and the hypocrites," since obedience is a form of fear. Thus the combination of the two clauses conveys the meaning: "O Prophet, do not fear anyone but Allah." He departed from the form of restriction, which is more famous in eloquent speech and more concise, to mentioning two clauses, one of command and one of prohibition, in order to make explicit that it is a restriction relative to a specific case, meaning that he should not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites. For had it been said merely, "Do not fear anyone but Allah," the hearing would not have attended to it with any special attention, since the Prophet's ﷺ piety toward his Lord is a known matter. So he took the path of elaboration for this purpose, like the saying of al-Samaw'al:

Our souls flow over the edges of swords, and they do not flow over anything other than swords.

He brought two clauses: an affirmation of flowing under a condition, and its negation in other than that condition, to make explicit that they do not dislike their blood flowing on the swords, but their blood does not flow on anything other than swords.

The original form of the restrictive construction is derived from two clauses of affirmation and negation, and because this clause is like a completion of the one before it, it is joined to it by conjunction, since the purpose of both is one. By this it is established that the command in His saying "fear Allah" and the prohibition in His saying "do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites" are both used to request continuance in what is constantly attached to him of the fear of Allah. This indicates that a great legislation will be delivered to him, which will not be free of hardship for him and for some of his community, and that he will encounter the reproaches of the disbelievers and the hypocrites.

The benefit of this command and prohibition is to make it known to them that the Prophet ﷺ will not accept their words, so that they may despair of that, because they were plotting with the polytheists and pretending that they were advising the Prophet ﷺ and persistently pressing him with requests, under the guise of counsel, as a display of Islam.

The intended meaning of "the disbelievers" is those who openly disbelieve, because they are contrasted with the hypocrites. It may be that they are the polytheists, as is the more common application of this term in the Qur'an, and this is most suitable given what follows in His saying: "Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body," through to the rest of the rulings on adoption. It also agrees with what is narrated about its occasion of revelation, though that narration is weak, as we will show. It may also be that they are the Jews, as the narration about its occasion of revelation seems to imply. And if it were taken to include both kinds of open disbelievers, it would not be far-fetched.

Obedience is acting in accordance with what another commands or indicates for the sake of a desired outcome. Its reality varies, and it is predicated by gradation. The occurrence of the term in the context of a prohibition requires the prohibition of every instance in which its least degree is realised, such as abandoning the marriage to the divorced wife of one's adopted son because of the saying of the hypocrites: "Muhammad forbids marrying the wives of sons," and he married the wife of his adopted son Zayd ibn Harithah. This is the meaning in which His saying occurs: ﴿And you feared the people, while Allah has more right that you should fear Him﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37], and His saying: ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and disregard their harm﴾ [al-Ahzab: 48], following the matter of Zayd's wife. It also covers abrogating what the polytheists had of making zihar (the pre-Islamic divorce formula of likening a wife to one's mother) render the one who is compared a "mother" to the one who makes the comparison, so that intercourse with her would be forbidden to him forever. For this reason the clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ was appended to the sentence, as a justification for the prohibition.

The meaning: Allah alone is worthy of obedience, not the disbelievers and the hypocrites, because He is Knowing and Wise, so He commands only what contains righteousness. The entry of "inna" upon the clause serves in the place of the causal "fa'" and performs its function, as explained in more than one place. Its well-known witness is the verse of Bashshar:

Go early, my two companions, before the midday heat, for that success lies in early rising.

Al-Wahidi in Asbab al-Nuzul, and al-Tha'labi, al-Qushayri and al-Mawardi in their tafsirs, mentioned that His saying, exalted is He, "﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾" was revealed because after the Battle of Uhud, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, 'Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl and Abu al-A'war al-Sulami, 'Amr ibn Sufyan, from Quraysh came to Medina, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ granted them safe conduct in Medina and permission to stay with 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. Then they came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ together with 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, al-Jadd ibn Qays, and Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq, and they asked the Messenger of Allah to leave off mentioning the gods of Quraysh. The Muslims became angry, and 'Umar intended to kill the Qurashi group, but the Messenger of Allah prevented him, because he had granted them safe conduct, and he ordered them to leave Medina. Then this verse was revealed, meaning: fear Allah in keeping the safe conduct, and do not obey the disbelievers, who are the Qurashi group, and the hypocrites, who are 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and those with him. But this report has no chain of transmission, and the critics such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir did not give it any attention.

This is a preface to what follows of the revelation concerning the rulings of adoption (tabanni) and what relates to them. For this reason the verb is in the present form, which is suitable for the future, and it is stripped of the future marker because it is close to the present time. The purpose of the command to follow it is that it is a specific command to follow, emphasizing the general command to follow the revelation. It also signals that what will soon be revealed to him is something that is hard on him and on the Muslims: the annulment of the ruling of adoption. They had become accustomed to it, it had settled into their customs, and they had treated adopted sons as true sons.

For this reason the clause ﴿Follow what is revealed to you﴾ is followed by the clause ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do﴾, as a reason for the command to follow and as a comfort to him, because Allah is aware of what is in your customs and your souls. So when He annuls any of that, its annulment is connected to the knowledge that it necessitates changing it. Therefore do not hesitate in carrying out His command in this matter. The clause ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do﴾ has the function of a cause, and it is therefore separated (from what precedes) because the emphatic particle serves the function of the conjunction fa' of consequence, as has passed just before.

In addressing the Prophet ﷺ in the singular with His words ﴿follow﴾, and in the plural with what includes him and his community in His words ﴿what you do﴾, there is an indication that among what will be sent down of revelation is what contains an obligation that includes changing a state in which the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, shared with some of the community in being involved, namely the ruling of adoption, since the Prophet had adopted Zayd ibn Harithah before his mission.

[Page 253]

Al-Jumhur (the majority of the reciters) read ﴿what you do﴾ with the second-person ta' (taa' al-khitab), addressing the Prophet ﷺ and the community, because this matter is more closely connected to the community. Abu 'Amr alone read ﴿what they do﴾ with the third-person ya' (the absent form), taking it as referring to all people, including the Muslims, the disbelievers and the hypocrites. This reading conveys, along with the reason given for the command to follow, an allusion to the polytheists and hypocrites that Allah will call them to account for the plots they hatch, and it is also a metonymy for Allah informing His Messenger of what He knows of them regarding this matter, as will come: ﴿If the hypocrites, and those in whose hearts is a disease, and the agitators in Medina do not desist, We will surely incite you against them﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60], meaning: We will surely inform you of what they plot, and We will permit you to expose their affair.

The meaning produced by this reading is not lost in the reading of al-Jumhur with the second person, because each group of those addressed takes its share of it.

Verse 3: **And put your trust in Allah; and Allah is sufficient as a Guardian** ﴿وتَوَكَّلْ عَلى اللَّهِ وكَفى بِاللَّهِ وكِيلًا﴾. This is an addition that prepares and paves the way for receiving a duty, one from which harm from the hypocrites is expected, such as their saying: "Muhammad forbade marrying the wives of sons, yet he married the wife of his son Zayd ibn Harithah." This is what His saying, the Exalted, points to: **And leave off their harm, and put your trust in Allah; and Allah is sufficient as a Guardian** ﴿ودَعْ أذاهم وتَوَكَّلْ عَلى اللَّهِ وكَفى بِاللَّهِ وكِيلًا﴾ [al-Ahzab: 48]. So He commanded him to fear his Lord alone, followed this with the command to follow His revelation, and reinforced it with the command to do what supports him, which is to entrust his affairs to Allah.

Tawakkul (reliance, trust): a person's leaning on another to take charge of his matter and affair, the one who will carry out his work. It was discussed at His saying, the Exalted: **So when you have resolved, then rely upon Allah** ﴿فَإذا عَزَمْتَ فَتَوَكَّلْ عَلى اللَّهِ﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159], in Surat Al 'Imran.

Wakil (guardian, trustee): the one to whom another entrusts his affair. It was discussed at His saying, the Exalted: **And they said, "Sufficient for us is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs"** ﴿وقالُوا حَسْبُنا اللَّهُ ونِعْمَ الوَكِيلُ﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173], in Surat Al 'Imran.

His saying "(wakilan)" [وكِيلًا] is a tamyiz (specification, a grammatical accusative clarifying the scope of a statement) of relation, meaning: Allah suffices as a guardian, that is, as His guardianship. Its parallel was discussed at His saying, "And put your trust in Allah; and Allah is sufficient as a Guardian" ﴿وتَوَكَّلْ عَلى اللَّهِ وكَفى بِاللَّهِ وكِيلًا﴾ in Surat An-Nisa.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 4 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body.﴾ This is an initial, independent resumption, like the introduction to a subject after a preface made by what precedes it. The introduction (muqaddimah) is more specific than the preface (tamhid), because it contains what clarifies the purpose, unlike the preface. So this is an introduction to what the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to follow of what is revealed to him, namely the legislation of contemplating the realities of things and their meanings, and that the true natures of matters are not altered by the statements attached to them that contradict realities, and that those attachments to realities are what veil minds from understanding the true realities, and what cover hearts through the confusion of things.

Two kinds of realities are mentioned here. The first is realities of beliefs, for the sake of establishing the Law upon sound beliefs and rejecting fabricated realities that contradict what is actual, because correcting thinking is the key to correcting action. This is what made its foundation the nullification that Allah placed in the creation of some people an order He did not place in the creation of others.

The second of the two kinds is realities of actions: so that the Law may be established upon considering the true natures of actions by what they are actually established upon in reality, not merely by assumption and pretension. This goes back to the principle that the realities of things are fixed, and this is what is pointed to by the words of the Exalted: (﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers, nor has He made your adopted sons your sons. That is your saying by your mouths. And Allah says the truth, and He guides to the way.﴾), meaning He does not say falsehood like some of your statements of that kind.

The intent is to draw attention to the falsity of matters that the people of ignorance (jahiliyyah) had asserted and claimed. Beginning with that which the evidence of its falsity is sensory perception and experience, so that it may be known from this that those who invent claims which the senses testify to be false will find it easy to invent claims with doubts and confusion of falsehood in the form of truth, which are then accepted with submission and compliance.

The reference in the words ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body﴾ is to one of the fabrications of the jahiliyyah. They claimed that Jamil ibn Ma'mar (it is said: ibn Asad) ibn Habib al-Jumahi al-Fihri (he was a shrewd man of strong memory) had two hearts that act and cooperate, and they called him "the one with two hearts," meaning two minds, because they used to think that perception is by the heart and that the heart is the seat of the intellect. This deceived him, or he took pride in it, so out of his extreme disbelief he would say: "Within me are two hearts, with each of which I act a deed better than the deed of Muhammad." They also called by the name "the one with two hearts" 'Abd Allah ibn Khatal al-Taymi, who was called 'Abd al-'Uzza in the jahiliyyah. When he embraced Islam the Messenger of Allah ﷺ named him 'Abd Allah; then he disbelieved and was killed in cold blood on the day of the Conquest of Mecca. He is the one who clung to the curtains of the Ka'bah, and he was not pardoned. So the verse negated their claim with general negation, meaning: Allah has not made for any man among the people two hearts, neither for Jamil ibn Ma'mar nor for Ibn Khatal. The occurrence of "man," which is indefinite in the context of negation, implies generality; and the occurrence of the verb "made" in the context of negation implies generality, because the verb in the context of negation is like the indefinite noun in the context of negation. The particle min before "two hearts" emphasizes the generality of two hearts within the body of a man. These three generalities indicate the negation of every individual instance of the making, for every individual of what is described as two hearts, concerning every man among the people; so Jamil ibn Ma'mar and others are included in the generality, such that this claim is not asserted for anyone whoever he may be.

The word "man" (rajul) has no restrictive implication (mafhum), because it is intended to mean the human being, in accordance with their customary usage in discourse of attaching human rulings and attributes to men, following the general pattern of speech, except for attributes specific to women. It is also known that it is not claimed for a woman that she has two hearts, by the implication of the address (fahwa al-khitab) or its allusive sense (lahn al-khitab).

The making that is negated here is the innate making, meaning: Allah did not create a man with two hearts within his body. He made the refutation of this claim a preface to the refutation of what they agreed upon of making someone a son of one who is not his son, and making a woman a mother of one who is not her mother, by way of analogical reasoning (qiyas al-tamthil): that is, those who invent what is not in creation do not hesitate to invent what is of that kind regarding fatherhood and motherhood, and their building upon their invention all the effects of invention. For fatherhood and motherhood are attributes of the natural constitution, and they are not among the things people agree upon by contract, like clientage (wala') and alliance (hilf).

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And his wives are their mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6], it is in the sense of likeness in the rulings of kindness and the prohibition of marriage. Do you not see what came in the hadith: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ proposed to 'A'ishah from Abu Bakr, Abu Bakr said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, I am only your brother.' The Messenger of Allah said: 'You are my brother, and she is lawful to me.'" Meaning that brotherhood does not go beyond the state of resemblance in sincere counsel and good companionship, and the effects of natural brotherhood do not follow from it, because those effects have their source in natural constitution. That is the meaning of his saying: "You are my brother, and she is lawful to me."

Al-jawf: the inner part of a person, his chest and belly, and it is the place of the principal organs apart from the brain.

The benefit of mentioning this container is to increase the depiction of what is signified by the heart and to make it manifest to the listener. When he hears it, he is quicker to be convinced of the denial that the inside of the body contains two hearts. This is like His saying ﴿but it is hearts within the breasts that become blind﴾ [al-Hajj: 46] and similar known restrictions; mentioning them is only a reminder of what is known and a renewal of its conception. Of this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There is no creature crawling on the earth, nor bird flying with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38], which has been discussed in Surah al-An'am.

* * *

﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers﴾.

This is a conjunction (atf) of a second refutation of some of their claims: that in the jahiliyyah, when a man wished to separate from his wife with a separation that admits no return in any way, he would say to her: "You are to me like the back of my mother" (anti 'alayya ka-zahri ummi). This was their well-known formula. It necessitates the divorce of the woman and the prohibition of marrying her thereafter, because she has become his mother. The intent here is not to legislate the nullification of the effects of that prohibition, because that was nullified in Surah al-Mujadilah, which was revealed before Surah al-Ahzab as will come. Rather, the intent is that it be a preface to the legislation of the nullification of adoption, by way of comparison between these delusions. Yet this second preface is closer to the intent, because it is among the legislative rulings.

Al-la'i: a relative pronoun for a group of women; it is the plural of allati, since it is not according to the pattern of plural forms. There are dialectal variants: al-la'i with a kasrah on the hamzah always, on the pattern of al-bab; al-la'i on the pattern of al-da'i; and al-la with the definite article prefixed without a yā'.

Qalun from Nafi', Qunbul from Ibn Kathir, and Abu Ja'far read (al-la'i) with an unstressed kasrah hamzah, and this is a dialect. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read (wa-lla'i) with a yā' after the hamzah on the pattern of al-da'i. Abu 'Amr, al-Bazzi from Ibn Kathir, and Ya'qub read it likewise.

And (al-lay) with a sakin yā' after the alif in place of the hamzah; this is a substitution attested by usage, and it is said to be the dialect of Quraysh. Warsh read with easing of the hamzah between the hamzah and the yā', with madd and qasr. This is also narrated from Abu 'Amr and al-Bazzi.

The mention of "back" (zahr) in their saying "You are to me like the back of my mother" is an imaginative depiction (takhyil) of the comparison hidden in the soul, in the manner of implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah), since he likens his wife, when he approaches her, to a riding animal when its rider mounts it. He mentioned the back by way of imagery, just as the claws (azfar) of death are mentioned in the well-known verse of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali. Its explanation will come at the beginning of the commentary on Surah al-Mujadilah.

Their saying "You are to me" contains an elided genitive, indicated by the meaning of marital relation present in the address, and the estimated sense is: "your intercourse." The word "to me" ('alayya) indicates the meaning of prohibition, meaning: you are forbidden to me. So the sentence, with the elision attached to it, became a sign of the meaning of permanent prohibition. The verb is transitive to the name of the woman whose prohibition is intended by the preposition min of origin (ibtida'iyyah), because it is implicitly construed with the meaning of separation from her.

When Allah the Exalted said: ﴿those whom you divorce by zihar﴾, the people knew that He meant their saying: "You are to me like the back of my mother."

The making that is negated in His saying ﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers﴾ is also the innate making, like that in His saying "Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body." That is: He did not create them as your mothers, since in reality they are not so. This is a metonymy (kinayah) for the negation of the legal effect which is one of the effects of the natural making, because Islam is the fitrah upon which Allah created people. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Their mothers are none but those who bore them﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 2]. Allah has elaborated this in Surah al-Mujadilah, and by this we know that Surah al-Mujadilah is the one in which the nullification of zihar and the rulings of its expiation appear. So we know that the verse of Surah al-Ahzab came after the establishment of the nullification of zihar, and its mention there is a preface to the nullification of adoption by way of resemblance, since both establish effects in an artificially made manner, not based on a divine making. This convinces us that Surah al-Ahzab was revealed after Surah al-Mujadilah, contrary to what Ibn al-Duraysi and Ibn al-Hassar held, and what Muhammad ibn al-Harith ibn Abyad transmitted from Jabir ibn Zayd, which is mentioned in the type of Meccan and Medinan surahs in the section on what was first revealed, from al-Itqan. Al-Suyuti said: "In this ordering there is room for examination." We will mention that in the commentary on Surah al-Mujadilah, if Allah wills.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (tazzahharuna) with a fatha on the ta' and a shaddah on the zay, fatha, without an alif, and a shaddah on the ha' with fatha. Hafs from 'Asim read (tuzahiruna) with a damma on the ta', a fatha on the zay lightened, followed by an alif, and a kasrah on the ha'. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Khalaf read (tazahiruna) with a fatha on the ta', a fatha on the zay lightened followed by an alif, and a fatha on the ha'.

* * *

﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾. This is the intended matter, which was prepared for by the two verses before it, and for this reason the discourse after it is expanded with the details of legislation concerning it. This sentence is conjoined to the two before it because all three share in negating claims that have no realities behind them.

The discussion of the intended meaning of "made" (ja'ala) is like the discussion of its counterpart in His saying ﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers﴾.

The meaning: you attribute adopted sons as sons, saying of the adopted one: "He is the son of so-and-so," to the one who adopted him, and you give him all that belongs to sons.

Al-ad'iya': plural of da'i, on the pattern of fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, derived from the root of ida'a'. Ida'a' is a claimant's asserting that something is his right, of property, lineage, or the like, truly or falsely. The description da'i came to be applied to the claimant who claims that he is the son of one whom he knows is not his father. So whoever claims to be the son of one who might possibly be his father, that is the laHiq or mustalhiq (one acknowledged). The da'i is one whom Allah did not make a son of the one who claimed him, since it is known he is not his father. As for the mustalhiq, Allah has made him a son of the one who acknowledged him by the ruling of acknowledgment, while it remains possible that he is his father.

It was pluralized as af'ila', because it is defective in its final radical, so it is not pluralized as fa'la. The more correct view is that af'ila' is regular for the plural of defective fa'il, whether it has the sense of active or passive participle.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 4 (part 2 of 2):**

This verse was revealed to annul adoption (*tabanni*, the taking of a child as one's own son), meaning the annulment of granting the legal effects of true sonship in matters of inheritance, lineage, and marriage prohibitions through affinity (*al-sihr*). In the Jahiliyya, people gave the adopted child all the rulings of sonship. Among the most famous adoptions in the Jahiliyya was Zayd ibn Harithah, whom the Prophet (ﷺ) adopted. 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah was adopted by al-Khattab, the father of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. Salim was adopted by Abu Hudhayfah. Al-Miqdad ibn 'Amr was adopted by al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth. Each of these four was called the son of the one who adopted him.

[Page 259]

Zayd ibn Harithah, about whom the verse was revealed, was a foreigner from the Banu Kalb of Wabarah, from the people of al-Sham. His father Harithah died and left two sons, Jabalah and Zayd, who remained in the custody of their grandfather. Then their two uncles came and asked the grandfather to take charge of them. He gave Jabalah to them, and Zayd remained with him. Then horsemen from Tihamah raided the tribe and took Zayd captive. His grandfather began searching for his fate and recited verses, among them:

*I wept for Zayd and did not know what had become of him,*
*Is he alive, so that hope may be held, or has the term of death come upon him?*

It was later learned that Zayd was in Makkah, and that those who had captured him had sold him in Makkah. Hakim ibn Hizam ibn Khuwaylid bought him and gave him as a gift to his aunt Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ). Khadijah then gave him to the Prophet (ﷺ). He remained with him for a time. Then his grandfather and uncle came, desiring to ransom him. He refused the ransom and chose to remain in slavery with the Prophet (ﷺ). At that point, the Prophet (ﷺ) called on the Quraysh to witness that Zayd was his son, that each would inherit from the other. His father and uncle were content and left. From then on he came to be called Zayd ibn Muhammad.

This was before the Prophethood (*al-ba'tha*). Zayd was killed at the Battle of Mu'tah in the land of al-Sham in the eighth year after the Hijrah.

\* \* \*

﴿That is your saying with your mouths, and Allah says the truth, and He guides to the way.﴾

This is a parenthetical resumptive sentence (*isti'naf i'tirad*) placed between the preface and the purpose of the legislation. It is a concluding summary (*fadhlakah*), as previously explained, of the three clauses that negated their making what was not actual into something actual. For this reason the sentence is detached (*fusilat*), since it serves as an explanation that achieves the purpose of what came before.

The demonstrative refers to something implicitly mentioned in the preceding discourse, namely what was negated: that Allah had made a man to have two hearts, that a wife whom one has likened to one's mother (*zihar*) becomes one's mother, and that adopted children become the sons of those who adopted them. Since these three negated matters arose from statements they uttered, it is correct to describe the matters referred to as "sayings." The meaning is that they are mere sayings, with no external realities corresponding to their implications, as the true statements of speech correspond to external relations. Otherwise there would be no point in describing those claims as "a saying with the mouths."

To convey this meaning, the phrase is restricted by "with your mouths." It is known that speech is only with the mouths, so mentioning "with your mouths" despite this being known indicates that it is a saying whose significance does not go beyond the mouths to reality and the actual state of affairs. Existence for it is only in the tongue and in minds, not in external observation. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By no means! It is only a word he is saying﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100], meaning it does not exceed that limit, i.e., its content does not come into being externally, namely the return to the world in the words of the disbeliever: ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99], ﴿that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100]. Thus it is understood from restricting it to "with your mouths" that it is a false saying that does not correspond to reality. He reinforced this by stating ﴿and Allah says the truth﴾, thereby indicating that their saying is false. For this reason the clause ﴿and Allah says the truth﴾ is conjoined to it, because it is included in the concluding summary of what came before, namely His saying "Allah did not make..." and so on. The meaning of their being sayings is that some people say, "So-and-so has two hearts," some say to their wives, "You are to me like the back of my mother," and some say to the adopted child, "So-and-so son of so-and-so," meaning the one whom they adopted.

The word *al-haqq* ("the truth") is in the accusative because it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*) that is the object of *yaqulu* ("says"). Its estimated form is: "the true speech," because the verb "to say" only governs sentences or what has the meaning of a sentence, as in ﴿Indeed, it is a word he is saying﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100]. The pronoun attached to *qa'il* ("sayer") refers back to *kalimah* ("word"), which is the object that has been made a genitive construction with it.

The subject, the name of Allah (*ism al-jalalah*), and its pronoun, being predicated with two verbal predicates, convey restriction by inversion (*qasr al-qalb*). That is: He says the truth, not those who established for you those claims; and He guides to the way, not those who misled people with delusions. Since both verbs are transitive, their objects are also restricted by context. Then, since Allah's saying in the three places is the truth and the way, it is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for the falsity and the misguidance of its opposite. The meaning is: they do not say the truth, and they do not guide to the way.

*Al-sabil* ("the way") is the well-trodden, clear road, that is, one that is evident to be frequented, so it is safe for conveying the traveler on it to his destination.

Since it has been established that these three claims are nothing more than bare words with no realization of their meanings in external reality, this requires the negation of the two matters that were made a preliminary and introduction to the purpose, and the negation of the third matter that is the purpose, namely adoption. Thus the introduction and the purpose share in the negation of truthfulness, and this is a more complete equivalence between the purpose and the introduction.

[Page 260 is not included; see below]

All of this is an added exhortation to receive Allah's command with acceptance and compliance, and to reject what contradicts it.

ادْعُوهم لِآبائِهِمْ هو أقْسَطُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ فَإنْ لَمْ تَعْلَمُوا آباءَهم فَإخْوانُكم في الدِّينِ ومَوالِيكُمْ

[Call them by their fathers' names; that is more just in the sight of Allah. But if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers in religion and your clients.]

This is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf, a new clause that opens the main subject of the legislation) for the purpose of abolishing adoption (tabanni, the taking of a child as one's own son), and a detailing of what Muslims should do concerning it.

This command is an obligation, by which the claim of the adopter that his adoptee is his son is annulled. The word "calling" (duʿaʾ) here means ascription of lineage (nasab).

What is meant by calling them by their fathers' names is the application of the consequences of that, namely that they are the sons of their fathers and not the sons of those who adopted them.

The lam in li-ābāʾihim is the lam of ascription (lam al-intisab), and its original meaning is the lam of entitlement (lam al-istihqaq). It is said: "Fulan li-Fulan," meaning he is his son, that is, he is ascribed to him. From this is the saying: "Fulan li-rishdah and Fulan li-ghayyah," meaning his lineage is attributed to her, that is, from a lawful marriage or from fornication. Al-Nabigha said:

If there is indeed for the two graves a grave at Jillaq,
and a grave at Saida, the one near Harib,

meaning: from the sons of the two companions of the two graves. ʿAlqama ibn ʿAbd, praising the king al-Harith, said:

You are not of human lineage, but of an angel
who descended from the air of the sky, swooping down.

In the hadith of Abu Qatada: ("The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed carrying Umama, the daughter of his daughter Zaynab, and (she was) to Abu al-As ibn Rabiʿa"). So the lam made it unnecessary to say "and the daughter of Abu al-As."

The pronoun in huwa aqsatu refers to the verbal noun (masdar) implied by the verb "call them" (ud'uhum li-ābāʾihim), that is, the calling (of them) by their fathers' names.

The clause huwa aqsatu ʿinda Allah is an explanatory resumptive (istiʾnaf bayani), as if a questioner said: "Why should we not call them by the names of those who adopted them?" It is answered by showing that this is the justice. The comparative form (ism al-tafdil) here is stripped of the sense of comparison, meaning: it is complete justice, and anything else is injustice to the true fathers and to the adoptees, because it entails the loss of their true lineages. The purpose of this resumptive clause is to confirm what is indicated by His words: ﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons. That is your saying with your mouths. But Allah says the truth, and He guides to the way.﴾ (Q. 33:4), so that the care of Allah the Exalted may be known in abolishing the judgments of the Jahiliyya concerning adoption, and so that the souls of Muslims, both adopters, adoptees, and those connected to them, may be reassured in accepting this legislation, which is difficult for them because it removes from them a familiarity to which they had become accustomed.

For this subtle meaning, the following was made a consequence: ﴿But if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers in religion and your clients.﴾ It combines in it an emphasis on the legislation, by not being lax in allowing what they had been doing, under the excuse that they do not know the fathers of some adoptees, and a comfort to people, that they may substitute for that false ascription a true connection that does not lose what was in the former ascription of connection, and that they may keep away from what was in it of corruption. So they began to call Salim, the adoptee of Abu Hudhayfa, "Salim the client of Abu Hudhayfa," and others likewise. None deviated from this except the people who said to al-Miqdad ibn ʿAmr: "al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad," in ascription to al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghuth, who had adopted him in the Jahiliyya, as has been mentioned before.

Al-Qurtubi said: When this verse was revealed, al-Miqdad said: "I am al-Miqdad ibn ʿAmr." Yet the (old) designation remained applied to him, and it was not heard that anyone among those who came before disobeyed by applying it to him, even if he did so deliberately.

In al-Qurtubi's words "even if he did so deliberately," there is an objection, since it is not possible to know whether one who uses that designation for him does so deliberately. Perhaps it passed over people's tongues as "al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad," so he was included in His words: ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you have done in error.﴾ (Q. 33:5), because what passes over the tongue is liable to be forgotten, and blame for forgetfulness is lifted.

The nominative of ikhwanukum is given as a predicate of an omitted subject, which is the pronoun referring to the adoptees, meaning: they can only be described as brothers in Islam if they are not clients, or as clients if they are clients by alliance or by the patronage of manumission. This is a complete inductive survey (istiqraʾ tamm). The statement that they are brothers and clients is a metonymy (kinaya) for guidance toward calling them by one of these two descriptions.

The waw in wa-mawalikum is the waw of division (li-l-taqsim), and it has the meaning of "or" (aw), so it may carry the sense of choice (takhyir), meaning: if you do not know their fathers, then call them, if you wish, "brothers," and if you wish, call them "clients," if they are such. This is a widening of latitude for people.

The fi in fi al-din is the fi of metaphorical containment (zarfiyya majaziyya), meaning: brothers by a brotherhood obtained through religion, just as a container gathers what is inside it; or it may be taken as the fi of causation (taʿlil wa-tasabbub), meaning: brothers because of Islam, like His words: ﴿When he is harmed for the sake of Allah﴾ (Q. 29:10), that is, for the sake of Allah, in accordance with His words: ﴿The believers are only brothers﴾ (Q. 49:10).

There is no doubt or confusion in calling them by the description of brotherhood, unlike calling them by the description of sonship, because the calling by brotherhood in such cases is apparent, since the description of brotherhood in them has an interpretation of intending the religious connection. By contrast, the description of sonship is merely loyalty and alliance. So the right course is that they be called by this description, and in that there is a consolation for the hearts of the adoptees and those who adopted them.

The "clients" (mawali) mentioned in His words "and your clients" means the clientage of alliance (wala' al-muhalafa), not the clientage of manumission (wala' al-ʿitq). So alliance is like brotherhood. This verse abrogates what had been practiced among the Muslims and by the Prophet (ﷺ) of calling adoptees by the names of those who had adopted them. This is an abrogation of the practical Sunna and the tacit approval (taqrir) by the Qur'an. This is what is meant by the one who said: "This verse abrogated the ruling of adoption." Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: In the separation and connection of these clauses there is a beauty and eloquence that is not hidden from one who knows the methods of composition.

Al-Tibi explained this, saying: He means in the omission and mention of the conjunction between the clauses, from the beginning of the sura until here. Its explanation is that the commands and prohibitions are in (be mindful — do not obey — follow — rely upon). The opening with His words ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾ (Q. 33:1) indicates that the address comprises a matter of importance, whose significance is evident in its arousing of the soul. For this reason He joined to it "do not obey," as the specific is joined to the general, and He followed it with the prohibition. Then He commanded reliance on Allah as encouragement to oppose the enemies of the religion. Then He followed each of these commands with what corresponds to it, by way of completion. He gave as cause for ﴿do not obey the disbelievers﴾ (Q. 33:1) His words ﴿Indeed Allah is ever All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾ (Q. 33:1), as a completion for restraint. He gave as cause for His words ﴿follow what is revealed to you﴾ (Q. 33:2) His words ﴿Indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾ (Q. 33:2), as a completion. He concluded His words ﴿and rely upon Allah﴾ (Q. 33:3) with His words ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs﴾ (Q. 33:3), as confirmation and emphasis, in the manner of: "So-and-so speaks the truth, and the truth is clear." He detailed His words ﴿Allah has not made for a man two hearts within his chest﴾ (Q. 33:4) by way of resumption, as an alert to some of their falsehoods. His words ﴿That is your saying with your mouths﴾ (Q. 33:4) are a summation of those situations, indicating that they are of falsehood and that the one who says them deserves blame. He joined His words ﴿But Allah says the truth, and He guides to the way﴾ (Q. 33:4) to this summation by the common element of contrast, in the manner of what preceded regarding "do not obey" and "follow." He detailed His words ﴿Call them by their fathers' names; that is more just in the sight of Allah﴾, and His words ﴿The Prophet is more worthy of the believers﴾ (Q. 33:6), and so on to the end of the sura, as a detailing of the statement of truth and of being guided to the straight path. End of quotation.

* * *

﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you have done in error, but [there is blame for] what your hearts have intended. And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (Q. 33:5)

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause "call them by their fathers' names," because the command in it is an obligation, so it implies a prohibition of its opposite, given its prohibition. As if it were said: "Do not call them by the names of those who adopted them, except by error."

The jунаḥ (blame) is sin, and this is explicit that the command in "call them by their fathers' names" is a command of obligation.

The meaning of "what you have done in error" is what passes over the tongues, occurring in the common manner in what they were accustomed to say: "So-and-so son of So-and-so," referring to the adoptee and his adopter. For this reason He contrasted it with "but what your hearts have intended," that is, what your beliefs have intended with intention and will.

With this the nullification of the judgment of adoption is established, and no one should say to his adoptee: "He is my son," nor say: "I have adopted so-and-so." If anyone says it, his saying has no effect and is not considered a bequest. What is considered is the statement of a man: "I have placed so-and-so in the station of a son of mine who inherits what my son inherits." This is what is called "tanzil" (assignment of status), and it is in the form of a bequest, taking the share of an heir, if he assigns him a third of the deceased's estate. But if he says to one who is not his son: "He is my son," in the sense of acknowledging paternity (istilhaq), then the ruling applies to him, if the one ascribed is of unknown lineage and the speaker does not intend mere affection and approximation.

According to Abu Hanifa and his companions, if a man says: "He is my son," and he is younger than the speaker and of unknown lineage, his lineage is established from him. If he was his slave, he is also freed. And if such a child cannot be born to a man like him, the lineage is not established, but he is freed by him according to Abu Hanifa, in contrast to his two companions, who said: he is not freed by him.

As for one of known lineage, his lineage is not established by the speaker. If he is a slave, he is freed by him, because his designation (as son) is prohibited except on the basis of lineage. So if he says to his slave: "He is my brother," he is not freed by him if he says: "I did not intend by it brotherhood of lineage," because this is applied to brotherhood in Islam, by the explicit text of the verse. And if anyone says to his adoptee: "O my son," as a gentle expression, it is treated as an error, and one should not be lax about it if there is suspicion in it.

His words "call them by their fathers' names": the pronoun of the command refers to the adoptees, so the command does not include calling grandchildren "sons," because they are sons. The Prophet (ﷺ) said about al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him: "Indeed this son of mine is a master," and he said: "Do not interrupt my son," meaning, do not cut off his urination. Likewise, it does not include what one says to another who is not his adoptee: "O my son," as a gentle expression and an approach. There is no harm in that, because the one so addressed was not his adoptee, and people have continued to call their contemporaries "brother" or "sister." The poet said:

You are my sister, and you are the sacred right of my neighbor,
and betraying the neighborhood is forbidden to me.

And they often call one who is older "uncle" (ʿamm). Al-Namir ibn Tawlab said:

The young women called me "uncle" of theirs,
and I imagined I had a name, so I am not called by it.

Here he means that they used to call him "O my brother."

The occurrence of "junah" (blame) in a negative context with "laysa" implies generality, so it conveys the generalization of the removal of sin from an erroneous act, based on the rule that a general statement is not restricted to the specific cause for which it was revealed. This is also supported by many provisions in the Sharia, among them His words: ﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we forget or make errors﴾ (Q. 2:286), and the Prophet's (ﷺ) words: "Error and forgetfulness are lifted from my community, and what they have been compelled to do."

From His words "call them by their fathers' names" is understood, by implication of the text (lahn al-khitab), a prohibition against anyone being ascribed to other than his father. In a hadith: "Whoever ascribes himself to other than his father, upon him is the curse of Allah, the angels, and all people. Allah will not accept from him any compensation (sarf) or ransom (ʿadl)."

Excluded from the prohibition is a man saying to another: "You are my father, and I am your son," intending honor and closeness, when there is no confusion. Like the words of Abu al-Tayyib, praising Sayf al-Dawla:

You are indeed a father, and the father is more tender
than the one who connects children.

His words ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (Q. 33:5) are a clause giving the reason for the removal of blame for error, namely that the removal of blame is among the effects of Allah's attribute of forgiveness and mercy toward His creatures.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 6 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves.﴾ This is an explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*), since His saying ﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4], and His saying "Call them by [the names of] their fathers," had included, among the first things it covered, the nullification of Zayd ibn Harithah's being a son of the Prophet ﷺ. This raised a question in people's minds about the extent of the believers' bond with their Prophet ﷺ, and whether it is the same as the bond between believers who are strangers to one another. Therefore, to teach the believers the rights and sanctity of the Prophet, this verse came to state that the Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves.

The meaning is that he is closer to every believer than the selves of the believers are.

The *min* here is comparative (*tafdiliyya*).

Now, the apparent meaning is that "selves" (*anfus*) is the plural of *nafs*, which is the human subtle essence, as in His saying ﴿You know what is in my self﴾. The plural is for distribution over every believer, applying to each individual self. That is, the Prophet is closer to every believer than that believer's own self is to him. That is, he has a stronger guardianship (*wilaya*), meaning nearness, toward every believer than the nearness of his own self to him. This is a figurative nearness, meaning its effects, such as love and support.

So *awla* is the comparative form of *wali*, which means nearness; that is, "more near."

This form (*ism al-tafdil*) implies the sense of having a greater claim to a thing, so its complement is attached to it with the *ba'* of accompaniment and association. The statement is elliptical, meaning "closer to the benefits of the believers" or "closer to the welfare of the believers." This omitted noun is elided in order to generalize to every good matter concerning the believers.

*[Page 267]*

And *anfus* means the persons themselves; that is, he has a greater right to dispose of their affairs than they have to dispose of their own affairs.

From this meaning is what is in the authentic hadith, the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab to the Prophet ﷺ: "You are dearer to me than everything except my own self that lies between my two sides." The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "None of you believes until I am dearer to him than his own self." 'Umar said: "By the One who revealed the Book to you, you are dearer to me than my own self."

It is possible that *anfus* means the whole of their kind, as in His saying ﴿When He sent among them a messenger from among themselves﴾. It is also possible that *anfus* means people.

The meaning then is that he is closer to the believers than the guardianship (*wilaya*) of some of them over others; that is, closer than the guardianship of all of them over one another, in the manner of His saying ﴿Then you are those who kill your own selves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85], meaning some of you kill others, and His saying ﴿Do not kill your selves; indeed Allah is ever Merciful to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 29].

The first aspect is stronger and more general in regard to the sanctity of the Prophet ﷺ, and it indicates his priority over those believers other than the selves, through the implication of the address (*fahwa al-khitab*). As for the second possibility, it does not indicate that he is closer to every believer than that believer's own self, except through analogical reasoning from the lesser (*qiyas al-adna*). For this reason 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, at the outset, excepted his own self, saying: "You are dearer to me, except my own self that lies between my two sides."

On both aspects, the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, is closer to the believers than their fathers and their sons. On the first possibility, he is closer to every believer than his own self. We will draw attention to this when we reach His saying "and his wives are their mothers." Thus the guardianship of the Prophet ﷺ over the believers, after the nullification of adoption, is equal toward all believers.

There is also a hadith: "There is no believer but that I am the closest of people to him in this world and the Hereafter. Recite, if you wish: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves.﴾" Since you have learned that this guardianship returns to his sanctity and honor, you know that it does not extend beyond that to matters of people's ordinary dealings and the rights of some of them over others, such as the inheritance of a deceased Muslim, for his estate belongs to his heirs. This has been made clear by the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "I am closer to the believers than their own selves. Whichever believer leaves property, let his heirs inherit it, whoever they may be. If he leaves debt or dependants, let him come to me, for I am his guardian (*mawla*)."

This is the core meaning of this verse.

\* \* \*

﴿And his wives are their mothers.﴾

He has joined to the rights of the Prophet ﷺ the rights of his wives over the Muslims, owing to the connection with the mention of the Prophet's right, upon him be prayers and peace. Allah has granted them what the mothers have, namely the prohibition of marrying them, by the indication of what preceded in His saying: ﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4].

As for what is other than the ruling on marriage, such as the forms of goodness toward them and their support, this refers to the magnifying of the Prophet's ﷺ affairs and sanctities. The Companions of the Prophet and the Rightly Guided Caliphs continued to take care to treat the wives of the Prophet ﷺ well and to give them preference in goodness, honor and reverence. Ibn 'Abbas said, when carrying the bier of Maymunah: "This is the wife of your Prophet. When you lift her bier, do not shake or jolt it, and be gentle." Narrated by Muslim.

Likewise, whatever is other than the ruling on marriage among the forms of dealing with them, excluding what relates to reverence. For this subtle point the eloquent simile was used, to emphasize their resemblance to mothers for the believers, such as in inheritance and in the prohibition of marrying their daughters. So it should not be supposed that their estates are inherited by all Muslims, nor that their daughters are sisters to the Muslims with respect to the prohibition of marrying them.

As for the description of Mu'awiyah, the Caliph, as "maternal uncle of the believers" because he was the brother of Umm Habibah, Mother of the Believers, this is among the forms of magnifying, as one says: "The Banu so-and-so are the maternal uncles of so-and-so," when they are the tribe of his mother.

The intended sense of "his wives" is those whom he married by marriage contract, so this does not include possession by right hand (*milk al-yamin*). The Companions said on the day of Qurayza, when the Prophet ﷺ married Safiyya bint Huyayy: "Is she one of those whom his right hand possesses, or is she one of the Mothers of the Believers?" They said: "We shall see. If he veils her, she is one of the Mothers of the Believers; and if he does not veil her, she is among those his right hand possesses." When he consummated the marriage with her, he drew the veil over her, and they knew she was one of the Mothers of the Believers. For this reason Maria the Copt was not one of the Mothers of the Believers.

For the recognition of this motherhood, it is required that the Prophet ﷺ had consummated the marriage with the woman. As for the one he divorced before consummation, such as al-Jawniyya, namely Asma' bint al-Nu'man al-Kindiyya, Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned that a woman to whom the Prophet ﷺ had been contracted married during the caliphate of 'Umar. 'Umar intended to stone her. She said: "Why? The Prophet did not draw a veil over me, nor was I called Mother of the Believers!" So he refrained from her. This woman is the daughter of al-Jawn al-Kindi, whom al-Ash'ath ibn Qays married. This is the more correct view, and it is the implication of the school of Malik. Imam al-Haramayn and al-Rafi'i among the Shafi'is also affirmed it. From Muqatil: it is forbidden to marry any woman to whom the Prophet ﷺ was contracted, even if he did not consummate the marriage. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, and al-Nawawi affirmed it in *al-Rawda*. As for those whom the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, divorced after consummation, there are two opinions concerning them. It is said: the prohibition of marrying them is established, in preservation of the sanctity of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It is said: this does not apply to them. The first is more preponderant.

The ruling on the motherhood of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ toward the believers has been reinforced by His saying: ﴿And when you ask them for something, ask them from behind a screen﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53], and by the prohibition of marrying any of them upon the believers, through His saying: ﴿Nor that you should marry his wives after him, ever. Indeed that would be an enormity in the sight of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53]. The explanation of this will come when we reach these two verses at the end of this surah.

It is reported that Ibn Mas'ud recited after it: "And he is a father to them." The same is reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b and from Ibn 'Abbas. It is reported from 'Ikrimah that it was in the first recitation: "And he is a father to them."

The interpretation of this is that it is an explanation and clarification. Otherwise, His saying ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves﴾ has conveyed more than what this reading conveys.

\* \* \*

﴿And those of blood relationship are closer to one another in the Book of Allah than the believers and the emigrants, except that you do kindness to your close friends. That was written in the Book.﴾

This follows the abrogation (*naskh*) of the rulings of adoption, among which is the inheritance of the adopted son from the one who adopted him, and the reverse, by the nullification of its counterpart, namely the brotherhood (*mu'akhah*) that existed between certain emigrants and certain Helpers. When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Medina with those who had emigrated with him, he assigned to each emigrant a Helper as a brother. He established brotherhood between Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Kharijah ibn Zayd, between al-Zubayr and Ka'b ibn Malik, between 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf and Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', between Salman and Abu al-Darda', and between 'Uthman ibn Maz'un and Abu Qatada al-Ansari. The paired brothers inherited from one another by that brotherhood for a time, as siblings inherit. Then this was abrogated by this verse, just as inheritance by adoption was abrogated by the verse ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers﴾. This verse made clear that kinship is the cause of inheritance, excluding a constructed (*ja'li*) affiliation.

Thus what is meant by "those of blood relationship" (*uli al-arham*) is the true brothers. They were described as "those of blood relationship" because a full brother takes precedence over a half-brother in inheritance, and they are the majority. The verse therefore makes clear that those of blood relationship are closer to one another in inheritance than the guardianship of the brothers by pact among the emigrants and Helpers. This covers all those of blood relationship, and it is restricted by His saying "of the believers and the emigrants," according to one of the two interpretations of *min* in the two verses. This is like a general ruling (*'amm*) that came upon a particular occasion (*sabab khass*). It is absolute regarding priority, and the absolute is of the category of the unspecified (*mujmal*). Since no explanation accompanies it, the interpretation of its absoluteness is that of generality, because priority is a state of those of blood relationship, and the generality of the persons implies the generality of the states. So the meaning is that those of blood relationship are closer to one another in all guardianships, except what the proof specifies or restricts.

The verse makes clear that true kinship is weightier than constructed brotherhood. It is unspecified regarding the detailed division among those of blood relationship, and that is detailed in the Book and the Sunnah in the rulings of inheritance.

The discussion of the word *uluw* (in "those of") has already been given at His saying ﴿And fear Me, O people of understanding﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning of "in the Book of Allah" is "in what He prescribed," that is, what He ordained and decreed.

It is possible that by it is meant the Qur'an, referring to what the verses of inheritance contain. The parallel of this verse has already been mentioned at the end of Surat al-Anfal. The discussion of the inheritance of the wider kin (*dhawu al-arham*) when the deceased has no known heir with a fixed share has also already been given.

*[Page 271]* 

"Those of blood relationship" is the subject (*mubtada'*), "some of them" is a second subject, "closer" is the predicate of the second, and the whole clause is the predicate of the first subject. "In the Book of Allah" is attached to "closer."

And His saying, ﴿among the believers and the emigrants﴾, may be connected to the elative form (ism al-tafdil, the comparative/superlative form) "more entitled" (awla), so that "min" is a comparative particle (min tafdiliyyah). The meaning is: those of the kinship ties are more entitled to the inheritance of their relatives than the inheritance of those who share the bond of faith and emigration, by that bond, meaning the bond that existed between the Helpers (al-Ansar) and the Emigrants. By "the believers" is meant specifically the Helpers, as indicated by its being contrasted with the conjunction "and the emigrants," in the sense of those of complete faith. This is to honour the faith of the Helpers, because they preceded many of the Emigrants who believed after them. The Helpers believed all at once when their chieftains (nuqaba') conveyed to them the call of Muhammad (ﷺ) after the Second Pledge of al-'Aqaba. God the Exalted said: ﴿And those who had settled in the abode and in faith before them﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], meaning before many of the poor Emigrants, except those whose faith had preceded (theirs). So the meaning is: every person with a kinship tie is more entitled to inherit from his relative than a Helper would be, if the deceased was an Emigrant, or than an Emigrant would be, if the deceased was from the Helpers. This abrogates the inheritance by emigration that was legislated by the verse of al-Anfal: ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate, you have no guardianship from them at all until they emigrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72]. Thus the Muslims inherited through emigration, so a Muslim bedouin would not inherit from his emigrant relative. Then this was abrogated by the verse of this surah.

It may also be that the phrase "among the believers" is a stationary adverbial phrase (zarf mustaqirr) in the position of a qualifier, meaning: "And those of kinship ties who are among the believers and the emigrants, some of them are more entitled than others." That is, a person of kinship ties does not inherit from his relative unless both are believers and emigrants. In this case the verse abrogates the inheritance by the pact (hilf) and brotherhood (mu'akhah) that was legislated upon the arrival of the Emigrants in Medina. When this verse was revealed, they returned to their inheritances, and this verse clarified that kinship is more entitled than the pact and brotherhood. In any case, the verses on inheritance abrogated all of this.

It may also be that "min" is explanatory (bayaniyyah), meaning: "And those of kinship ties are the believers and the emigrants." That is, those of kinship ties who are unbelievers do not inherit, and neither does one among the believers who has not emigrated, due to His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved, some of them are guardians of others﴾ [al-Anfal: 73], then He said: ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate, you have no guardianship from them at all until they emigrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72].

[p. 272]

The exception in His saying ﴿except that you do for your close friends a kindness﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), and "illa" here means "but" (lakin), because what follows "illa" is not of the same kind as what precedes it. The entitlement affirmed for those of kinship ties is a specific entitlement, namely the entitlement to inheritance, by the indication of the context, and not the entitlement of good companionship and the bestowing of kindness.

This is a qualification (istidrak) against what might be supposed from the cutting off of benefit from the wealth of the close relatives for those who had the guardianship through brotherhood and pact. So it clarifies that what was annulled and abrogated is the benefit of inheritance, while the principle of mutual support and the performance of kindness remains, such as spending, gifting and bequeathing.

The clause ﴿That was in the Book inscribed﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for these rulings, and a closing that signals the end of the purpose of the rulings legislated from His saying "call them by their fathers" up to here. The demonstrative "that" refers to the rulings mentioned that were legislated. This concluding statement is more general than what His saying ﴿some of them are more entitled than others in the Book of God﴾ requires. By this consideration it is not a repetition of it, but it includes it and includes other things, so it confirms and emphasises it secondarily. This is the nature of concluding statements.

The definiteness in "the Book" is for a known reference, namely the Book of God, meaning what He wrote upon people and obligated, like His saying "the Book of God over you" [al-Nisa': 24]. So "the Book" is used metaphorically for legislation, by the common feature of its being established and recorded, which precludes alteration and forgetting, as al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

*"Fearing oppression and ... and can the desires abolish what is in the tablets?"*

The meaning of this is like His saying: ﴿And those of kinship ties, some of them are more entitled than others in the Book of God﴾ in surat al-Anfal.

So "the Book" is an implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah), and the particle of location (harf al-zarfiyyah) "in" is a reinforcement (tarshih) of the metaphor.

"Maskhur" (inscribed) means written in lines, and this is also a supporting element (tarshih) for the metaphor, and in it there is an imaginative evocation (takhyil) of the implicit metaphor.

The verb "kana" (was) in His saying "That was" is for strengthening the affirmation of ﴿in the Book inscribed﴾, because "kana," when it is not intended to mean that its subject was characterised by its predicate in past time, is generally for emphasis, like ﴿And God was ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ahzab: 5], meaning He has never ceased to be so.

[Page 273]

﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, son of Mary. And We took from them a solemn covenant﴾ ﴿that He may question the truthful about their truthfulness. And He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment﴾.

This is a continuation (ʿaṭf, coordination) of His saying: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab: 1], up to His saying: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs﴾ [al-Ahzab: 3]. Therefore it includes the command to establish the religion as Allah willed it and revealed it to His Messenger ﷺ, and to reject the explicit ways of the disbelievers and hypocrites, which stem from desires and delusions.

When He mentioned that and followed it with three of the misguided judgments of their pre-Islamic ignorance, after a long discourse, the direction of the speech turned back to inform that what Allah commanded him is from the covenants that Allah took from the prophets and messengers from the earliest of the religious laws. This discourse is connected to the discourse it is coordinated with by the relevance of His saying: ﴿That was written in the Book as a decree﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6]. Because of this connection between the two discourses, there was no need to explain the covenant that Allah took from the prophets. So it is understood that the meaning is: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾ to fear Allah, to reject obeying the disbelievers and hypocrites, and to follow what Allah revealed. His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Ahzab: 1 context] and ﴿that He may question the truthful about their truthfulness. And He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment﴾ follow. When the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to limit himself to fearing Allah and to turn away from the claims of the disbelievers and hypocrites, he was informed that this was the practice of the prophets before him. For this reason He placed His saying ﴿and from you﴾ right after mentioning the prophets, as an alert that the matter of the messengers is one and that Allah's practice regarding them is unified. Thus these verses have the sense of a concluding statement (tadhyil, appended conclusion) to the verse ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab: 1] and the three verses after it, but they came joined by the conjunction "wa" (and) because of the distance between them and the three preceding verses.

His saying ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾ and the two verses have the role of an introduction to the story of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), because among what Allah took the covenant of the prophets upon is that they should support the religion Allah sends with them, and that they should support the religion of Islam. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you will surely believe in him and surely support him."﴾ [Al ʿImran: 81]. So Muhammad ﷺ is commanded to support his religion with those Muslims who are with him, by His saying in this verse ﴿that He may question the truthful about their truthfulness. And He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment﴾. And in the following verse, in praise of the believers who fulfilled what they pledged to Allah, He said: ﴿that Allah may reward the truthful for their truthfulness and punish the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab: 24], and so on.

His saying ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾ came following the style of many Qur'anic narratives that begin with "idh" (when), with the implied verb "udhkur" (remember). 

"Idh" (إذ) is a noun of time that is stripped of the meaning of adverbial location. So the estimate is: "And remember a time," and by the attachment of "idh" to the clause after it, the meaning becomes: "Remember the time when We took a covenant from the prophets." This covenant is stated briefly here, but many verses explain it. Its summary is that they should speak the truth and convey what they were commanded, without flattering the disbelievers and hypocrites, without fearing them, without following their desires, and without sharing with the people of misguidance in leaving some of their misguidance intact. And Allah made a covenant with them and promised them victory upon that. Because this surah contains such purposes, the covenant has an increased impact on the Prophet ﷺ, and it is strongly similar to the covenants taken from the messengers before him.

As an example of this, His saying here: ﴿Allah says the truth, and He guides to the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4], and His saying regarding the covenant of the People of the Book: ﴿Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them, that they would not say about Allah except the truth?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 169] in Surat al-Aʿraf.

In placing the command to the Messenger ﷺ to fear Allah, to oppose the disbelievers and hypocrites, and to hold firm in following what is revealed to him, and his command to rely upon Allah, before His saying ﴿O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you when hosts came to you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 9], etc., there is an indication that this support with which Allah strengthened His Messenger ﷺ and the believers with him, when He repelled from them the confederate forces of the disbelievers and hypocrites, who returned in their rage without attaining any good, is nothing but one of the effects of the covenant that Allah took from His Messenger when He sent him.

The covenant (mīthāq, مِيثاق) is the name for an agreement and the fulfilment of a promise. It is derived from "wathiqa," meaning to be certain and assured. It is a metaphorical transfer from the form of an instrument noun, which became dominant over the verbal noun. It was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿those who break the covenant of Allah after its confirmation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 27] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The attachment of "mīthāq" to the pronoun of the prophets is an attachment of the verbal noun to its agent, in the sense that the covenant is specific to them regarding what they were obligated to and what Allah promised them for fulfilling it. It is also attached to the pronoun of Allah's Name in His saying: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you and His covenant which He established with you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 7].

His saying ﴿And from you, and from Noah,﴾ etc., is the mention of some individuals of a general category for the sake of giving them importance, for these mentioned are the most excellent of the messengers. The pronoun of Muhammad ﷺ was mentioned before them as an indication of his superiority over all of them. Then the mention of the rest was arranged according to their order in existence. Because of this subtle point, the Prophet's pronoun was specifically given the preposition "min" (from) on its own, and then the preposition "min" was applied to the group of the rest. Thus he was given two kinds of emphasis: the emphasis of precedence, and the emphasis of showing the joining of the beginning with a pronoun specifically, not merged with the rest of them, peace be upon them.

It will come that what is in Surat al-Shura, of placing what He enjoined upon Noah before "and that which We revealed to you," is another path, and it is more fitting to the purpose of that surah in His saying: ﴿He has prescribed for you of religion what He enjoined upon Noah, and that which We revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham﴾ [al-Shura: 13], etc.

The clause ﴿And We took from them a solemn covenant﴾ repeats the content of the clause ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾ for the sake of stronger emphasis, and so that the description of the covenant as "ghalīẓ" (solemn) can be built upon it, meaning great and of lofty status within its kind. Every covenant has greatness, so when this one was described as ghalīẓ, it indicated that it has a special greatness. And so that the purposive "lam" (لام) in His saying ﴿that He may question the truthful﴾ can be connected to it.

The true meaning of "ghalīẓ" (غليظ) is strong and sturdy in creation. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿so it became thick and stood on its stalk﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. The word "ghalīẓ" was borrowed for what is great and lofty within its kind, because the thick of every category is the strongest in the attributes of its kind.

The "lām" in His saying ﴿li-yas'ala al-ṣādiqīn ʿan ṣidqihim﴾ (لِيَسْألَ الصّادِقِينَ عَنْ صِدْقِهِمْ) is the "lām" of purpose (lām kay), meaning: "We took from them a solemn covenant in order to magnify the reward for those who fulfil the covenant of Allah and do not break the pledge, and in order to intensify the punishment for those who disbelieve in what Allah's messengers brought them." So among the reasons for mentioning this covenant here is that it is a preparation for the mention of the reward of the truthful and the punishment of the disbelievers, in addition to what we mentioned earlier of such reasons.

This is one of the reasons for taking the covenant from the prophets, and it is the last of the reasons in occurrence. Its mention signals that this covenant has reasons that occur before the truthful are questioned about their truthfulness. These are what is in the deeds upon which the covenant was taken, of bringing benefits and warding off harms. This is what the doers are questioned about regarding their deeds, good and bad.

The pronoun in "yas'alu" (يَسْألُ) refers to Allah the Exalted, following the stylistic device of iltifat (shift of grammatical person) from first person (speech) to third person (absent).

By "the truthful" (al-ṣādiqūn) is meant the nations of the prophets to whom what was taken as a covenant from their prophets reached. Opposed to them are the disbelievers, who denied their prophets, or those who affirmed them and then broke the covenant afterward; the term "disbelievers" includes them.

The "questioning" (al-suʾāl) is a metonymy for accountability, because it is among the results of answering the question, namely assigning reward to the truthful and punishment to the disbelievers. This is similar to His saying: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya: 23], meaning no one holds Him accountable for His act or takes Him to account for what does not suit Him. And there is the saying of Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr:

*And it was said: "Indeed you are one who is held to account and questioned."*
