The clause ﴿And He has prepared for the disbelievers﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿that He may question the truthful﴾, and the style was changed in it to indicate the certainty of the punishment of the disbelievers, so that it is not imagined that they will be questioned as one whose answer is heard or whose excuse is accepted, and to convey that the preparation of their punishment is a matter that has already passed and been decreed in the knowledge of Allah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 9:

﴿O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you when there came to you armies, so We sent upon them a wind and armies you did not see. And ever is Allah, of what you do, Seeing.﴾

This is an introduction to one of the great purposes for which this surah was revealed, a matter surrounded by signs and lessons from its beginning to its outcome, as instruction for the believers and a reminder that increases them in certainty and insight. The address is therefore opened by directing the discourse to them, because they are its people and deserve it, and because in it is the perpetuation of their dignity, their certainty, Allah's care for them, His kindness toward them, and the belittling of their enemy and of those who plot against them. They were commanded to remember this favor and not to forget it, because in remembering it there is a renewal of pride in their religion, of trust in their Lord, and of affirmation of their Prophet (ﷺ).

This day was chosen for reminding them, in connection with the command not to obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites, because among the favors that surrounded the believers on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab) was that Allah turned back the plotting of the disbelievers and the hypocrites. So the believers were reminded of the earlier plotting of the hypocrites in that crisis, so that they would beware of their schemes and rumors concerning the matter of adoption (tabanni) and the marriage of the Prophet (ﷺ) to the divorced wife of his adopted son. For this reason the hypocrites were singled out in His saying: ﴿And when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease say...﴾ [al-Ahzab: 12] and what follows; moreover, the matter of nullifying adoption and permitting marriage to the wives of adopted sons (al-adi'a) occurred close to the battle of the Confederates.

"Idh" (when) is an adverbial of past time, related to "ni'mah" (favor) because it contains the meaning of bestowing, meaning: remember what Allah bestowed upon you at the time when armies came to you, and Allah defeated them with armies you did not see.

This verse and what follows refer to the great handiwork of Allah toward the believers in the Battle of the Confederates (ghazwat al-Ahzab). Let us therefore set out a summary of what the people of biography (ahl al-siyar) and exegesis (ahl al-tafsir) have mentioned, so that there may be an explanation of the hidden meanings of these verses.

The cause of this battle was that after the Battle of Uhud, Quraysh made a truce with the Muslims for a period of one year, on condition that they meet at Badr in the following year. But no fighting took place at Badr because Abu Sufyan failed to keep the appointment. Neither party harassed the other except for the incident of the treachery of the polytheists against the Muslims, which was the incident of Bi'r Ma'unah, when the tribes of 'Usayyah, Ri'l, and Dhakwan from Banu Sulaym betrayed forty of the Muslims, after 'Amir ibn Malik asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to send them to the people of Najd to call them to Islam. That was a plot devised by 'Amir ibn Malik, and it took place four months after the end of the Battle of Uhud.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) expelled Banu al-Nadir, because of their treachery toward him and their breaking of the covenant they had with the Muslims, the great men of the Jews of Qurayzah were enraged after the expulsion and after they had settled in the homes of Banu Qurayzah and in Khaybar. Sallam ibn Abi al-Huqayq (with the l of Sallam doubled, the h of al-Huqayq vowelled with a damma and its q with a fatha) and Kinanah ibn Abi al-Huqayq, Huyayy ibn Akhtab (with a damma on the h of Huyayy, and a fatha on the hamza and the t of Akhtab), and others among a band of Banu al-Nadir went out and came to Quraysh for this purpose.

They conspired with Ghatafan that they should attack Medina. Quraysh went out with its Ahabish and Banu Kinanah, numbering ten thousand, led by Abu Sufyan; Ghatafan went out with a thousand, led by 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn; and Hawazin went out with them, led by 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl.

The news of their intention to besiege Medina reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), conveyed to him by Khuza'ah, and the Muslims feared the multitude of their enemy. Salman al-Farisi suggested that a trench be dug encircling Medina as a fortification against the entry of the enemy. The Muslims dug it, with the Prophet (ﷺ) digging with them and carrying earth. The Battle of the Trench occurred in the fourth year according to the narration of Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim from Malik. Ibn Ishaq said: in the fifth year. This is what became famous among the people, and Ibn Rushd followed it in Jami' al-Bayan wa al-Tahsil, following what had become well known; but the statement of Malik is more sound.

When the digging of the trench was complete, the armies of the polytheists came and named themselves "the Confederates" (al-Ahzab), because they were a number of tribes that formed a faction (tahazzabu), meaning they became one party. Banu Qurayzah joined them. Quraysh arrived from the lower part of the valley on the western side, and Ghatafan and Hawazin arrived from the upper part of the valley on the eastern side. The army of Quraysh camped at the gathering place of the rivulets of Rumah between al-Jurf and Zughabah (with a dammed z, a dotted gh; some narrate it with an undotted 'ayn, and some say al-Ghabah; the correct form is the first, as in al-Rawd al-Unuf). The army of Ghatafan and Hawazin camped at the tail of Naqma beside Uhud. The Muslim army numbered three thousand. The Muslims went out of Medina and encamped beneath Mount Sal', placing their backs to the mountain with the trench between them and the enemy. The Muslims placed their women and children in the fortresses (atam) of Medina. The Prophet (ﷺ) appointed 'Abd Allah ibn Umm Maktum over Medina. The situation continued thus for some twenty nights, with no fighting between them except a duel between three horsemen who forced their mounts through a narrow gap in the trench and fought in the salt flat between the trench and Sal'. One of them was killed by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and his two companions fled. An arrow shot at random struck Sa'd ibn Mu'adh in his arm vein (akhal), and he died of it in Medina. The Muslims were struck by severe hardship from the siege and fear because of the great number of their enemy, until "the Prophet (ﷺ) resolved to make peace with the Confederates by giving them half the dates of Medina for that year, to be taken when they ripened, and he almost wrote a document with them to that effect. He consulted Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh said:
"We were, we and these people, upon polytheism, and they did not hope to eat from it a single date except as hospitality or by purchase. Now that Allah has honored us with Islam and strengthened us through you, shall we give them our wealth? By Allah, we will give them nothing but the sword until Allah judges between us and them." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set aside what he had resolved upon."

Allah sent upon the army of the polytheists a fierce wind, which uprooted their tents, overturned their cooking pots, and extinguished their fires. Their affairs were thrown into disorder, their horses and camels perished, discord arose among them and between them and Qurayzah, and Quraysh thought that Qurayzah had made peace with the Muslims and would join the Muslims against the Confederates. So the Confederates resolved to depart; they departed from Medina, and the Muslim army returned to Medina.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿when there came to you armies﴾ is mentioned as a preparation for His saying ﴿so We sent upon them a wind﴾ and so on, because that is the locus of the favor.

The wind mentioned here is the eastern wind (al-saba), which was cold; it uprooted the tent pegs and ropes, blew dust into their eyes, the horses surged against one another, and many of their horses, camels and sheep perished. Concerning it the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was given victory by the eastern wind, and 'Ad was destroyed by the western wind (al-dabur)."

The armies they did not see were the hosts of angels who sent the wind and cast discord among the Confederates, and they were the means of casting terror into their souls.

The clause ﴿and ever is Allah, of what you do, Seeing﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the divine name in His saying "favor of Allah", and it is a hint that Allah gave them victory over their enemies because He knows what the Muslims endured of hardship and perseverance in digging the trench, in leaving their homes for their encampment outside Medina, and in offering their lives in support of the religion of Allah. So Allah rewarded them with manifest victory, as He said: ﴿And Allah will surely support whoever supports Him﴾ [al-Hajj: 40].

The majority read ﴿بِما تَعْمَلُونَ بَصِيرًا﴾ with the ta of address (taʿmalūna). Abu 'Amr alone read it with the ya of the third person (yaʿmalūna), and its interpretation is as an iltifat (shift of grammatical person). The first "junud" is the plural of "jund," which is a united and mutually supporting group; for this reason it came to dominate the assembled host gathered for fighting, so "jund" became current in the sense of "army." Here "junud" is used in the plural form, although its singular already implies a collectivity, like His saying: ﴿A host of the confederates will be routed there﴾ [Sad: 11]. He used the plural here because they were gathered from a number of tribes, each tribe with its own army, who went out allied together to attack the Muslims in Medina. A parallel is His saying: ﴿So when Saul set out with the armies﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The second "junud" is the plural of "jund" in the sense of a group of one kind. By them are meant the angels who were sent to support the believers and to cast terror and fear into the hearts of the polytheists.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verses 10–11:

﴿When they came upon you from above you and from below you, and when the eyes shifted and the hearts reached the throats, and you imagined about Allah assumptions.﴾ ﴿There the believers were tested and shaken with a severe shaking.﴾

﴿Idh jA'ukum﴾ ("when they came upon you") is a substitute (badal) for ﴿idh ja'atkum junud﴾ ("when hosts came upon you") [al-Ahzab: 9], a detailed substitute (badal mufassal) for a general one (mujmal).

What is meant by "above" (fawq) and "below" (asfal) is the upper side of Madinah and its lower side.

﴿Wa idh zaghati al-absar﴾ ("and when the eyes shifted") is coordinated (ʿatf) upon the substitute, and it belongs to the detailed part. The definite article in al-absar (the eyes), al-qulub (the hearts) and al-hanajir (the throats) is for prior reference (ʿahd), meaning the eyes, hearts and throats of the Muslims. Or the lam may be taken as a replacement (ʿiwad) for the genitive pronouns attached to them, meaning: your eyes shifted and your hearts reached your throats.

Zaygh (shifting) is the inclination away from straightness toward deviation. The shifting of the gaze is that it does not see what it is directed toward, or that it intends to turn toward one direction but falls on another from the intensity of terror and alarm.

Al-hanajir is the plural of hanjara, with a fatha on the unpointed ha, sukun on the nun and fatha on the jim: the end of the windpipe (hulqum), and it is the top of the Adam's apple (ghalsama). The reaching of the hearts to the throats is a metaphor for the severe agitation of the hearts from fear and panic, to the point that, because of their agitation, they seem to exceed their places and rise up seeking to leave the chests; when they reach the throats they cannot pass beyond them because of the constriction. Thus the state of the heart of one who is terrified and trembling is likened to the state of a heart that has passed its place and gone upward seeking to exit, so the thing compared is the heart itself, considering the difference between the two states.

Page 281
The speech is not literal, for hearts do not pass beyond their place. Close to this is the expression: "He breathed a long sigh" (tanaffasa al-su'da'), and "the soul reached the collarbones" (balaghat al-ruh al-taraqi).

The clause ﴿wa tazunnuna billahi al-zununa﴾ ("and you imagined about Allah assumptions") may be coordinated upon the clause ﴿zaghati al-absar﴾, and it may be that the waw is for the circumstantial (hal) and the verb is in the present tense to indicate the renewal of those assumptions with the renewal of their causes, as a metonymy for the long duration of this affliction.

In the present tense there is a sense of wonder at their assumptions, to combine reproach with favour. For the severity of the panic that shifted the eyes and made the hearts like reaching the throats indicates that they feared being defeated, because of what they saw of the strength of the confederates and the narrowness of the siege, or feared the length of the war and the annihilation of souls, or feared that the defeat would embolden the polytheists against the Muslims, or other kinds of assumptions and different degrees of their holders.

The believer, although he trusts in the promise of his Lord, does not feel secure from His wrath because of his shortcomings, and fears that victory may be deferred to another time, for what is in Allah's knowledge and wisdom cannot be encompassed.

The two objects of (tazunnuna) are omitted without any evidence indicating their estimate; this is an omission to make the verb take the place of an intransitive verb. Grammarians call this omission "ellipsis for restriction" (al-hadhf iqtisaran), meaning restricting the attribution of the verb of assuming to its subject. The purpose of this treatment is that the listener's mind may go in every possible direction. This omission is frequently used in eloquent speech, and most grammarians permit it, and from it is the Exalted's saying: ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 35] and His saying ﴿and you assumed an assumption of evil﴾ [al-Fath: 12], and the proverb: "Whoever listens, imagines" (man yasma' yakhal); Sibawayh and al-Akhfash forbade it.

The verb (tazunnuna) is taken to imply the meaning of (talhaquna) ("you attach yourselves to"), so it is followed by the preposition bi-, and the bi- is for accompaniment (mulabasa). Sibawayh said: the saying "I assumed about him" (zanantu bihi) means: I made him the object of my assumption; the bi- here is not like its use in ﴿wa kafa billahi hasiba﴾ [al-Ahzab: 39], meaning it is not superfluous, and its governed noun is an object of the verb before it, as if you said: "I assumed in the house," and similarly: "I doubted in it," meaning the bi- for him means "in." The better view is that it is for accompaniment, as in the saying of Duraid ibn al-Simma:

So I said to them: "Assume about two thousand armoured men whose chiefs are in the sewn coats of mail."

Page 282
The detailed treatment of this will come under the Exalted's saying ﴿So what is your assumption about the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Saffat: 87] in Surat al-Saffat.

Al-zununa is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) specifying the number, and it is the plural of zann. Its definiteness with the article is the definiteness of the genus, and its plural is to indicate kinds of assumption, as in the saying of al-Nabigha:

I came to you naked, my garments worn out, in fear, while suspicions are imagined about me.

It is written al-zununa in the Imam (the standard codex) after the nun; this alif was added in pronunciation for the sake of observing the rhyme-endings at pause, because the verse-endings, like rhymed prose (asjaʿ), are treated as pause-points since the speaker intended them so. This surah is built on the alif rhyme, like the qasidas of the maqsura type. In the same way the alif is added in the Exalted's saying (﴿wa ata'na al-rasula﴾ [al-Ahzab: 66]) and His saying (﴿fa adallsuna al-sabila﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67]).

From Abu 'Ali in al-Hujja: whoever keeps the alif in continuous recitation does so because it is so in the Mushaf, and it is the end of a verse, and verse-endings are likened to rhyme-words insofar as they are cadences; as for whoever drops the alif in continuous recitation, he holds that this applies to rhyme-words, and verse-endings are not rhyme-words.

As for the readers: Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr from 'Asim and Abu Ja'far read with the alif in both continuous recitation and pause. Ibn Kathir and Hafs from 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read with the alif omitted in continuous recitation and kept in pause. Abu 'Amr, Hamza and Ya'qub read with the alif omitted both in continuous recitation and in pause. Khalaf read with the alif kept after the nun in pause and omitted in continuous recitation. This is a difference of the type concerning the modes of performance, not in the wording of the Qur'an. All of them are eloquent and in use, and the better course is to pause on them, because the verse-endings are like rhymed cadences and the cadences are like rhyme-words.

The demonstrative (hunalika) refers to the place contained in His saying ﴿there came upon you hosts﴾ [al-Ahzab: 9] and His saying ﴿when they came upon you from above you and from below you﴾. The more apparent view is that the demonstrative refers to the time indicated by idh in His saying ﴿and when the eyes shifted﴾. Often one of the two adverbs is treated as the other. For this reason Ibn 'Atiyya said: "hunalika is an adverb of time, and its governing verb is ubtuliya." I say: from this is the entry of (lata) upon (hanna) in the verse of Hajl ibn Nadla:

Nawar has wept, and it is not the time of weeping; she wept, and what Nawar concealed has appeared.

For (lata) is specific to negating nouns of time, so hanna is a demonstrative for an indefinite time, and it is a dialectal form of (huna). They say: "yawm huna," meaning "a day of the first," so they point to a near time, and the origin of this is a metaphor that was extended and spread.

Al-ibtila' (testing) originally means examination, and it is used metaphorically for the striking of hardship, because examining the state of steadfastness and patience is necessarily connected with it; God called what afflicted the believers a testing, indicating that He did not shake their faith.

Al-zilzal is the shaking of the earth, and it is the intensive form of zalla, giving the sense of emphasis. Here it is a metaphor for the severe disruption of the situation, to the point that it is imagined as agitated with a violent agitation like that of the earth; and it is more violent agitation because it affects the greatest body in this world. It is said: "Fulan was shaken" (zulzila fulan), in the passive form, following the saying: "the earth was shaken" (zulzilat al-ard), since the doer of this act is not known by custom. This is the most common usage of it; the Exalted said: ﴿and they were shaken until the Messenger said﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214], the verse.

The shaking of the believers means the severity of their disturbance and terror, because the hosts of the enemy surpassed them in number and equipment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 12–13:

﴿When the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease say, "Allah and His Messenger promised us only delusion."﴾ ﴿And when a faction of them said, "O people of Yathrib, there is no place for you, so return," and a party of them sought permission from the Prophet, saying, "Indeed our houses are exposed," while they were not exposed. They only intended to flee.﴾

This is an conjunction with ﴿And when the eyes shifted﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10], for all of that was among what befell the Muslims as a trial: part of it from the condition of war and part of it from the harm of the hypocrites, so that they would beware of the hypocrites in what occurs afterward, and so that they would not fear their scheming, for Allah diverts it just as He diverted its greatest form on the Day of the Confederates.

Page 284
The statement of these hypocrites may have been made openly among the Muslims, intending by it to introduce doubt into the hearts of the believers, perhaps they would turn them back from their religion. By their saying ﴿what Allah and His Messenger promised us﴾ [al-Ahzab: 22] etc., they gave the impression that they were among those who believe in Allah and His Messenger. So the attribution of delusion to Allah and His Messenger is either by way of eloquent metaphor (tashbih baligh), or because in their ignorance they permitted that Allah might deceive His servants.
