**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 14:**

﴿And if they had been entered upon from its every side, then asked to commit strife, they would have given it, and they would not have hesitated over it except briefly.﴾

The placement of this verse is to confirm further the content of the clause ﴿And they are not exposed; they intend only to flee﴾ [al-Ahzab: 13]. It is a refutation of their claim, in showing fear for their houses, when their real aim is to abandon the Muslims. In what I have seen of the words of the exegetes (mufassirun) and of the people of linguistics (ahl al-lughah), I have not found anyone who clarified the meaning of (al-dukhul, "entering") in a verse like this. They mention only the meaning of entering a place, such as entering houses or cities, which is the literal meaning. What I hold is that dukhul has frequently been used for a specific kind of entering, namely the incursion of an army or raiders into a land or town in order to attack its people. God the Exalted said: ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, remember God's blessing upon you when He made prophets among you and made you kings"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 20], up to His words ﴿"O my people, enter the holy land which God has prescribed for you, and do not turn back on your heels"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 21]. It is also generally followed by the preposition ʿala (upon) when the object is the people attacked. From this is His saying: ﴿Two men of those who feared, on whom God had bestowed favour, said, "Enter upon them through the gate, for when you enter it, you will be victorious"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 23], up to His words ﴿They said, "O Moses, we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24]. The meaning here can only be the entering of battle and war, because of His saying ﴿when you enter it, you will be victorious﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 23]. It is evident that what is not meant is entering as a guest, wandering, or spying.

[Page 287]

Thus, the entering in such a context is understood to mean invasion and conquest, as we say: "the year of the entry of the Tatars into Baghdad." Accordingly, the dukhul in His saying ﴿And if they had been entered upon﴾ is the dukhul of invasion. Therefore the pronoun in (dukhilat, "had been entered") must refer to the city of Yathrib, not to the houses mentioned in their saying ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed﴾ [al-Ahzab: 13]. The meaning is: "If the city were attacked from its sides, etc."

His saying ʿalayhim (upon them) is connected to (dukhilat), because the passive form (dukhilat) requires an implied agent. So the intended meaning is the entering of the invaders upon the people of the city, as it comes in its basic form in His saying ﴿enter upon them through the gate﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 23] in Surah al-Ma'idah.

Al-aqtar (the sides) is the plural of qutr, with a dammah on the qaf and a sukun on the ta', meaning a region or direction of a place. Its being annexed to (aqtar), which is a plural, conveys generality, that is, from all the sides of the city. This is the strongest form of enemy assault on the city, as in His saying: ﴿when they came upon you from above you and from below you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10]. The verb (dukhilat) is stated in the passive because it is evident that the agent of the entering is a group of raiders. The exegetes have offered various possibilities for the structure of this verse, differing in the meanings of the words and in the intended overall meaning. The closest of them is what Ibn ʿAtiyyah said, though it is somewhat obscure. Next is what is in al-Kashshaf.

What should be followed in interpreting it is that the clause ﴿And if they had been entered upon﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the pronoun in (yuridun, "they intend") or from the pronoun in ﴿And they are not exposed﴾ [al-Ahzab: 13], as an added refutation of their saying ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed﴾ [al-Ahzab: 13].

The implicit pronoun in (dukhilat) refers to the city, because the annexation of (aqtar) suits cities and localities, and does not suit houses. So the meaning becomes: "If the raiders had entered upon them into the city while they were residing in it."

Thumma (then) denotes a sequence of rank (al-tartib al-rutbi). The apparent expectation was that it would be joined with waw, not with thumma, because what comes after thumma here falls under the verb of the conditional particle law (if) and is the response to it. So it deviates from waw to thumma to draw attention to the fact that what comes after thumma is more important than what came before it, as is the case with (thumma) in the conjoining of sentences. That is, they would, despite all that, come to strife. The strife (fitnah) is that they would tempt the Muslims, that is, plot against them and cast discord into the Muslim army. Some exegetes interpreted fitnah as shirk (polytheism), but there is no basis for this, and others interpreted it as fighting, which is far-fetched.

(Al-ityan, "coming") means arriving at a place. This verb conveys that they would go out from the city in which they were, in order to tempt the Muslims. The pronoun of the object in (atawha, "they would come to it") refers to strife, and what is meant is its place, which is the place of the Muslims: that is, they would come to its place and its likely location. The pronoun in (biha, "with it") refers to strife, and the bi (with) is for transitivity.

The clause ﴿and they would not have hesitated over it﴾ is conjoined to the clause (la-atawha). Al-talabbuth means al-lubth, that is, settling or remaining in a place, and here it is used figuratively for delay: that is, they would not have delayed in striving for strife, nor would they have feared that their houses would be seized.

The meaning is: if the armies of the confederates had entered the city while the army of the Muslims remained outside it (for example, since the speech is on a hypothetical assumption), and the entering army had asked the group seeking permission to cast strife among the Muslims through division and weakening, they would have gone out for that purpose hastening, and fear for their houses would not have restrained them, lest thieves enter them or the army plunder them. This would be either because they are secure from encountering harm from the entering army, since they are its allies and helpers, being of them and with them, or because their aversion to Islam makes them unconcerned about the plundering of their houses.

The exception in His saying ﴿except briefly﴾ shows that it is sarcastic toward them, so the intended meaning is the emphasis of negation through the form of exception.

It may also be taken in its apparent sense, that is, "except for a moment in which they deliberate," so that the purpose of mentioning it is to emphasize the brevity of their delay. This is the interpretation most harmonious with the composition of the Qur'an.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Ja'far read (la-atawha) with a hamzah followed by a ta' with a dot above. Ibn ʿAmir, Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Khalaf read (la-ataw-ha) with an alif after the hamzah, in the sense of "they would have given it," that is, they would have given strife to those who asked for it. So the use of the verb (atawha) is a mushakalah (rhetorical correspondence, harmonization) with the verb (su'ilu, "they were asked").

[Page 289]

﴿And they had already made a covenant with Allah before, that they would not turn their backs. And the covenant of Allah will be questioned.﴾

These were the Banu Harithah and the Banu Salamah, and they are the ones about whom a group among them said, ﴿Indeed, our houses are exposed﴾ [al-Ahzab: 13], and they asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission. That is, on the Day of Uhud they lost their nerve, then repented and made a covenant with the Prophet ﷺ that they would not turn their backs in any expedition after it. These are also the ones concerning whom Allah's statement was revealed: ﴿When two groups among you were about to lose heart, while Allah was their ally﴾ [Al 'Imran: 122]. A slackening (nifaq) and weakness of faith came upon a number of the Banu Harithah, so Allah reminded them of this and showed them that among them was a fickle group that does not keep a covenant and whose conviction is not steady, and that this was due to the weakness of their certainty and the dominance of cowardice over them, to the point that it would call them to cast off the covenant of Allah. This is a warning to both tribes, so that they would restrain whoever among them had broken it.

The emphasis of this report by the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), the particle of confirmation (harf al-tahqiq), and the verb kana, is used even though the address is directed to the believers, as a way of treating the listeners as those who might doubt that they had made a covenant with Allah to remain steadfast.

The addition of min qablu ("before") indicates that this covenant is ancient and established, and it is the covenant of the Day of Uhud.

The clause ﴿they would not turn their backs﴾ explains the clause "they had made a covenant".

Tawliyah (turning) means directing oneself toward something, and it derives from al-wali, which means nearness. Allah says: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144].

Al-adbar (the backs, sing. dubur) means the backsides. Tawliyat al-adbar (turning the backs) is a metonymy (kinaya) for fleeing, since what they had sought permission for in the Battle of the Trench was the desire to flee. Do you not see His statement: ﴿They intend only to flee﴾ [al-Ahzab: 13], and fleeing is what they had covenanted with Allah to abandon.

The clause ﴿and the covenant of Allah will be questioned﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to the clause ﴿they had already made a covenant﴾, etc. What is meant by the covenant of Allah is every covenant a person binds himself to with his Lord.

Al-mas'ul (questioned) is a metonymy for being held accountable for it, like the Prophet's ﷺ saying: «And each of you is responsible for those under his care», and as has passed just before, at His statement ﴿that He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness﴾ [al-Ahzab: 8]. This is a threat.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 16:

Page 290
﴿Say, "Flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing; and in that case you will not be given enjoyment except for a little."﴾

This is a response to their saying ﴿Indeed, our houses are exposed﴾ [al-Ahzab: 13]. For this reason it is separated (from what precedes), since it follows the pattern of dialogue and back-and-forth. What lies between the two sentences, from His saying ﴿And if they had been entered upon from its surroundings﴾ [al-Ahzab: 14] to His saying ﴿and they would have been questioned﴾, is a parenthetical insertion, as has already been explained. This supports that the Prophet ﷺ did not permit them to return to Madinah, and that he answered them with what Allah commanded him to say to them. That is, Allah knew that you intended nothing but fleeing out of cowardice, and fleeing does not avert from you death or killing. So the meaning of negating its benefit is negating what is intended by it, because the benefit of a thing is that what is intended from it is achieved.

Thus His saying "from death" relates to ﴿al-firar﴾ (the flight) and ﴿farartum﴾ (you flee), and it does not relate to ﴿yanfa'ukum﴾ (will benefit you), because the object of ﴿yanfa'ukum﴾ is not mentioned, being evident from the context; so the sense is complete without the complement, meaning: it will not benefit you with deliverance.

The meaning of negating the benefit of flight, even though it involves taking up a means of deliverance, is that this means is not permitted, because standing firm against the enemy alongside the Prophet ﷺ is obligatory. Therefore, in this flight, consideration of the reality is made pure, namely what has been decreed for the human being by Allah, since there is no opposing it. Had flight been permitted, it would have been permissible to take into account the means of deliverance it contains. The Muslims were commanded to stand firm one against ten of the enemy; then flight from a force ten times the number of the Muslims was not permitted, and it was permitted for what exceeded that. When Allah abrogated that by requiring the Muslims to stand firm against an enemy of twice their number, flight beyond that became permitted. Likewise, when the Muslims were in a marching column (zahf), flight was then forbidden.

I think that the situation at the Battle of the Trench was before the abrogation, and therefore Allah rebuked those who concealed the intention to flee; for the number of the army of the confederates that day was about four times the army of the Muslims, and the Muslims were not then in a marching column, since the situation was one of siege.

It is also possible that the meaning is: if you flee and thereby escape killing, flight will not benefit you from death at its appointed term, and perhaps your terms are near.

Page 291
By "death" is meant the death by natural causes (al-mawt al-zu'am), that is, dying in one's bed (hatf anfihi), because it is contrasted with killing. The meaning is that flight does not avert the death which Allah knows will befall the fleeing person at the time in which He knows the fleeing person will die or be killed. If it seems to the fleeing person that flight has averted danger from him, that is only in those circumstances in which Allah knows that no harm will befall him, and he must in any case die by natural causes or be killed at the appointed time which Allah knows he will die or be killed.

For this reason He followed it with the sentence ﴿and in that case you will not be given enjoyment except for a little﴾, as an answer to an implied statement indicated by what was mentioned. That is: if it seems to you that flight benefited the one who fled at some time, then it is only a meager benefit, because it is a postponement of the term of life, and that is little enjoyment, that is, granting life for a limited period. Indeed, (idhan) may be a response to an omitted element indicated by the preceding speech, as in the verse of al-'Anbari:

"If you had been at Ma'zin, the sons of the foundling of Dhuhl ibn Shaiban would not have plundered my camels.
Then a rough company would have risen to support me, at the moment of anger, if a man with a sprain were to be lame."

Here his saying "idhan laqama bi-nasri ma'shar" (then a company would have risen to my support) is an answer and a conditional response to an implied element indicated by "lam tastabih ibili" (you would not have let my camels be plundered). The implied sense is: if they plunder my camels, then a company would have risen to my support. This is what al-Marzuqi's statement appears to favour, contrary to what is in Mughni al-Labib.

Most commonly, when (idhan) occurs after the coordinating particles wa and fa, the following present verb is not put in the subjunctive, though its subjunctive use is attested rarely.

The purpose of the verse is to instil in the Muslims the trait of regarding the life of this world as slight, and to turn their resolve toward striving for the perfection through which eternal happiness is attained, pursuing the teachings of the religion which lead souls to the summit of angelic rank.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 17:

﴿Say: "Who is it that can protect you from Allah if He intends for you harm, or intends for you mercy?"﴾

It appears that this sentence stands in the position of a reason (ta'lil) for the sentence ﴿Flight will not benefit you if you flee﴾ [al-Ahzab: 16] and what follows it. It is as if it were said: "Who is it that can protect you from Allah?", meaning: there is no protector for you against the enforcement of His will upon you. The repetition of the verb "Say" serves to draw attention to the content of the sentence.

The meaning is: because the power and will of Allah encompass the created beings, whenever He wills He nullifies the effect of causes or obstructs them by impediments. So if He wills evil, He deprives them of benefit from causes or of protection through preventive measures, and misfortunes may come from the very directions of what was expected to benefit. And whenever He wills a particular good for someone, He graciously facilitates for him by preparing causes and making them easy, until he encounters ease that he had not anticipated. And whenever His will is not attached to any particular matter, He lets circumstances take their course and leaves people to what He has made the cause of the conditions of beings, so each person attains a share according to his acuteness, his capacity and his guidance. For Allah has deposited in souls degrees of thinking and reflection. Therefore, if you disobey Allah and His Messenger and forsake the believers, you expose yourselves to His will to inflict harm upon you, and there is no protector for you from His purpose. The interrogative here is denunciatory, carrying the sense of negation, because they believed that the stratagem against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would benefit them and that flight would save them from death if there was fighting.

The sentence ﴿Who is it that can protect you﴾ etc. is the answer to the condition in His saying ﴿if He intends for you harm﴾ etc. It is the indicator of the answer according to the grammarians of Basra.

Al-'isma (عصمة) means protection and prevention from what the one protected dislikes.

Harm (su') is contrasted with mercy (rahma) because the intended harm is a specific harm, namely the harm that is made a punishment for them for disobeying the Messenger (ﷺ), which is the harm of vengeance. It is thus a specific harm decreed by Allah for the purpose of punishing them, should He intend it, and it proceeds contrary to the customary laws.

The conjunction of ﴿or intends for you mercy﴾ to "intends for you" (which is made the condition) requires a implied statement in the answer mentioned earlier, for His intending mercy suits the verb "protect you," since mercy is desired. So the implied meaning is: "or deprives you of it, if He intends for you mercy." This is from the type of implication (dalalat al-iqtida') for conciseness of speech, like the words of the poet:

When the coquettes appear one day, having arched their brows and their eyes,
its implied meaning is: "and have applied kohl to the eyes," since eyes are not arched, but they are kohled at the time the brows are arched, and that is part of adornment.

* * *

﴿And they will not find for themselves, besides Allah, any ally or helper.﴾

This is coordinated with the sentence ﴿Say: Who is it that can protect you from Allah?﴾, or it is parenthetical between the parts of the speech; the two estimations are close, because the parenthetical waw returns to the conjunctive waw. The address is directed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is not of the category of iltifat. The intended meaning is the necessary implication of the report, which is to inform the Prophet (ﷺ) of the falsity of their stratagems and that they will not find a helper other than Allah, and Allah has deprived them of victory because they did not set their hearts on supporting His religion and His Messenger. By "ally" is meant one who takes charge of benefiting them, and by "helper" is meant one who helps in war, so it is more specific.

[Page 294 is not marked here; the page break follows below.]

**Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 33, verse 18 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿Indeed, Allah knows those among you who hinder others, and those who say to their brothers, "Come to us," and who come to the fighting only a little.﴾ ﴿Stingy towards you. When fear comes, you see them looking at you, their eyes rolling like one who faints from the agony of death. But when the fear departs, they lash you with sharp tongues, stingy regarding the good.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19]

This is a *istinaf bayani* (explanatory resumptive sentence) arising from His words, ﴿Who is it that can protect you from Allah?﴾ [al-Ahzab: 17], because that raises a question that occurs to their minds: that they conceal their intentions from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so he does not perceive their purpose in seeking permission. Therefore he was commanded to say to them, ﴿Indeed, Allah knows those among you who hinder others﴾, meaning: Allah informs His Messenger about you, that the conduct of those people is a hindering of the believers. This resumptive sentence has been made a transition (*takhallus*) to mentioning another group of hinderers.

The particle *qad* here conveys *tahqiq* (affirmation), because, owing to their hypocrisy and the sickness of their hearts, they doubt the necessary implication of this report, namely that Allah informs His Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, about them. Or, because of their ignorance arising from disbelief, they assume that Allah does not know the hidden things of the hearts. This is not surprising in the creeds of the people of disbelief. In the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari, it is related from Ibn Mas'ud: "Two men from Quraysh and one from Thaqif, or two from Thaqif and one from Quraysh, gathered at the House. Their bellies were full of fat, but their hearts had little understanding. One of them said, 'Do you think that Allah hears what we say?' The other said, 'He hears if we speak aloud, but He does not hear if we speak quietly.' Another said, 'If He hears when we speak aloud, then He hears when we speak quietly.' So Allah, exalted, revealed: ﴿You did not conceal yourselves so that your hearing, your sight, and your skins would not testify against you; but you thought that Allah does not know much of what you do.﴾ [Fussilat: 22]."

[Page 294]

So the emphatic particle of affirmation has a place here.

The entry of *qad* upon the imperfect verb does not remove it from the meaning of affirmation according to the verifying scholars of Arabic grammar. What they supposed of diminution (*taqlil*) is indicated by the context in some places, not by the meaning of *qad* itself. Similar is the case of its conveying multiplicity (*takthir*). This was discussed under His words, ﴿We see the turning of your face towards the heaven﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144] in Surah al-Baqarah, and His words, ﴿He knows what you are upon﴾ [al-Nur: 64] at the end of Surah al-Nur.

*Al-mu'awwiq* is an active participle from *'awwaqa*, which indicates intensity in the occurrence of hindering. It is said: *'aqahu 'an kadha*, when he prevented him and discouraged him from something. So the doubling (*tadh'if*) in it indicates intensity and multiplicity, like *qattaʿa al-habl* ("he cut the rope"), when he cut it into large pieces, and ﴿they bolted the doors﴾ [Yusuf: 23], meaning they secured their bolts well. It may also indicate multiplicity in an intransitive verb, like *mawwata al-mal* ("the property died off"), when death increased among the camels, and *tawwafa fulan* ("so-and-so circled much"), when he circumambulated a great deal. The meaning is: Allah knows those who are eager to discourage people from fighting. The address in His words *minkum* ("among you") is to the hypocrites, who were addressed in His words, ﴿Fleeing will not benefit you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 16].

It is also possible that "those who say to their brothers, 'Come to us'" are the very same hinderers themselves, so that it is the conjoining of attributes of a single subject, as in the saying:

*"To the king, the lion of the battlefield, and the son of the noble."*

It is also possible that they are a different group, and "their brothers" are those who agree with them in hypocrisy. Then the intended meaning is brotherhood in opinion and religion. This is because 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, and those with them, of those who withdrew from the army of the Muslims on the day of Uhud and returned to Madinah, used to send to those hypocrites who remained in the army of the Muslims, saying to them, "Come to us" ("*halumma ilayna*"), that is, "Return to us." Qatadah said: "These are people among the hypocrites who say to them: 'Muhammad and his companions are only a mouthful of a head' (that is, a small group who eat the head of a camel), and if they were flesh, Abu Sufyan and those with him would have devoured them." (This is an image meaning that it would be easy for Abu Sufyan to overpower them.)

*Halumma* is a verbal noun (*ism fi'l*) of command meaning "come forward," in the dialect of the Hijaz, which is the eloquent dialect. Therefore this word remains in one fixed form among them and does not change: they say *halumma* for the singular, the dual, the plural, the masculine, and the feminine. But in the dialect of Banu Tamim it is a verb, so they attach to it the markers of conjugation: they say *halumma*, *halummi*, *halumma* (dual), *halummu*, and *halumman* (feminine plural). This was mentioned under His words, ﴿Say: Bring your witnesses﴾ [al-An'am: 150] in Surah al-An'am.

The meaning is: withdraw from the army of the Muslims and come to us.

The clause ﴿and they do not come to the fighting except a little﴾ is an independent statement. It may be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from "those who say to their brothers, 'Come to us'." It may also be conjoined to "those who hinder" and "those who say," because the verb may be conjoined to the participle, as in His words, ﴿then those who charge at dawn and raise dust﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 3], and His words, ﴿Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity, and who lend to Allah﴾ [al-Hadid: 18]. So the implied sense here is: "Allah knows those who hinder, and those who say, and those who do not come to the fighting," or "and those who do not come to the fighting." There is no difficulty in the verb of knowledge taking *la ya'tuna* ("they do not come") as its object, because it is according to an interpretation, just as the operation of the abrogating particle in His words *wa aqradu* ("and they lend") is according to an interpretation. That is, Allah knows that they do not come to the fighting except a little. That is, He knows that by gathering their brothers with them they do not intend to strengthen them in the war, but rather to keep them away from fighting.

The meaning of *illa qalilan* ("except a little") is "except for a little time," which is the time of their presence with the Muslims who are stationed on the frontier. This is like His words, ﴿so they do not believe except a little﴾ [al-Nisa': 46], meaning outward belief, and like His words, ﴿or by an outward statement﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33]. *Qalilan* is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a little coming," and its littleness is apparent in the brevity of its duration and the smallness of its benefit.

*Al-ba's* means war. This was mentioned under His words, ﴿to protect you from your violence﴾ [al-Anbiya': 80] in Surah al-Anbiya'. "Coming to the war" is intended to mean coming to the people of war or to its place. The intended meaning is: the violence with the Muslims, that is, deceit against the Muslims, not cowardice.

*Ashihhatan* ("stingy") [al-Ahzab: 19] is the plural of *shahih*, in the pattern *af'ilah*, which is irregular but eloquent; its regular plural would be *ashiha'*. The pronoun of address in His words *'alaykum* ("towards you") refers to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, and to the Muslims. This is a shift from the speech that the Messenger was commanded to say to them to disclosing their condition to the Messenger and the Muslims, in connection with the shift from address to third person in His words, ﴿and they do not come to the fighting﴾. *Shuhh* was mentioned under His words, ﴿and souls are present with stinginess﴾ [al-Nisa': 128] in Surah al-Nisa'.

[Page 295]

*Ashihhatan* ("stingy") [al-Ahzab: 19] is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun of *ya'tuna*. *Shuhh* is stinginess with what is within one's capacity that benefits others. Its original meaning is not giving wealth, and it is used figuratively for withholding what is within one's power of help or assistance. It is transitive to the thing withheld by means of *bi* and *'ala*, as in His words, ﴿stingy regarding the good﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19]. It is also transitive to the person withheld from by *'ala* as well, because *shuhh* contains the sense of aggression (*i'tida'*). So its transitivity in His words, ﴿stingy towards you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19], is transitivity to the one withheld from.

The meaning is: they withhold from you whatever wealth or assistance is within their power. That is, when they are present in the violence, they withhold their benefit from the Muslims as much as they can. Among this is their stinginess with themselves and with everything that is grudged.

It is also possible to make *'ala* here transitive to the thing grudged (*al-mudnun bihi*), as in the verse quoted by al-Jahiz:

*"You were among a people stingy towards you with yourself, except that whatever perishes, perishes."*

The meaning then is: stingy outwardly. That is, they show that they fear for you destruction, so they turn you away from fighting and make your withdrawal from fighting seem good. This is what al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's commentary) has taken.

Upon describing them with stinginess towards the Muslims, His words are made a consequence: ﴿When fear comes﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19], to its end.

*Al-maji'* ("coming") is a well-known figurative usage for the occurrence and coming about of a thing, as He said, ﴿When the promise of the Hereafter comes﴾ [al-Isra': 7].

*Al-khawf* ("fear") is the expectation of fighting between the two armies, and from it the prayer of fear (*salat al-khawf*) is named.

The intended meaning is describing them with cowardice: that is, when they see the armies of the enemy approaching, ﴿you see them looking at you﴾. The apparent meaning is that the verse alludes to what occurred on some days of the Confederates (al-Ahzab) in the fighting between the three horsemen who forced their way into the trench at its narrowest point, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and those with him of the Muslims, as was mentioned earlier.

The address in "you saw" (*ra'aytum*) is to the Prophet ﷺ, and it implies that this is a narration of a state that occurred, not a supposition of its occurrence. For this reason the verb *ra'aytuhum* is used, and it was not said, "when fear comes, they look" [*yanzuruna*] ... to you. Their looking at him is the look of one who is reading his face, to see what he will do; their state seems to say: "Did we not tell you that you have no strength to fight the Confederates? So withdraw!" They see it as though they were in the right when they warned him against fighting the Confederates. For this reason their looking was specified as being at the Prophet ﷺ, and it was not said "they look at you."

The imperfect form is used to indicate the repetition and renewal of this looking.

The clause ﴿their eyes roll﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19] is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of *yanzuruna*, portraying the appearance of their looking: the look of one who is afraid and terrified, who stares with his eyes at directions from which he fears calamities may come upon him from one of them.

*Al-dawr* and *al-dawaran* are the rotating motion of a body like a millstone (that is, like the motion of a mill), moving from one place to another until it returns to where it began. I think this verb and its derivatives are derived from the noun *dar*, which is the enclosed place surrounding its inhabitants so that it is around them. From it the term *dara* is used for any land surrounded by mountains. They say: "The millstone turned around its axis." They also named an idol *duwar*, with the first letter either vowelled with *damma* or *fatha*, because its visitors circle around it like circumambulation. The Ka'bah was also called *duwar*, and they called what surrounds the moon a *dara*. The calamity of war was called *da'ira* ("circle") because they imagined it encompassing the one who was struck by it, so he finds no escape from it. 'Antarah said:

*"I feared that I would die and that there would not turn, in the war, a circle upon the two sons of Dhamdham."*

So the meaning of ﴿their eyes roll﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19] is that they quiver in their eyelids, like the rotating motion of a body, from a speed that moves them, staring, towards the surrounding directions.

He compared their looking to the look of one who has fainted from the agony of death, because his eyes move.

*Dhahab al-khawf* ("the departure of fear") is a well-known figurative usage for ending, that is, the removal of its causes, either by abandoning the fighting or by making it clear that no fighting will occur. This happened when the Confederates withdrew from besieging Madinah, as His words will indicate: ﴿They think the Confederates have not withdrawn﴾ [al-Ahzab: 20].

[Page 296]

*Al-salq* is the strength and loudness of the voice. The meaning is: they raised their voices in blame for exposing themselves to the great danger of the enemy and for not complying with their own suggestion to the Muslims to make peace with the polytheists. *Salq* has also been interpreted as harm by the tongue. It is said that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas about ﴿they lash you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19], and he said: "Stabbing with the tongue." Nafi' said: "Do the Arabs know that?" He said: "Yes. Have you not heard the words of al-A'sha:

*'Among them are fertility and generosity, and nobility is among them, and the eloquent orator (al-mislaq).'"*

*Hidad* is the plural of *hadid*, and *hadid* is everything with a penetrating effect of its kind. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿So your sight today is piercing﴾ [Qaf: 22].

The phrase ﴿stingy regarding the good﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19] is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of raising in ﴿they lash you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19]. That is: they dispute with you and blame you, while they are stingy regarding that in which there is good for the Muslims. That is, their disputing with them is not as it appears, out of fear for the Muslims and concern for them, but rather it comes from hatred and rancour. For some blame and dispute is motivated by love for the one blamed and a wish to give him sincere advice, and the sayings of the wise and poets on this meaning are many.

It may also be that "good" (khayr) here means wealth, as in His saying: ﴿If he leaves behind wealth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], and His saying: ﴿And indeed, he is intense in his love of wealth﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 8]. That is, in times of peace they rush to blame you, and they do not share their wealth with you for equipping for the enemy should it return against you. Here the preposition 'ala (against/upon) is used with the thing withheld (al-mabkhul bihi).

[Page 299]

The demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishara*) is used here to single them out by those base attributes that were described earlier, and to draw attention to the fact that they deserve the ruling that follows the demonstrative noun, as in His saying, ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:5] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The ruling of the negation of faith has been applied to them by His saying, ﴿they have not believed﴾, to expose their inner intentions, because they used to give the Muslims the impression that they were among them, as He said, ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:14] in Surah al-Baqarah.

[Page 300]

Because their faith was negated, Allah nullified their deeds as a consequence.

*Ihbat* (nullification) means making something *habit* (void, nullified). The *hamzah* in it is for causation, like *idhab* (causing to go away). *Habt* in its literal sense is the corruption of what is intended to be beneficial and useful.

It is used figuratively for corrupting what was beneficial, or for a thing being corrupt while it is thought to be beneficial. It is said: "The right of so-and-so became void (*habita haqqu fulan*)," if it was nullified. This figurative usage occurs frequently in the Qur'an. Its verb comes from the patterns *sami'a* and *daraba*. Its verbal noun is *al-habt*, and the noun of the verbal noun is *al-hubut*.

It is said: "So-and-so nullified the thing (*ahbata al-shay'*)" if he invalidated it. From this is *ihbat dam al-qatil*, that is, the nullification of the right of retaliation (*qawad*) for the blood of the slain.

Thus, *ihbat al-a'mal* (nullification of deeds) means invalidating the consideration of deeds that were intended as acts of devotion and presumed to be righteous deeds, due to an impediment that prevents them from being counted in religion.

The term *habt* and *hubut* has become one of the technical legal-theological terms (*al-alfaz al-shar'iyyah al-istilahiyyah*) among the scholars of *fiqh* (jurisprudence) and *kalam* (theology). It is applied to the non-consideration of good deeds because of apostasy (*ridda*), that is, returning to disbelief, or because of the excess of evil deeds over good deeds, such that the doer of those deeds deserves punishment because his evil deeds exceed his good deeds, according to what Allah has decreed for that, and He knows it best. For this reason, the question of *hubut* is counted among the theological questions. Or it is applied where one considers the benefit he gained from the obligatory acts he performed if he apostatized from Islam and then returned to Islam, like one who performed the Hajj, then apostatized, then returned to Islam. For this reason, the question of *hubut* is counted among the questions of *fiqh*.

Malik and Abu Hanifa said: apostasy nullifies deeds by the mere occurrence of it. So if he returns to Islam, and he had performed the Hajj, for example, before his apostasy, it becomes obligatory upon him to repeat the Hajj, adhering to the unrestricted (*mutlaq*) sense of this verse, since it linked nullification to the negation of faith. They did not consider this among the matters in which the unrestricted is interpreted in light of the restricted (*mutlaq* by *muqayyad*), out of caution, because this ruling pertains to beliefs, and conjecture (*zann*) does not suffice in them.

Al-Shafi'i said: if he returns to Islam, his good deeds that he performed before apostasy return to him, adhering to His saying, ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever - those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:217] in Surah al-Baqarah. This is by interpreting the unrestricted verse in Surah al-Ahzab and similar verses in light of the restricted verse in Surah al-Baqarah, giving preference to the legal (*furu'i*) side in this question over the doctrinal (*i'tiqadi*) side.

[Page 300, continued]

This question is known as the question of *muwafat* (continuance until death), that is, the apostate's persistence in apostasy until the end of his life, so that he meets [Allah] on the Day of Resurrection as an apostate. Malik and Abu Hanifa did not consider the condition of *muwafat*, while al-Shafi'i considered *muwafat* a requirement. The Mu'tazila (the rationalist theological school) held the same view as Malik and Abu Hanifa. Al-Fakhr [al-Razi] reported from the Mu'tazila that they considered *muwafat* upon disbelief. Refer to what has preceded in His saying, ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever - those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:217] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The meaning is: their acts of devotion and their striving will not benefit them.

The clause ﴿And that was ever, for Allah, easy﴾ is a statement used in its necessary implication, which is their belittlement: that when Allah removed them from the enclosure of Islam and nullified their deeds, He did not give them any weight, nor did He consider that a breach in the community of the Muslims.

The hypocrites used to take pride in displaying faith, and they supposed that the Muslims would be strengthened by them. Allah said, ﴿They consider it a favor to you that they have accepted Islam. Say, "Do not consider your Islam a favor to me. Rather, Allah has bestowed favor upon you that He guided you to faith, if you should be truthful."﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:17]

[Page 301]

When the state of the hypocrites and of those in whose hearts is a sickness was mentioned, along with their trial among the Muslims, and how they were when the armies came and when "the eyes turned aside and the hearts reached the throats," the discourse now turns back to their condition at the time when God favoured the Muslims by the withdrawal of the armies from them. This indicates that the withdrawal of the confederates occurred at a moment of heedlessness on the part of the hypocrites. That is why they used to be vehement in blaming the Muslims and would lash at them with sharp tongues, [urging them] to expose themselves to the large enemy. At that time God had already routed the confederates, so they withdrew, and God sufficed the believers against their evil. The hypocrites had no intercession (wasatah) in that matter.

Perhaps they did not wish the return of the confederates without their taking Medina. Thus the sentence ﴿يَحْسَبُونَ﴾ ("they think") is a fresh, independent resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i) linked to God's words, ﴿Remember the favour of God upon you when armies came against you, so We sent against them a wind﴾ [al-Ahzab: 9] and so on. It comes as a return to the beginning, occasioned by the mention of the hypocrites' conditions. For His words, ﴿they think the confederates have not departed﴾ indicate that the confederates had been defeated and had turned back on their heels, that is, this occurred while the hypocrites were unaware of it.

It is also possible that the meaning is: they used to lash at the believers out of pride in the confederates, because the confederates were allies of Quraydhah, and the hypocrites were close friends of the Jews. Their lashing at the Muslims therefore occurred at the time when the confederates had gone, while they did not know this. Had they known it, they would have lowered their harshness toward the Muslims. In this case the sentence ﴿يَحْسَبُونَ﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the nominative pronoun in ﴿سَلَقُوكُمْ﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19], meaning: they did that while thinking that the confederates were encircling Medina and that they were strengthened by them, so their disappointment in what they had estimated became evident.

As for His words, ﴿and if the confederates should come, they would wish that they were out in the desert among the Bedouins﴾, this is a description of the cowardice of the hypocrites. That is, if the confederates came once more, the hypocrites would take their precautions and go out to the desert among the Bedouins who dwell around Medina, namely Ghifar, Aslam and others. God said: ﴿It was not fitting for the people of Medina and those of the Bedouins around them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 120], and so on.

The word "wudd" (wishing, loving) is used here as a metonymy (kinaya) for striving to obtain the thing desired, because a beloved thing is not kept from being obtained except by an overwhelming obstacle; so it is a necessary consequence of wishing.

Al-bad (بادٍ): a dweller of the desert (badiyah). It was mentioned earlier at His words, ﴿equal for the resident therein and the desert-dweller﴾ [al-Hajj: 25] in Surat al-Hajj.

Al-a'rab: these are the inhabitants of the deserts by origin. That is, they wish to join the dwellings of the Bedouins, as long as they are not incapacitated, as indicated by His words that follow: ﴿and had they been among you, they would not have fought except a little﴾. That is, if they were unable to do that and remained among you, they would fight only a little.

Law (لو) is a particle that expresses a wish (tamanni) after a verb of wishing and the like. Al-Jahiz and Abd al-Qahir recited:

They would wish, if their skins were sewn over you,
And the miserly souls do not prevent death.

It was mentioned earlier at His words, ﴿each one of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 96] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The asking about the news is for the purpose of spying on the Muslims on behalf of the polytheists, and to delight them by whatever defeat might befall the Muslims.

[Page 302]

The meaning of ﴿and had they been among you, they would not have fought except a little﴾ is that, supposing they could not get out to the desert and remained in Medina with the Muslims, they would fight with the Muslims only a little fighting, that is, weak fighting that is of no account. It is merely a pretext and show (riya'), and its parallel was mentioned just above.

Al-anba' (الأنباء) is the plural of naba', which is: an important piece of news. It was mentioned earlier at His words, ﴿And there has certainly come to you news of the messengers﴾ [al-An'am: 34] in Surat al-An'am.

The majority of readers recite ﴿يَسْألُونَ﴾ with a sukun on the sin followed by a hamzah, the imperfect of sa'ala ("to ask"). Ruways, from Ya'qub, recited ﴿يَسّاءَلُونَ﴾ with a fatha on the sin, shaddah, and an alif after it followed by a hamzah, the imperfect of tasa'ala ("to ask one another"). Its original form is yatasa'alun, and the ta' was assimilated into the sin.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 21:

﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of God you have a good example (uswah hasanah) for whoever hopes for God and the Last Day and remembers God much.﴾

After the rebuke of the hypocrites and of those in whose hearts is a disease, the discourse turns to addressing the believers in general, praising their steadfastness and their emulation of the Messenger ﷺ, while their degrees of that emulation vary. The statement is thus a report, but its conjunction with the two emphatic particles in "laqad" (indeed/certainly) hints at an indirect rebuke of those who did not benefit from the good example, namely among the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease. For this reason the pronoun was used in a general way at the start, with "lakum" (for you), and then it was specified by apposition through His words ﴿for whoever hopes for God and the Last Day and remembers God much﴾, meaning: unlike those who were not like those (the first group). The lam in His words ﴿for whoever hopes for God﴾ is a reinforcement of the lam in the substituted term (mubdal minhu), like His exalted words: ﴿It shall be a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 114]. So the meaning of this verse is close to the meaning of His exalted words in Surah Bara'ah concerning the story of Tabuk: ﴿They were content to be with those who stay behind, and a seal was set upon their hearts, so they do not understand. But the Messenger and those who believed with him strove with their wealth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 87], and so on.

Al-uswah, with a kasrah or a dammah on the hamzah, is a noun for that which one emulates, i.e., that which one is followed in and whose action one does in the same manner. The essence of uswah is that the one emulated be the model (qudwah), and therefore the particle "fi" in "fi" came in the style of what is called al-tajrid (abstraction), which is useful for emphasis, since one is abstracted from a described one a similar described one, so that they are like two persons, as in the saying of Abu Khalid al-Khariji:

"And in the Most Merciful there is a sufficiency for the weak"

That is, the Most Merciful is sufficient. The original is: "The Messenger of God is an uswah," and then it was said: "in the Messenger of God is an uswah." The object of emulation was made the very person of the Messenger ﷺ, without a specific attribute, so that it includes emulating him in his sayings by complying with his commands and avoiding what he forbade, and emulating him in his deeds: patience, courage, and steadfastness.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "uswah" with a kasrah on the hamzah. 'Asim read it with a dammah on the hamzah, and both are dialects.

And ﴿li-man kana yarju Allah﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "lakum," a substitution of part from whole (badal ba'd min kull) or like inclusion (shibh al-ishtimal), because those addressed by the pronoun "lakum" include those who hope for God and the Last Day. Or it is an exact substitution (badal mutabiq) if the intended sense of the pronoun "lakum" is specifically the believers. Repeating the lam in the substitute adds multiplicity to the meanings mentioned, through the multiplicity of possibilities, and each takes its share of them.

Those who emulated the Messenger ﷺ on that day were thereby confirmed as among those who hope for God and the Last Day and remember God much. In this there is an indirect rebuke of a group of those who were kept from emulating him, from among the hypocrites or those in whose hearts is a disease of doubt concerning the religion.

The verse indicates the excellence of following the Prophet ﷺ, and that he is certainly the good example. However, it contains no detailed explanation or specification of the degrees of emulation, what is obligatory in it and what is recommended; its detailing is in the science of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). The usage of the scholars of usul is to make ta'assi (emulation) a technical term for following the Messenger in those actions which he did not require of the community in the manner of legislation.

Al-Qurtubi mentions, from al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, that it was narrated from 'Uqbah ibn Hassan al-Hajari, from Malik ibn Anas, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar regarding ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of God you have a good example﴾ that he said: "In the hunger of the Prophet ﷺ."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 22:

Page 304
﴿When the believers saw the confederates, they said, "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us, and Allah and His Messenger have spoken the truth." And it did not increase them except in faith and submission.﴾
When the sayings of the hypocrites and of those in whose hearts is a disease were mentioned, which indicate what fear entered their hearts and their weakness of faith and doubt concerning what Allah had promised His Messenger ﷺ and the believers of victory, beginning with His words ﴿And when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease said﴾ [al-Ahzab: 12], the sayings of those were matched by the sayings of the believers when the confederates descended upon them, and they saw their large numbers and multitude, and they were aware of their superiority over them in strength and number many times over, and they knew that they had been tested and shaken. All of that did not weaken their resolve, nor did it introduce any doubt into them regarding what Allah had promised them of victory.

Allah had promised them victory on more than one occasion, among them His words in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise without there having come to you the like of those who passed on before you? They were touched by misfortune and adversity and were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of Allah?" Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214]. So when the Muslims saw the confederates, and were tested and shaken, and saw the same condition described in that verse, they knew that they would be made victorious over them, and they knew that this was the promise Allah had made them through the verse of Surah al-Baqarah. The verse of al-Baqarah had descended a year before the battle of the Confederates, as is related from Ibn 'Abbas. Also, the Prophet ﷺ informed the Muslims: "The confederates are marching toward you after nine or ten [days]." So when the believers saw the confederates and were shaken, the steadfastness arising from the strength of faith returned to them, and they said ﴿This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us﴾, that is, from the looking and from the report of the march of the confederates. They affirmed Allah's promise to them of victory and the Prophet's ﷺ report of the march of the confederates. So the demonstrative "this" refers to what they witnessed of the armies of the confederates and to what follows from that of hardship and patience in enduring it, and all of that is the promise of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. Then they were told about the truthfulness of Allah and His Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, in what they had reported, and they affirmed Allah concerning what He had promised them of victory, in contrast to the saying of the hypocrites ﴿Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion﴾ [al-Ahzab: 12]. So the promise refers to both matters, and the truthfulness likewise.

The promise (al-wa'd): the informing of one who informs that he will do an action for the one informed (with fatha on the 'ayn-less form, i.e., the promisee being the one addressed).

So the verb ṣadaqa in what is related of the believers' saying ﴿and Allah and His Messenger have spoken the truth﴾

Page 305
is used in reporting a truthfulness that has already occurred and a truthfulness that will occur in the future, whose occurrence is certain, such that its future is treated as past, like ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1]. Thus it is used with the meaning of certainty (al-tahaqquq).
Or it is the use of the word in both its literal and figurative senses. There is no doubt that interpreting the verb as truthfulness in the future is more fitting to the context of praise for the believers and more closely tied to the attachment of their saying to the verb ﴿the believers saw the confederates﴾, rather than saying "and when the confederates came." If you refuse the use of the word in both its literal and figurative senses, then restrict it to the figurative and set aside the possibility of reporting a past truthfulness.

The hidden pronoun in zādahum refers back to what the demonstrative referred to, that is: and what they saw did not increase them except in faith and submission, in contrast to the state of the hypocrites, for it increased them in doubt regarding the fulfillment of the promise. The meaning: that did not increase the believers except in faith, that is, it did not increase in the thoughts of their souls anything but faith, meaning it did not add to them fear upon the fear that naturally arises in everyone who expects a strong enemy to attack him. Rather, the preoccupation of inference from it regarding the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ in what he informed them, and in what Allah promised them through His Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, of victory, occupied them away from fear and dread, so their souls turned away from thoughts of fear toward rejoicing in the anticipated victory.

Submission (al-taslim): compliance and obedience, because it is the surrender of the self to the one to whom it submits. It has already been mentioned in His words ﴿and submit in full submission﴾ [al-Nisa': 65] in Surah al-Nisa'. Among the forms of submission here is surrendering oneself to meet a strong enemy without seeking to cast down their hands before the enemy or to make peace with him with their wealth. Ibn Ishaq and others related that "when the affliction intensified upon the Muslims, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ consulted the two Sa'ds, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, about giving 'Uyayna ibn Hisn and al-Harith ibn 'Awf, the two leaders of Ghatafan, one third of the produce of Madinah that year, on condition that they withdraw from Madinah. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is this a matter you love, so that we do it, or a thing Allah has commanded you, which we must act upon, or a thing you are doing for us?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Rather, it is a thing I do for you. By Allah, I do it only because I saw the Arabs had shot at you from a single bow and were circling you from every side, so I wanted to break their power from you for a while.' Sa'd ibn Mu'adh said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we and these people were upon polytheism with Allah, not worshipping Allah nor knowing Him, and they did not hope to eat a single date from it except as hospitality or by sale. So when Allah honored us with Islam and guided us to it and strengthened us through you and by Him, shall we give them our wealth? We have no need of this. By Allah, we will give them nothing but the sword until Allah judges between us and them.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Then you decide.'" This was the stance of the Muslims in that hardship, and this was their submission of themselves to fighting.

Among submission is contentment with what the Messenger ﷺ commands of steadfastness with him, as Allah said: ﴿and submit in full submission﴾ [al-Nisa': 65]. Since it is known that they are believers by His words ﴿When the believers saw the confederates﴾ to the end, it is established that the faith that this increased them is an increase beyond their faith, that is, faith together with their faith.

The faith that increased them was intended as a manifestation of their strong faith. The repetition of the manifestations of faith and its effects is treated as an increase in faith, because the repetition of deeds strengthens the motive toward them in the soul and keeps its possessor far from doubt and apostasy, so it is as if it increases that motive. This is of the same kind as His words ﴿that they may increase in faith along with their faith﴾ [al-Fath: 4] and His words ﴿As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124], as was mentioned in Surah Bara'ah. The same applies to the opposite of increase, which is decrease. Otherwise, the reality of faith, which is affirmation of a thing, when it is attained with its constituents, is established; so its increase is the attainment of what is already attained, and its decrease is a deficiency in it and the negation of its root. This is the sense of what is reported in the Book and the Sunnah of attributing increase to faith, and likewise what is attributed to disbelief and hypocrisy of increase, as in His words ﴿The Bedouins are more intense in disbelief and hypocrisy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 97] and His words ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it has added to them filth upon their filth, and they died while they were disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125].

To this interpretation the dispute of the scholars returns concerning whether faith admits increase and decrease, so it reverts to a verbal disagreement.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 23:

﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted with God. Some of them have fulfilled their vow [to death], and some of them still await [their turn]. And they have not changed in the least.﴾

He follows the praise of all the sincere believers for their steadfastness, their certainty, and their readiness to meet the large enemy on that day, and their determination to give up their lives, while it was not decreed for them to meet it, as will come in His saying ﴿And God sufficed the believers in fighting﴾ [al-Ahzab: 25]. [He does this] by praising a group of them who had fulfilled what they covenanted with God, both in deed and in intention, so that through praising them there would be praise also for their brethren who were not able to meet the enemy on that day. [This is] so that it may be known that the truthfulness of those indicates the truthfulness of these, because the believers are one hand.

Describing them as "men" (rijal) is an added expression of praise, because the word rijal (men) is derived from rijl (foot), which is the strength of a person's reliance, just as the word aid (strong, supporter) is derived from yad (hand). If this verse was revealed together with the rest of the verses of the surah after the Battle of the Trench, then it is a reminder of what the believers had done earlier. If it was revealed on the Day of Uhud, then its placement in this surah is only by the direction of the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is an alert to the meaning we have mentioned, on the supposition that it was revealed together with Surat al-Ahzab. Whatever the time of the revelation of the verse, its intended meaning is: men among the believers who stood firm against the enemy on the Day of Uhud, namely: 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Anas ibn al-Nadr, Talhah ibn 'Ubayd Allah, Hamzah, Sa'id ibn Zayd, and Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr. As for Anas ibn al-Nadr, Hamzah, and Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, they were martyred on the Day of Uhud. As for Talhah, his hand was cut off that day while he was defending the Messenger of God (ﷺ). As for the rest of them, they fought and survived. The context and placement of the verse require that it was revealed after the Battle of the Trench. Al-Qurtubi mentioned the narration of al-Bayhaqi from Abu Hurayrah that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) returned from Uhud, he passed by Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, who was lying slain on his path, so he stopped, prayed for him, and then recited ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted with God; some of them have fulfilled their vow [to death]﴾, the verse.

The meaning of ﴿have been true to what they covenanted with God﴾ is that they fulfilled what they pledged, for a covenant is a promise, and it is information that one will do something in the future; when he does it, he has been true. The verb ṣadaqa (to be true) is used intransitively, which is the more common usage, and it is used transitively to the one informed (with a fatha on the ba'): one says ṣadaqahu al-khabar, i.e., the report told him the truth. Accordingly, its transitivity here to ﴿what they covenanted with God﴾ is by the removal of the preposition, i.e., they were true in what they covenanted with God, like the people's proverb: ṣadaqanī sinna bakrihi (he told me the truth about the age of his young camel), i.e., regarding the age of his young camel.

Al-nahb means a vow and what a person commits himself to by a pledge or the like. That is, among the believers is one who fulfilled what he pledged of jihad, like the statement of Anas ibn al-Nadr when he did not witness Badr with the Messenger of God (ﷺ); this was hard on him, and he said: "The first engagement the Messenger of God witnessed, I was absent from it. By God, if God shows me an engagement with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) hereafter, God will surely see what I do." He then witnessed Uhud and fought until he was killed. Likewise those who witnessed the days of the Trench, for they fulfilled their vow on the Day of Qurayzah.

Some exegetes have taken ﴿qaḍā naḥbahu﴾ in this verse to mean death in jihad, by way of metaphor, likening death to a vow in its inevitability. Some exegetes have gone further and made naḥb one of the names of death, but what is narrated in the hadith of al-Tirmidhi precludes this: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said about Talhah ibn 'Ubayd Allah: 'He is among those who have fulfilled their vow,'" and he had not died during the lifetime of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

As for His saying ﴿And they have not changed in the least﴾, it has the same meaning as ﴿have been true to what they covenanted with God﴾. It is mentioned here only as an allusion to the hypocrites, who had covenanted with God that they would not turn their backs, then they turned and fled on the Day of the Trench and went back to their houses in Madinah.

Tabdilan is in the accusative as an absolute object emphasizing the negated verb baddalu. Perhaps this emphasis is directed as an allusion to the hypocrites who changed the covenant of faith when they thought that victory would belong to the polytheists.

﴿So that Allah may reward the truthful for their truthfulness, and punish the hypocrites if He wills, or turn to them in forgiveness. Indeed Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful.﴾

The lam of causation (*lam al-ta'lil*, the lam expressing purpose or cause) governs the verb in the phrase ﴿so that Allah may reward the truthful﴾, and it may be linked to either of two verbs: *ṣadaqū* (they were truthful) or *mā baddalū* (they did not change). That is, the believers were truthful to their covenant, and the hypocrites changed it, so that Allah may reward the truthful and punish the hypocrites.

As for the lam of causation in relation to the verb ﴿may reward the truthful﴾, it is used in its literal meaning. In relation to the verb *wa-yu'adhdhiba* (and punish), it is used figuratively in the sense of the *fā'* of consequence (*fā' al-'āqiba*, the fa' indicating result), by likening the consequence of their action to the cause that prompts an act, for what they committed of altering and breaking the covenant. This comparison conveys their concern with what they did of altering, to the point that they seem to be striving to seek the punishment that was due to them for their deed. Or it is a comparison of them, in their obstinacy and scheming, to one who is intent on a reward that is sought even though it will lead to his own destruction.

*Al-jaza'* (reward) here means recompense for good, because the verb *jazā* is used most often for good, and because mentioning the cause of the reward, which is ﴿their truthfulness﴾, indicates that it is a reward for good deeds. The reward has come in the opposite sense in the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾ [al-An'am: 93], in Surat al-An'am.

The mention of the name of Allah (*ism al-jalāla*) explicitly, in a place where a pronoun could have been used, serves to indicate the magnitude of the reward.

Making the punishment conditional upon His will ("if He wills") is a reminder to them of the vastness of Allah's mercy, and that it does not cut off their hope in striving toward the forgiveness of what they have committed, by repenting so that Allah turns to them in forgiveness. Since He paired His punishment of them with His turning to them, it is established that punishment remains in place if they do not repent, in accordance with His words in another verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 48].

Repentance here is repentance from hypocrisy, that is, the sincere adoption of faith. Many of the hypocrites repented after that, among them Mu'attib ibn Qushayr.

The sentence ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾ is a justification for both the reward and the punishment, distributed between them: He is Forgiving toward the sinner who turns to Him in repentance, and Merciful toward the doer of good by rewarding him according to the measure of his effort.

In the mention of the verb *kāna* (was/is) there is an indication that forgiveness and mercy are essential attributes of Him, as we have mentioned more than once, among them at the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿Is it a wonder to the people that We revealed﴾ [Yunus: 2], at the beginning of Surat Yunus.

[Page 309]

﴿Allah repelled those who disbelieved in their rage; they gained no good.⁠﴾ [Please see note below.] ﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in combat.⁠﴾ ﴿And Allah is ever Strong and Mighty.⁠﴾

This is a coordination (*'atf*) on the clause ﴿So We sent upon them a wind﴾ [al-Ahzab: 9], and it best fits the context of the verses that follow. That is, He sent upon them a wind and repelled them. It may also be a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) from the pronoun in ﴿they think the confederates have not withdrawn﴾ [al-Ahzab: 20], meaning: they think the confederates have not withdrawn, when in fact Allah has repelled the confederates and they have withdrawn.

[p. 310]

Repelling (*al-radd*) is returning someone to the place from which they came. Their return to their homes was part of the completion of the blessing upon the Muslims, following the blessing of the wind being sent against them, because their return was more conducive to the Muslims' peace of mind. He expressed the confederates as "those who disbelieved" to point out that their disbelief was the cause of their strange and remarkable failure.

The *bā'* in *bi-ghayẓihim* (بِغَيْظِهِمْ) denotes accompaniment (*mulābasah*), and the phrase is a fixed adverbial complement (*ẓarf mustaqirr*) in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*ḥāl*). That is, He repelled them while they were enraged.

The explicit mention of the Name of Allah (*ism al-jalālah*) rather than a first-person pronoun serves to draw attention to the great magnitude of this remarkable repulsion, as was mentioned previously in His saying: ﴿That Allah may reward the truthful for their truthfulness⁠﴾ [al-Ahzab: 24].

*Al-ghayẓ* is anger and fury. Their anger was great, befitting their state of disappointment, because they had borne the hardship of assembling, spending, and a long stay around Madinah for nothing. Their hopes of conquering Madinah, eating its produce, and annihilating the Muslims were dashed, while they had assumed it would be a battle of a few days. Then what afflicted them of calamity through the wind and the defeat, whose cause they did not know, enraged them further.

The clause ﴿they gained no good⁠﴾ is a second circumstantial phrase. You may also take the clause ﴿they gained no good⁠﴾ as an explanatory resumption (*istiʾnāf bayānī*) clarifying the cause of their rage.

*Kafā* here means "sufficed," i.e., He relieved them of the hardship of fighting by turning away the confederates. With this meaning, *kafā* takes two objects, as in the saying: "I sufficed you your task" (*kafaytuka muhimmaka*). It is not the *kafā* in which the *bā'* is added to its object, which carries the meaning of "enough" (*ḥasb*).

In His saying ﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in combat⁠﴾ there is an omitted genitive construct (*ḥadhf muḍāf*), meaning the hardship of combat or the calamities of combat. The believers at that time needed to preserve their numbers and equipment after the disaster of the Day of Uhud. Had they met the army of the polytheists, their calamities would have been great, even if they had been victorious over the polytheists.

The discussion of the explicit mention of the Name of Allah in ﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in combat⁠﴾ is like the discussion of it in ﴿And Allah repelled those who disbelieved in their rage⁠﴾.

[p. 311]

The clause ﴿And Allah is ever Strong and Mighty⁠﴾ is a concluding summary clause (*tadhyīl*) for the clause ﴿And Allah repelled those who disbelieved⁠﴾ through its end.

*Al-quwwah* is power, as mentioned previously in His saying ﴿If only I had power against you⁠﴾ [Hud: 80] in Surah Hud.

*Al-'izzah* is majesty and invincibility, as mentioned previously in His saying: ﴿Pride led him into sin⁠﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The verb *kāna* ("is") is mentioned to indicate that might and power are attributes that belong to Allah, the Exalted, permanently. Among the manifestations of His power and might is that He turned away that great army disappointed and disgraced, and cast doubt between them and their allies from Qurayzah, and sent upon them the wind and the cold, and guided Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ghatafani to Islam without his people noticing, so that he was able to give sincere advice to the Muslims by scheming against the polytheists. All of that is a miracle (*mu'jizah*) of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verses 26–27:

﴿And He brought down those of the People of the Book who had supported them from their fortresses, and cast terror into their hearts. A party you killed, and a party you took captive.﴾ ﴿And He caused you to inherit their land, their homes, and their wealth, and a land you had not trodden. And Allah is ever over all things competent.﴾

The Jews of Banu Qurayza had aided the confederates (al-Ahzab), and they besieged the city with them. Huyayy ibn Akhtab, of Banu al-Nadir, had joined them, and he was the one who incited Abu Sufyan to attack Madina. When Allah turned back the confederates, Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to campaign against Qurayza, a group of Jews known as Banu Qurayza, whose dwellings and fortresses were in the south-eastern part of Madina, and their settlement is known by their name. «The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had returned to Madina from the trench at midday, and he was about to bathe and rest. When the revelation came to him to campaign against Qurayza, he called out to the people: "None of you should pray the 'asr except in Banu Qurayza."» The army that had been at the trench went out with him, and they alighted at the village of Qurayza. The people of the village took refuge in their fortresses, and the Muslims besieged them for about twenty nights. When the siege exhausted them and fear of the Muslims conquering their land and uprooting them overcame them, they desired to ask to surrender their land on condition that a judge (hakam) decide the manner of that surrender. This type of settlement is called "descending upon the judgment of an arbiter" (al-nuzul 'ala hukm hakam). They sent Shas ibn Qays to the Prophet ﷺ, offering to descend on the same terms on which Banu al-Nadir had descended, namely exile, on condition that they may carry away whatever their camels could bear, except weapons. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ refused to accept that. After deliberations, they descended upon the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, and Sa'd ruled that the fighting men be killed, the women and children be taken captive, and that their homes be for the Muhajirun, to the exclusion of the Ansar. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ approved what Sa'd had ruled, as is detailed in the Sira.

The meaning of zahara-hum is that they supported them and aided them, and it has been mentioned in His words: ﴿And they have not supported anyone against you﴾ [al-Tawba: 4] in Surat Bara'a.

Al-inzal (إنزال) is bringing down, i.e., from the fortresses or from the strongholds such as mountains.

Al-sayasi (الصَّياصِي) means fortresses. Its origin is that it is the plural of siysiya (صِيصَيَة), which is the horn of a bull or the like. The poet ʿAbd Banī al-Ḥasḥās said:

"So the bulls became dead in the water, and the women of Tamim were gathering horns (al-sayasi)."

That is, horns, which they sold. They used horns in the combs for wool, and they also made from them containers for kohl and the like. Since the horn is what a bull uses to defend itself, the stronghold in which an army takes refuge was called siysiya, and fortresses were called sayasi.

Al-qadhf (القذف) is swift casting. That is, Allah cast terror into their hearts by His creative command, so they surrendered and descended upon the judgment of the Muslims.

The party who were killed were the men, and they were about seven hundred. The party who were taken captive were the women and children.

The address in His words ﴿A party you killed﴾ to the end is to the believers, as a completion of the blessing alluded to by His words ﴿O you who believe, remember the favour of Allah upon you when hosts came against you, so We sent upon them a wind﴾ [al-Ahzab: 9], etc., i.e., He destroyed the hosts, turned them back in their rage, and gave you power over their allies and supporters.

The fronting of the object in ﴿A party you killed﴾ is for the sake of emphasis on mentioning it, because that party were the men of the tribe, and by killing them the seizure of the land, wealth, and captives is completed. For this reason the object of "you take captive" was not fronted, since there is no need to front it, so it remains in its original place.

His words ﴿and a land you had not trodden﴾ mean a land you had not entered as raiders. It is a land other than the land of Qurayza, described by the clause ﴿you had not trodden﴾, i.e., you had not walked in it. It has been said that Allah gave them good news of another land they would inherit later. Qatada said: "We were told that it is Makka." Muqatil and Ibn Rumman said: "It is Khaybar." It was also said: "It is the land of Persia and Rome." The most apparent of these views is that it is the land of Khaybar, for the Muslims conquered it a year and a month after the campaign against Qurayza.

In the concluding phrase ﴿And Allah is ever over all things competent﴾ there is an allusion to good news of a great conquest that would come after it.
