"You trampled us in rage, a trampling of one bound, with the decrepit camel's stride."

From this is His saying: ﴿And had there not been believing men and believing women whom you did not know, that you might trample them﴾ [al-Fath: 25]. The land of Banu al-Nadir was among what Allah granted to His Messenger without any cavalry or camel charge.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verses 26–27:

﴿And He brought down those of the People of the Book who had supported them from their fortresses, and cast terror into their hearts. A party you killed, and a party you took captive.﴾ ﴿And He caused you to inherit their land, their homes, and their wealth, and a land you had not trodden. And Allah is ever over all things competent.﴾

The Jews of Banu Qurayza had aided the confederates (al-Ahzab), and they besieged the city with them. Huyayy ibn Akhtab, of Banu al-Nadir, had joined them, and he was the one who incited Abu Sufyan to attack Madina. When Allah turned back the confederates, Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to campaign against Qurayza, a group of Jews known as Banu Qurayza, whose dwellings and fortresses were in the south-eastern part of Madina, and their settlement is known by their name. «The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had returned to Madina from the trench at midday, and he was about to bathe and rest. When the revelation came to him to campaign against Qurayza, he called out to the people: "None of you should pray the 'asr except in Banu Qurayza."» The army that had been at the trench went out with him, and they alighted at the village of Qurayza. The people of the village took refuge in their fortresses, and the Muslims besieged them for about twenty nights. When the siege exhausted them and fear of the Muslims conquering their land and uprooting them overcame them, they desired to ask to surrender their land on condition that a judge (hakam) decide the manner of that surrender. This type of settlement is called "descending upon the judgment of an arbiter" (al-nuzul 'ala hukm hakam). They sent Shas ibn Qays to the Prophet ﷺ, offering to descend on the same terms on which Banu al-Nadir had descended, namely exile, on condition that they may carry away whatever their camels could bear, except weapons. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ refused to accept that. After deliberations, they descended upon the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, and Sa'd ruled that the fighting men be killed, the women and children be taken captive, and that their homes be for the Muhajirun, to the exclusion of the Ansar. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ approved what Sa'd had ruled, as is detailed in the Sira.

The meaning of zahara-hum is that they supported them and aided them, and it has been mentioned in His words: ﴿And they have not supported anyone against you﴾ [al-Tawba: 4] in Surat Bara'a.

Al-inzal (إنزال) is bringing down, i.e., from the fortresses or from the strongholds such as mountains.

Al-sayasi (الصَّياصِي) means fortresses. Its origin is that it is the plural of siysiya (صِيصَيَة), which is the horn of a bull or the like. The poet ʿAbd Banī al-Ḥasḥās said:

"So the bulls became dead in the water, and the women of Tamim were gathering horns (al-sayasi)."

That is, horns, which they sold. They used horns in the combs for wool, and they also made from them containers for kohl and the like. Since the horn is what a bull uses to defend itself, the stronghold in which an army takes refuge was called siysiya, and fortresses were called sayasi.

Al-qadhf (القذف) is swift casting. That is, Allah cast terror into their hearts by His creative command, so they surrendered and descended upon the judgment of the Muslims.

The party who were killed were the men, and they were about seven hundred. The party who were taken captive were the women and children.

The address in His words ﴿A party you killed﴾ to the end is to the believers, as a completion of the blessing alluded to by His words ﴿O you who believe, remember the favour of Allah upon you when hosts came against you, so We sent upon them a wind﴾ [al-Ahzab: 9], etc., i.e., He destroyed the hosts, turned them back in their rage, and gave you power over their allies and supporters.

The fronting of the object in ﴿A party you killed﴾ is for the sake of emphasis on mentioning it, because that party were the men of the tribe, and by killing them the seizure of the land, wealth, and captives is completed. For this reason the object of "you take captive" was not fronted, since there is no need to front it, so it remains in its original place.

His words ﴿and a land you had not trodden﴾ mean a land you had not entered as raiders. It is a land other than the land of Qurayza, described by the clause ﴿you had not trodden﴾, i.e., you had not walked in it. [Page 314]

﴿O Prophet, say to your wives: If you desire the life of this world and its adornment, then come, I will provide for you and release you with a fair release.﴾ ﴿But if you desire Allah and His Messenger and the Last Abode, then indeed Allah has prepared for the good-doers among you a great reward.﴾

What can be drawn from what Ibn 'Atiyya related on the authority of Ibn al-Zubayr, and from what Abu Hayyan mentioned in al-Bahr al-Muhit and elsewhere, is that the connection of these verses to what precedes them is this: when the land of Qurayza was conquered for the Muslims and they seized their property, and the land of al-Nadir had been, shortly before that, fay' (property taken from the enemy without battle) belonging to the Prophet (ﷺ), the wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) thought that his situation was like that of any man: when provision is widened for them, they widen their spending, they and their dependants. So the wives of the Prophet (peace be upon him) did not ask him for more provision before Allah had granted him the people of al-Nadir as fay', and before he had the khums (one-fifth share) of the spoils. When they saw that the Prophet (ﷺ) had set aside for himself and his wives their sustenance from the wealth of Allah, and they saw the abundance of wealth that Allah had granted him as fay', they supposed that he would widen spending. So some of them began to ask him for more expenditure, as is indicated by the words of ʿUmar to his daughter Ḥafṣa, Mother of the Believers: ("Do not ask the Prophet for more, do not argue with him about anything, and ask me for whatever you wish.")

But Allah had placed His Messenger (ﷺ) in a great station, so his heart was not attached to the goods of this world except for what the sustaining of life requires. He used to say: "What have I to do with this world?" and he said: "Women and perfume have been made dear to me of your world." I have explained the reason for the exception of these two in a treatise I wrote on the divine wisdom in the Prophet's (peace be upon him) training of himself by reducing food.

ʿUmar said: ("The property of the Banu al-Nadir was among what Allah granted as fay' to His Messenger, which the Muslims had not pressed on with horse or camel. It was therefore exclusively for the Messenger of Allah, from which he would spend on his family the provision of a year; then he would place what remained in weapons and horses as a reserve for the Muslims.") You know that the land of Qurayza was divided among the Muhajirun (emigrants) by the judgment of Saʿd ibn Muʿadh. Perhaps when the sustenance of the Muhajirun was widened for their wives, the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) hoped to be like the Muhajirun. So Allah willed to teach them the conduct of the righteous women in living and in other matters. It has been related that some of them asked him for things from the adornment of this world, so He revealed to His Messenger these consecutive verses. This is what is indicated by

[Page 315]

the occurrence of these verses immediately after the mention of the event of Qurayza and the mention of the land that they had not trodden, which is the land of the Banu al-Nadir.

Since this course of conduct would be hard for most people, and especially for women, Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to inform his wives of it, and to give them the choice of following it in accordance with their condition, or of separating from him.

Therefore, opening these rulings with the address "O Prophet (ﷺ)" is an alert that what is mentioned after the address concerns him in a special way. This is the purpose of defining the conduct of his wives with him, a conduct befitting the rank of prophethood, and defining his marriage. This is the second of the purposes mentioned earlier in His words: ("O Prophet, fear Allah").

The wives referred to in this verse are his nine wives who survived him. They are: ʿĀ'isha bint Abi Bakr al-Siddiq; Ḥafṣa bint ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭab; Umm Habība bint Abi Sufyan; Umm Salama bint Umayya al-Makhzumiyya; Juwayriyya bint al-Ḥarith al-Khuzaʿiyya; Maymuna bint al-Ḥarith al-Hilaliyya of the Banu ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa; Sawda bint Zamʿa al-ʿĀmiriyya al-Qurashiyya; Zaynab bint Jaḥsh al-Asadiyya; and Ṣafiyya bint Ḥuyayy al-Nadariyya.

As for Zaynab bint Khuzayma al-Hilaliyya, known as Umm al-Masakin, she had died by the time this verse was revealed.

The meaning of ("If you desire the life of this world and its adornment"): if you prefer what is in this life of luxury over devoting yourselves to acts of worship and asceticism. The speech here involves the omission of a modifier (muḍāf), which is to be understood as general, since there is no evidence that a particular matter of worldly affairs is meant. This is the reason for the transitivity of the verb turidna ("you desire") directly to the noun of the life itself, without a qualifier of its affairs.

The conjunction of ("its adornment") is a specific conjunction after a general one. Its mention adds an alert that the omitted modifier is general. Also, the verb turidna indicates the choosing of one thing over another. So the meaning is: if you desire to immerse yourselves in the affairs of this world. This is indicated by its contrast with His words: ("But if you desire Allah and His Messenger"), as will follow.

[Page 316]

The word (تَعالَيْنَ, ta'alayna) is an imperative-form verb (ism fi'l amr) meaning "come hither (approach)". It is used here figuratively to represent the wives' readiness to receive the provision and the release, like one who comes to the place of the speaker.

The discussion of (تَعالَ, ta'āla) has already been made at His words: ("Say: Come, let us call our sons and your sons") [Āl ʿImrān 3:61] in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān.

Tamtīʿ (provision upon divorce) means that a husband gives his wife, when he divorces her, a gift to console her heart for what befalls her of brokenness. The discussion of it has been treated in detail at His words: ("And provide for them, the wealthy according to his means, and the straitened according to his means, a provision in kindness") [al-Baqara 2:236] in Sūrat al-Baqara.

The form (أُمَتِّعْكُنَّ, umatti'kunna) is in the jussive mood as the answer to (تَعالَيْنَ, ta'alayna). Since the latter is an imperative-form verb and not a clear imperative, the jussive of its answer is not obligatory. It is therefore given in the jussive so that it carries the meaning of a conditional, thereby conveying that the provision is achieved merely by one of them desiring the life of this world.

As-sarāḥ means divorce. It is one of its names and forms. Allah the Exalted said: ("Then either retain them in kindness or release them in kindness") [al-Baqara 2:231].

Al-jamīl means "the good", a goodness meaning what is acceptable to the soul, namely divorce without anger or aversion, since it is a divorce in which avoiding burdening the wife with what would be hard for her is observed. What is mentioned in the verse is not of the kind of the choice (takhyīr) and the granting (tamlīk), which are of the delegation of divorce to the wife. Rather, this is the wife being given the choice between two things, where her choosing one of them would prompt her husband to divorce her if he wishes that.

The meaning of ("But if you desire Allah and His Messenger") is: if you prefer Allah over the life of this world, that is, you prefer the pleasure of Allah in what He wills for His Messenger. So the speech involves the omission of a modifier. Seeking Allah's pleasure is doing what Allah loves and what brings one closer to Him. So the transitivity of the verb turidna to the noun of Allah's essence is according to an interpretation required by the correctness of attaching the desire to a noun of essence, since the essence itself is not desired literally. Therefore it is necessary to supply a modifier, and it must be understood as general, as already explained.

The desire for the pleasure of the Messenger (ﷺ) is similarly by way of such an interpretation, that is, everything that pleases the Messenger (peace be upon him). The first of that is that they remain in his company with good dispositions.

[Page 317]

As for the desire of the Last Abode, it is the desire for its success. So the speech involves the omission of a modifier which the context also requires. The style of speech proceeds by attaching the judgment to concrete entities, and this style requires an interpretation in the speech of the kind of implication necessary for meaning (dalālat al-iqtiḍāʾ).

In omitting the modifiers and attaching the desire to the names of the three entities, the purpose is that the desire be connected to the affairs of the one referred to, which stand in the place of its essence, along with fulfilling the requirement of brevity after fulfilling the requirement of inimitability (iʿjāz).

So the meaning is: if you prefer what pleases Allah and what His Messenger loves, and the good of the Last Abode, then choose that over what distracts from it, as is indicated by the contrast of the desire for Allah and His Messenger and the Last Abode with the desire for the life of this world and its adornment. For the contrast requires two desires, one of which is combined with the other. Attachment to the world necessitates occupation with many matters of worldly affairs, and it is inevitable that these distract its possessor from occupation with great matters of what pleases Allah and what pleases His Messenger (peace be upon him), and from enjoying many works which earn success in the Hereafter. Allah loves that the human soul rise to the ranks of angelic perfection, and the Messenger (ﷺ) desires to be the nearest of people to Him and the most knowing of Him, proceeding upon His way, because His way is the one Allah chose for him. In proportion to the abundance of this, success in the bliss of the Hereafter increases. People race in this arena, and the one most deserving of the prize in it is the one most attached to the Messenger (ﷺ). Thus were the aspirations of the excellent predecessors, and the most deserving of people in this are the wives of the Messenger (peace be upon him). Allah reminded them with a remarkable reminder in His words: ("And remember what is recited in your houses of the signs of Allah and the wisdom") [al-Aḥzāb 33:34], as will follow.

Since their desiring Allah, His Messenger, and the Last Abode necessitates their righteous deeds, and that deed varies in degree, He made the reward for it conditional on good-doing, saying: ("Indeed Allah has prepared for the good-doers among you a great reward"), so that they would know that this reward is attained by them in proportion to their good-doing. Thus this is the reason for mentioning the description "good-doers", and it is not for restricting the meaning.

The mention of "prepared" (aʿadda) conveys concern for this reward and emphasis upon it, in addition to describing it as "great".

The emphasis of the clause of the reward by the particle inna is not for removing doubt; rather, it displays concern for this reward.

[Page 318]

It has come in the books of the Sunna that when this verse was revealed, "the Prophet (ﷺ) began with ʿĀ'isha and said to her: 'I am going to mention a matter to you, and there is no harm if you do not hasten until you consult your two parents.' Then he recited this verse. ʿĀ'isha said: 'Regarding this, am I to consult my two parents? For I desire Allah, His Messenger, and the Last Abode.' He said the same to the rest of his wives, and they said the same as what ʿĀ'isha had said."

There is no benefit in occupying oneself with whether this choice was obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ) or recommended, for this is a matter that has already passed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was not one who would oppose the command of Allah the Exalted, whether by obligation or by recommendation.

Since their desiring Allah, His Messenger, and the Last Abode necessitates their righteous deeds, and that deed varies in degree, He made the reward for it conditional on good-doing, saying: ("Indeed Allah has prepared for the good-doers among you a great reward"), so that they would know that this reward is attained by them in proportion to their good-doing. Thus this is the reason for mentioning the description "good-doers", and it is not for restricting the meaning.

The mention of "prepared" (aʿadda) conveys concern for this reward and emphasis upon it, in addition to describing it as "great".

The emphasis of the clause of the reward by the particle inna is not for removing doubt; rather, it displays concern for this reward.

[Page 318]

It has come in the books of the Sunna that when this verse was revealed, "the Prophet (ﷺ) began with ʿĀ'isha and said to her: 'I am going to mention a matter to you, and there is no harm if you do not hasten until you consult your two parents.' Then he recited this verse. ʿĀ'isha said: 'Regarding this, am I to consult my two parents? For I desire Allah, His Messenger, and the Last Abode.' He said the same to the rest of his wives, and they said the same as what ʿĀ'isha had said."

There is no benefit in occupying oneself with whether this choice was obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ) or recommended, for this is a matter that has already passed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was not one who would oppose the command of Allah the Exalted, whether by obligation or by recommendation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 30:

﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear immorality, the punishment will be doubled for her twofold, and that is ever easy for Allah.﴾

God Himself addressed them directly after He commanded His Messenger to give them the choice (takhyir). So they chose God, His Messenger, and the Last Abode, and their Lord addressed them directly, because they had become bound by a covenant with God, the Exalted: ﴿that He will give them a great reward﴾. ʿUmar called it a covenant ('ahd). He would often recite Surat al-Ahzab in the dawn prayer, and when he reached this verse he would raise his voice with it. He was asked about this and said, "I remind them of the covenant." Since the promised reward is tied to good conduct, it was intended to warn them against sins, raising them to the rank of angels (al-malakiyyah) in emphasizing the warning, since the punishment for disobedience was made, on the supposition that one of them commits it, a doubled punishment.

Their being addressed by name serves to draw attention to what will be conveyed to them.

He addressed them by the description "wives of the Prophet" so that they would know that what is about to be conveyed to them is news befitting the loftiness of their status. Here "nisa'" (women) means wives (al-halā'il), and this was mentioned earlier in the words of the Exalted: ﴿our women and your women﴾ [Al 'Imran: 61] in Surat Al 'Imran.

The majority read "ya'ti" with a yaʾ at its beginning, taking into account the meaning of the conditional "man" (whoever), since its meaning is a thing, so its original form is non-feminine. Ya'qub read "man ta'ti" with a ta' at its beginning, taking into account the referent of "man", i.e., one of the women.

The majority read "yuda'af" with a yaʾ at its beginning for the third person, with a fatha on the ʿayn, in the passive voice, and "al-ʿadhab" in the nominative as the deputy subject. Ibn Kathir and Ibn ʿAmir read "nuda'if" with the first-person plural of majesty and a shadda on the ʿayn, kasra-vowelled, and "al-ʿadhab" in the accusative as the object. Thus the explicit mention of the Name of Majesty (Allah) in His words after it, ﴿and that is ever easy for Allah﴾, is an explicit mention in place of the pronoun. Abu ʿAmr and Ya'qub read "yudda'af" with a yaʾ for the third person and a shadda on the ʿayn, fatha-vowelled. The meanings of these readings are, on verification, one and the same.

Al-Tabari narrated from Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla' and from Abu ʿUbayda Maʿmar ibn al-Muthanna that there is a distinction between "ḍaʿafa" and "ḍaʿʿafa". As for "ḍaʿafa" (to double), it signifies making a thing its double, so it becomes three; and as for "ḍaʿʿafa" with the shadda, it signifies making a thing its equal. Al-Tabari said: We know of no one among the people of knowledge who claimed this distinction other than these two.

The dual form in His words "ḍiʿfayn" (twofold) is used to mean multiplicity, like His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Then return your gaze twice; your gaze will return to you humbled and weary﴾ [al-Mulk: 4], since it is evident that the gaze does not return humbled and weary from repeating the look twice. The dual is used in Arabic speech as a figure for repetition, as in their saying "labbayka wa saʿdayka" and their saying "dawalayka". For this reason, we do not occupy ourselves with specifying the doubling intended in the verse as a single doubling, such that this punishment would equal twice what is due for the like of the immorality, or three times that; and no one among the exegetes has engaged in that. Their turning away from it is only because their understanding went directly to the well-known usage in speech. Therefore what is narrated from Abu ʿAmr and Abu ʿUbayda is not to be heeded.

Al-fahisha (immorality): disobedience. The Exalted said: ﴿Say: my Lord has only forbidden the immoralities, what is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾ [al-A'raf: 33]. Whenever "fahisha" occurs in the Qur'an in indefinite form, it means disobedience; and when it occurs in definite form, it means fornication (zina) and the like.

Al-mubayyina (clear): in the form of the active participle, it is an intensification of the statement that it is an immorality and of its clarity, to the point that it seems to make itself clear. The majority read it thus. Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr read it with a fatha on the yaʾ, meaning that its doer makes it clear.

Al-mudaʿafa (doubling): the repetition of a thing of a certain quantity with its like quantity.

Al-dhiʿf (double): the equal of some number. It was mentioned earlier in the words of the Exalted: ﴿So give them a punishment doubled from the Fire﴾ [al-A'raf: 38] in Surat al-A'raf.

The meaning of the doubling of the punishment is that it will be double the punishment of the like of that disobedience if it proceeds from others; it is double in intensity and in duration, and the punishment of the Hereafter is intended.

The clause ﴿and that is ever easy for Allah﴾ is a parenthetical insertion, and the discussion of its counterpart was given earlier. The meaning: Allah fulfils His threat, and the fact that she is the wife of a Prophet does not prevent Him from that, as the Exalted said: ﴿They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them, and they availed them nothing against Allah﴾ [al-Tahrim: 10], to His words ﴿so they availed them nothing against Allah at all﴾ [al-Tahrim: 10].

The definiteness in "al-ʿadhab" is the definiteness of reference (ʿahd), i.e., the punishment that Allah appointed for the immorality.

[Page 5]

﴿And whoever of you devoutly obeys Allah and His Messenger and does righteous deeds — We will give her her reward twice, and We have prepared for her a noble provision.﴾

He follows the threat with the promise, in keeping with the Qur'an's practice, as was mentioned in the tenth introduction (al-muqaddimah al-‘āshirah).

Qunut (devout obedience) means obedience. Qunut to the Messenger means persistence in obeying him and seeking his pleasure, because in his pleasure is the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [al-Nisa’: 80].

The majority (al-Jumhur) read yaqnut with a yā’ at its beginning, in consideration of the meaning of the conditional man (whoever), as was mentioned in ﴿whoever of you commits a clear immorality﴾ [al-Ahzab: 30].

Ya‘qub read it with a tā’ at its beginning, in consideration of what man refers to, namely one of the women, as was mentioned in His saying, the Exalted, ﴿whoever of you commits a clear immorality﴾ [al-Ahzab: 30].

The verb of giving their reward is attributed to the pronoun of the Majesty (Allah) in a clear manner, to honour their receiving the reward, because it is what is hoped for from them. The same applies to the verb (wa-a‘tadnā, “and We have prepared”).

The meaning of marratayn (twice) is the abundance of the reward and its multiplication, as was mentioned in His saying, the Exalted, ḍi‘fayn (double).

The pronoun in ajrahā (her reward) refers to man (whoever), in view of the fact that it applies to one of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ.

Attaching the reward to her pronoun indicates the magnification of that reward, that it befits her station, and it also indicates her honour, that she deserves that reward.

The doubling of the reward for them for acts of obedience is an honour for their rank, and this doubling applies in both cases

[Page 6]

among the distinctive features of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, because of the greatness of their rank, since the increase in the ugliness of disobedience follows the increase in the merit of the one who commits it.

The rank of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ is great.

The majority read wa-ta‘mal with a tā’ at its beginning, considering the meaning of the relative man as referring to one of the women. What makes this acceptable is that it is coordinated with the verb yaqnut after the attached genitive pronoun (the pronoun of the women, niswah) became linked to it.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisā’ī and Khalaf read wa-ya‘mal with a yā’, in consideration of the meaning of man (whoever) in its original usage. The majority read nu’tihā with the plural of majesty (nūn al-‘aẓamah). Ḥamzah, al-Kisā’ī and Khalaf read it with a yā’, considering the pronoun of the absent third person to refer back to the name of the Majesty (Allah) in His saying before it, ﴿And that is ever easy for Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 30].

What is said about a‘tadnā lahā is like what is said about ﴿indeed, Allah has prepared for the doers of good among you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 29]. The tā’ in a‘tadnā replaces one of the two dāls of a‘adda, because of the closeness of their articulation points and for the purpose of lightening. The shift from the imperfect to the perfect verb in His saying a‘tadnā is to indicate the certainty of its occurrence.

The noble provision (al-rizq al-karīm) is the provision of Paradise. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whenever they are provided with a provision of fruit therefrom﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25], and so on in the verse. He described it as noble because it is the best of its kind. This has been discussed in His saying, the Exalted, ﴿indeed, I have been delivered a noble letter﴾ [al-Naml: 29], in Surat al-Naml.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 32:

﴿O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any of the [other] women, if you fear Allah.﴾

Their address was repeated from the side of their Lord, and their call was repeated, out of concern for this report, a concern that singles it out.

And aḥad (أحد): a noun meaning "one," like ﴿Say: He is Allah, One (aḥad)﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1]. Its hamza is a substitution for a wāw. Its original form is waḥad, on the pattern fa'al, meaning muttaḥid ("unique"), just as they said farad meaning munfarid ("alone"). Al-Nabigha said, describing his riding of his mount:

"As if my saddle, when the day declined with us on the Day of al-Jalil, was on a wild ass, wary and solitary (waḥid)."

He means: on a wild bull, solitary (munfarid). When beginning with the wāw became burdensome, they commonly said: aḥad.
صفحة ٧
It is most often used in a context of negation, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then none of you could withhold him from Us﴾ [al-Haqqah: 47]. When it occurs in a negative context, it indicates the negation of every single individual of the category.

The negation of resemblance here is intended as the negation of equality, expressed metaphorically as a denial of superiority over other women, like the negation of equality in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Not equal are those believers who sit [at home] — other than those with a disability — and those who strive in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 95]. Had the intention not been preference, there would be no point in the addition ﴿other than those with a disability﴾ [al-Nisa': 95], nor a reason for its revelation, as has been mentioned earlier in Surat al-Nisa'. So the meaning is: you are the best of women. Its apparent sense is the preference of all of them over the women of this community, and the reason for that is that they were closely attached to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in a way closer than any other attachment; they became his intimate companions, constant in his affairs, so they were singled out with knowledge of his conditions and character which no others shared, in times of ease and of hardship, and they took on his character more than others could acquire from him. And because his attention to them was a special attention. Do you not see his saying, may blessings and peace be upon him: "Women and perfume have been made dear to me of your world" [al-Nasa'i]? And the Exalted said: ﴿Good things are for good people﴾ [al-Nur: 26]. Then, the wives of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, also differ in excellence among themselves.

The restriction with His saying ﴿if you fear Allah﴾ is not meant to guard against the opposite of that, but is a spur and an exhortation to increase in piety. Close to this meaning is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Hafsa: "Indeed, ʿAbd Allah (meaning her brother) is a righteous man; if only he would stand in prayer at night." Hafsa conveyed that to ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, and he did not abandon the night prayer after that, because he understood that the intent was exhortation to stand in prayer.

The conditional verb is used to indicate continuity, meaning: if you persist in piety. The wives of the Prophet ﷺ were already God-fearing before this, and the answer to the condition is indicated by what precedes it.

Know that the apparent sense of this verse is the preference of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ over all the women of this community. There has been disagreement about the comparison between the wives and the daughters of the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Ash'ari is reported to have abstained on this, and perhaps that is because of the conflict of the textual proofs and the difference of the religious and spiritual aspects of the bases of preference, to the point that it is difficult to pin them down with fixed rules.

Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi pointed to a number of these in his commentary on al-Tirmidhi, in the hadith of a dream of a man among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ: that he saw a balance sent down from the sky, in which the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr were weighed, and the Prophet ﷺ outweighed; then Abu Bakr and ʿUmar were weighed, and Abu Bakr outweighed; then ʿUmar and ʿUthman were weighed, and ʿUmar outweighed; then the balance was raised. The aspects on which Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi based his reasoning are mostly among the affairs of men. It does not follow that the daughters of the Prophet ﷺ or his wives are equal in merit. Some scholars have firmly affirmed the preference of the daughters of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ over his wives, especially Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her, and this is the apparent sense of al-Taftazani's words in his book al-Maqasid. This is a question on which no action depends from its precise determination, so it is not appropriate to prolong the discussion of it.

The better view is that the pause is on ﴿if you fear Allah﴾, and His saying ﴿so do not be soft in speech﴾ is the beginning of a consequence, not the answer to the condition.

* * *

﴿So do not be soft in speech, lest one in whose heart is a disease should covet, but speak in a known manner﴾

Following from their preference and elevation of rank, there is guidance for them toward subtleties of conduct which heedlessness of observing them may befall, because the effect of them is hard to perceive, and because they are hidden, rare means that lead to what is unbecoming of their sanctity in the minds of some within the community, among whom are its hypocrites.

It begins with a warning about the manner of speech, for people vary in its softness, and women have a natural tenderness in their speech; some of them have such delicacy and softness of disposition that, when added to their innate softness, its manner comes close to the manner of coquetry, since such a manner is rarely practiced except in that state. When this appears in some women, some men who address them suppose that she is showing fondness toward him, so his soul may be emboldened to covet flirtation, and a rash act may escape from him that contradicts the sanctity of a woman, let alone the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, who are the mothers of the believers.

Khudu' (خضوع) is in its essential meaning humility, and here it is applied to softness because of its resemblance to humility.

The ba' in His saying "bil-qawl" may be transitive, in the role of the transitive hamza, meaning: do not make speech submissive, that is, do not make it humble and abased, that is, soft and loose. The placement of the ba' here is better than the placement of the transitive hamza, because the transitive ba' came from the ba' of accompaniment, as the investigating grammarians explained: the origin of your saying "I went with Zayd" is that you went accompanied by him, so you took him with you; then the sense of accompaniment was forgotten in such as His saying: ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]. Since loosening and beautifying of speech follows the loosening of the speaker, he attributed submission to them in a form, and the transitivity was conveyed by the ba'. The ba' may also mean "in," meaning: let there be no softness in speech from you.

The prohibition of submission in speech is an indication of a warning against what exceeds the usual softness of women's speech, namely softening the voice; that is, let your speech be firm.

Maraḍ (مرض) in its essential meaning is the disruption of the order of bodily temperament through weakness of strength, and here it is used figuratively for the disruption of the religious restraint, such as the hypocrites and those among the desert Arabs at the beginning of faith who had not yet firmly acquired the morals of Islam, and likewise those who take on ill opinion and thus slander chaste, heedless, believing women. The affair of the hypocrites' slander against ʿA'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, is evidence of this. It has been mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿in their hearts is a disease﴾ [al-Baqarah: 10] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The verb yaṭma' (يطمع) is in the subjunctive as an answer to the prohibition after the fa', because the thing prohibited is a cause of this covetousness.

The object of yaṭma' is omitted out of exalted reverence for the status of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, with the presence of the context indicating it.

The conjunction of ﴿and speak a known speech﴾ to ﴿do not be soft in speech﴾ serves as a safeguard lest they think that Allah has obligated them to lower their voices like the whispering of secret conversation.

Qawl (قول) means speech.

Ma'ruf (معروف) is that which people are accustomed to according to general custom. The known speech includes the manner of speech, which is what the context was brought for, and its implications include that they should not rebuke anyone who speaks to them or let them hear obscene speech, of the type: "Let him say what is good, or let him remain silent." By this, this sentence serves as a concluding summary.

[p. 10]

﴿And remain in your houses﴾. This is a command specific to them, namely the obligation to stay constantly in their houses, as a mark of honour for them and to strengthen their sanctity. Their staying in their houses is an act of worship, and the descent of revelation within them, and the Prophet's ﷺ coming and going among them, gives them sanctity. When the Prophet's Mosque became too crowded for the Muslims, they used to pray the Friday prayer in the houses of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, as in the hadith in al-Muwatta'. This ruling is an obligation upon the Mothers of the Believers, and for all other women it is a matter of perfection.

Nafi', 'Asim and Abu Ja'far read "qarna" with a fatha on the qaf. Abu 'Ubayda, on the authority of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, explained it as the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, from qarra, meaning "to remain and settle". They say "qarirtu fi al-makan" with a kasra on the ra' in the past tense, of the pattern 'alima, so its present tense has a fatha on the ra'. The original form of "qarna" was "iqrarna", and the first ra' was deleted for lightness, from the doubling, and its vowel was transferred to the qaf, as in the saying of the Arabs "ahsana" meaning "ahassna" in the verse of Abu Zubayd:

"Except that the swift mounts among the riding beasts sensed him, and they were fierce against him."

Al-Mazini and Abu Hatim denied that this is a dialect, claiming that "qarirtu" with a kasra on the ra' in the past tense only occurs in the sense of "the coolness of the eye". The reading is evidence against both of them. Al-Nahhas adopted their position and claimed that the interpretation of the verse according to this reading is that it derives from "qurrat al-'ayn" (the coolness of the eye), and that the meaning is: "and be cool-eyed in your houses", i.e. there is coolness for you in your houses, so do not look beyond that. This would be a metaphor for constant residence in their houses.

The rest of the ten readers read "wa-qirna" with a kasra on the qaf. Al-Mubarrad said: it is from al-qarar (settling), its original form being "iqrirna" with a kasra on the first ra', which was deleted for lightness, and its vowel transferred to the qaf, as they said "zalta" and "mast". Ibn 'Atiyya said: it may be "qirna" with a kasra on the qaf, as a command from al-waqar (dignity). It is said: "waqara fulan yaqirru", and the command from it is "qir" for one man and "qirna" for women, like "'idna". This would be a metaphor for constant residence in their houses, with an allusion to the reason for it, which is that it is a dignity for them.

The majority read "buyutikunna" with a kasra on the ba'. Warsh, on the authority of Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far read it with a damma on the ba'. [p. 11]

The attribution of the houses to them is because they are the ones who dwell in them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ settled them there, so the houses of the Prophet ﷺ were distinguished from one another by being attributed to the one who lived in each house. They say: "the chamber of 'A'isha" and "the house of Hafsa". This attribution is like the attribution to the pronoun of the divorced women in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not expel them from their houses﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]. This is because a man's wife is the mistress of his house, and the Arabs call the wife "the house". This does not imply that the houses belong to them, because the Prophet ﷺ built the houses as subordinate to the building of the Mosque. For this reason, when all the wives had passed away, their courtyards were incorporated into the Mosque during the expansion which the caliph al-Walid ibn 'Abd al-Malik carried out during the governorship of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz over Medina, and he did not give compensation to their heirs.

This verse requires that the wives of the Prophet ﷺ remain in their houses, and that they not go out except out of necessity. It has come in a hadith that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah has permitted you to go out for your needs", meaning the needs of a human being.

The meaning of this command is that they remain constantly in their houses, except in cases where going out is compelled, such as the death of one's parents. 'A'isha went out to the house of Abu Bakr during his illness in which he died, as his hadith with her about his gift, which he had given her from a palm tree, indicates, and his saying to her, "Indeed today it is the wealth of an heir", which is narrated in al-Muwatta'. They used to go out for the Hajj and in some of the military campaigns with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, because the place where the Prophet ﷺ stayed on his journeys is equivalent to his houses in his residence. Sawda refused to go out for the Hajj and 'Umra after that. All of this indicates that the general application of the command in His saying "and remain in your houses" is absolute.

For this reason, when Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas died, 'A'isha ordered that his funeral be brought past her in the Mosque so that she could supplicate for him, meaning to pray over him. This is narrated in al-Muwatta'.

The going out of 'A'isha to Basra in the strife known as the Battle of the Camel has been a source of difficulty for people. Many of the leading Companions did not object to it, among them Talha and al-Zubayr. Some of them objected to it, such as 'Ammar ibn Yasir and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and each has a view in ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning). The position of the verifiers, such as Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi, is that this was from her ijtihad, for she saw that in her going out to Basra there was a benefit for the Muslims, to mediate between the two factions of the strife [p. 12] for reconciliation. People had clung to her and complained to her of the great strife they had fallen into, and they hoped for her blessing, that she would go out and reconcile between the two sides. They thought that people would be shy before her. So she interpreted her going out as a benefit which corresponds to the general application of the remaining commanded in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And remain in your houses﴾, and is equivalent to going out for the Hajj. She took as evidence His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, then make peace between them﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9], and saw that the command to reconcile includes her and others like her who hope to be heard. So this was from her ijtihad. A number of the Companions advised her to do this and went out with her, such as Talha and al-Zubayr, and how excellent those two are. This is one of the matters of ijtihad of the Companions where we must take it upon ourselves to interpret it in the best of ways, and to hold the best opinion of them, as we say concerning their fighting at Siffin, when the matter was close to being settled, but those who call to strife spoiled it. 'A'isha did not realise until the fighting had already taken place between two factions of the Companions on the day of the Camel. It is not appropriate to take the words of the historians at face value, for among them are people of desires and those who gather the worthless and the valuable. As for what is mentioned of her, may Allah be pleased with her, that whenever she recited this verse she would weep until her veil became wet, there is no confidence in the soundness of its chain; and even if it were sound, its meaning would be that she was grieved by those events which compelled her to exercise ijtihad in interpreting the verse.

* * *

﴿And do not display yourselves in the manner of the former days of ignorance﴾. Tabarruj (display, ostentation) is a woman showing the beauty of her person, her clothing and her ornaments before the eyes of men. It was discussed previously in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿not displaying adornment﴾ in Surat al-Nur.

The phrase "tabarruj al-jahiliyya al-ula" is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq, a verbal noun used for emphasis or description), and it has the sense of a descriptive qualification, intended to deter from display. The purpose of the prohibition is continuous abstention from display, and that they are forbidden from it. It also contains an indirect rebuke to other Muslim women for display, for in Medina at that time there remained the women of the hypocrites, and perhaps some of them were still upholding some of their conduct from the time of ignorance. So the intention was a call to abolish that in the conduct of Muslim women. It appears that the Mothers of the Believers are forbidden from display absolutely, even in those circumstances in which women were permitted to display (in Surat al-Nur), in their houses, because abandoning display is a perfection and a purity from occupation with trivialities.

The ignorance is attributed to the people of the Jahiliyya, since it had been established among the Muslims to belittle what the state of the Jahiliyya was, except what Islam had approved.

[p. 13]

Al-Jahiliyya is the period in which the Arabs were before Islam. Its feminine form is because it is understood as "the period". Al-Jahiliyya is a nisba (relative adjective) derived from al-jahil (the ignorant), because the people who lived in it were ignorant of Allah and of the laws. It has already been discussed at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They think of Allah other than the truth, the thought of the Jahiliyya﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154] in Surat Al 'Imran.

Describing it as "the first" (al-ula) is a qualifying description clarifying that it was the first before Islam, and Islam came after it. It is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that He destroyed the first 'Ad﴾ [al-Najm: 50], and like their saying "al-'isha' al-akhira" (the last night prayer). There is no second and first jahiliyya. Some exegetes treated it as a restrictive description and made al-Jahiliyya into two jahiliyyas. Among them are those who said: the first is what came before Islam, and there will be another jahiliyya after Islam, meaning when the rulings of Islam are lifted, and we seek refuge in Allah. Among them are those who said: the first jahiliyya is the ancient one, from the era before Abraham, when there was no restraint for women or for men, and they fabricated stories about that, varying, exaggerated, or general. All of this is an artificial stretch which drove them to it, namely the attempt to treat the description as restrictive.

* * *

﴿And establish the prayer, give the zakat, and obey Allah and His Messenger﴾. These commands are intended to be continuous, because they are already engaged in their content. It is so that people know that those who are near to Allah and the righteous are not elevated in rank with Allah, may He be exalted, beyond the right of the obligations being placed upon them. In this there is a rebuke to some of the Sufis who claim that when the saints reach the highest levels of sainthood, the legal obligations are dropped from them.

He singled out the prayer and the zakat for the command, then the command came general to obedience, because these two acts of obedience, the physical and the financial, are the root of all other acts of obedience. Whoever attends to them with due care, they lead him to what lies beyond them. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed the prayer forbids indecency and wrong﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45], and we have explained it in Surat al-'Ankabut.

* * *

[p. 14]

﴿Indeed Allah desires only to remove from you the uncleanness, O people of the household, and to purify you with complete purification﴾. This is connected to what precedes it, since it is a reason (ta'lil) for what the previous verses included of commands and prohibitions, beginning with His saying, may He be exalted: (﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear immorality﴾ [al-Ahzab: 30]) and so on. The position of "innama" (indeed/only) conveys the linking of what follows to what precedes, because the particle "inna" is a part of "innama", and the particle "inna" by its nature serves the function of the causal fa' (so), as Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir explained. So the meaning is: Allah commanded you with what He commanded and forbade you what He forbade, because He desired for you the clearing away of deficiencies and the adorning with perfections. This reason came as a parenthetical insertion between the commands and prohibitions which are conjoined.

The definite article in "al-bayt" (the house) is the definite article of prior reference (al-'ahd), and it is the house of the Prophet ﷺ. The houses of the Prophet ﷺ are many, so what is meant by "the house" here is the house of each one of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, and each of these houses was inhabited by the Prophet ﷺ, and its wife is the one who owns it. For this reason, after it came His saying: (﴿And remember what is recited in your houses﴾ [al-Ahzab: 34]). The two pronouns of address are directed to the wives of the Prophet ﷺ in accordance with the pattern of the pronouns that came before. The two pronouns were given in the masculine plural form by way of ghalba (the prevailing of the masculine gender), because the Prophet ﷺ is taken into account in this address, for he is the lord of each of their houses, and he is present in the address, since he is the one who conveys it. In this prevalence there is an allusion that this purification is for them on account of the station of the Prophet ﷺ, so that his consorts may be similar to him in purity and perfection, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And good things are for good men﴾ [al-Nur: 26], meaning the wives of the Prophet for the Prophet ﷺ. This is a parallel to His saying in the story of Abraham: ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings upon you, O people of the house﴾ [Hud: 73], where the addressee is the wife of Abraham, and he is with her.

"Rijs" (uncleanness) in its original meaning is filth which defiles the bodies. It is used metaphorically here for sins and religious deficiencies, because they make a person's honour in this world and the next despised and hateful, like a body defiled with filth. It has been discussed previously at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿an abomination of Satan's work﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 90] in Surat al-'Uqud. "Tathir" (purification) is used metaphorically for the opposite of that, namely keeping away from sins and deficiencies, just as a body or a garment is pure.

"Idhhab" (removing) is used metaphorically for deliverance and distancing.

[p. 15]

The use of the imperfect verb indicates the renewal and continuity of the will. When Allah wills a matter, He decrees it, since none can repel His will.

The meaning is: God only intends, by what He has commanded and forbidden you, to protect you (the wives) from defects and to adorn you with perfections, and to make that lasting. That is, He does not intend by it to abhor you or to harm you. The restriction here is a restriction by reversal (qasr qalb), as the Exalted said: ﴿God does not intend to place upon you any difficulty, but He intends to purify you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. This is the reason the restrictive construction with innama comes here. The verse indicates that God protected the wives of His Prophet ﷺ from committing major sins and purified their souls.

"The People of the House" (Ahl al-Bayt) are the wives of the Prophet ﷺ. The address is directed to them, and likewise what comes before and after it. No one doubts this, and the Companions of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, and the Followers (al-Tabi'un) did not understand from it anything other than that the wives of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, are the intended meaning, and that the revelation was about them.

As for what al-Tirmidhi narrated from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from Umar ibn Abi Salamah, who said: "When it was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, ﴿God only intends to remove from you the impurity, O People of the House, and to purify you thoroughly﴾, in the house of Umm Salamah, he called Fatimah, Hasan and Husayn, and covered them with a cloak, while 'Ali was behind his back, and he covered him with a cloak. Then he said: 'O God, these are the People of my House, so remove from them the impurity and purify them thoroughly.'" Al-Tirmidhi said: "It is a gharib hadith from the narration of 'Ata' from Umar ibn Abi Salamah." Al-Tirmidhi did not grade it as sahih or hasan, and he labelled it gharib. In Sahih Muslim, from 'A'ishah: "The Messenger of God went out one morning wearing a striped cloak (mirt murahhal). Then al-Hasan came and he admitted him, then al-Husayn came and he admitted him, then Fatimah came and he admitted her, then 'Ali came and he admitted him. Then he said: ﴿God only intends to remove from you the impurity, O People of the House, and to purify you thoroughly﴾." This is more explicit than the hadith of al-Tirmidhi.

So its interpretation is that the Prophet ﷺ included the People of the Cloak (Ahl al-Kisa') under the ruling of this verse, and made them his household, just as he extended the sanctity of Madinah to Makkah, by his saying: "Indeed Ibrahim made Makkah sacred, and I make sacred what lies between its two lava plains (labatayha)." The interpretation of "house" (bayt) in its literal and figurative meanings is valid for the house of lineage, as they say: "The house and the number are among them," and this is from interpreting the Qur'an in all its non-contradictory meanings, as we indicated in the ninth introduction. It seems that the wisdom of covering them together with the cloak was to strengthen the metaphor of "house" with respect to them, bringing the image of a house closer by the greatest possible degree at that time; so that the cloak would stand in the place of the house. The presence of the Prophet ﷺ with them under the cloak, as in the hadith of Sahih Muslim, confirms that this cloak is attributed to him. By this it becomes clear that the wives of the Prophet ﷺ are his household by the explicit text of the verse, and that Fatimah, her two sons, and her husband are made by his supplication (or by the interpretation of the verse according to its meanings) to be his household. For this reason they are his household by the evidence of the Sunnah. All of them, God has removed from them the impurity and purified them thoroughly: some by the divine designation, and some by the prophetic designation. Similar to this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Salman is one of us, the People of the House."

Ibn Kathir collected many narrations of this report, which imply that the People of the House includes Fatimah, 'Ali, Hasan and Husayn. However, there is nothing in them that this verse was revealed concerning them, except for one hadith which Ibn Kathir attributed to al-Tabari. It is not found in his (al-Tabari's) tafsir, that from Umm Salamah: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib was mentioned in her presence, and she said: "It was about him that ﴿God only intends to remove from you the impurity, O People of the House, and to purify you thoroughly﴾ was revealed," and she mentioned the report of his being covered with Fatimah and her two sons with a cloak. [[The editor of the printed edition of Ibn Kathir's tafsir noted that there is disagreement in the text across all manuscripts, and the editor did not detail it.]]

The Shi'ah seized upon the hadith of the Cloak and appropriated the description of the People of the House, restricting it to Fatimah, her husband and her two sons, may God be pleased with them, and they claimed that the wives of the Prophet ﷺ are not of the People of the House. This is a contradiction of the Qur'an, by making this verse an interpolation between what was addressed to the wives of the Prophet ﷺ. There is nothing in the wording of the hadith of the Cloak that requires restricting this description to the People of the Cloak, since in his saying ("These are the People of my House") there is no restrictive construction. It is like the Exalted's saying: ﴿Indeed these are my guests﴾ [al-Hijr: 68], whose meaning is not "I have no guests other than them." And it implies that this verse is cut off from what precedes it and what follows it. It appears that this misconception dates from the era of the Followers, and that the source of reciting this verse on tongues separately, without connection to what precedes and follows it. What supports this is what the commentators narrated from Ikrimah, that he said: "Whoever wishes, I will contend with him over it: it was revealed concerning the wives of the Prophet ﷺ." He also said: "It is not as you go about saying; it is only the wives of the Prophet ﷺ," and that he used to shout this out in the market. The hadith of Umar ibn Abi Salamah is explicit that the verse was revealed before the Prophet made the supplication for the People of the Cloak, and that it was revealed in the house of Umm Salamah.

As for what occurred in the saying of Umar ibn Abi Salamah that Umm Salamah said: "And I am with them, O Messenger of God?" He said: "You are in your place, and you are upon good." The Shi'ah erred in this, thinking that he prevented her from being of his household. This is ignorance, because the Prophet ﷺ only meant what she asked about, which was already included: the verse was revealed concerning her and her co-wives, so she had no need to be added to them. Thus, the supplication for her that God remove the impurity from her and purify her is a supplication for the attainment of a matter that had already occurred, which contradicts the etiquette of supplication, as Shihab al-Din al-Qarafi explained in al-Furuq between the permissible supplication and the prohibited supplication. So the Prophet's ﷺ answer was a teaching for her. In some narrations it occurred that he said to Umm Salamah: "Indeed you are of the wives of the Prophet." This is clearer regarding the meaning of his saying "you are upon good."

When God answered his supplication, the Prophet ﷺ used to apply the term "People of the House" to Fatimah, 'Ali and their two sons. Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Anas ibn Malik that the Messenger of God ﷺ used to pass by the door of Fatimah for six months when he went out to the dawn prayer, saying: "The prayer, O People of the House! ﴿God only intends to remove from you the impurity, O People of the House, and to purify you thoroughly﴾." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hasan gharib hadith from this route."

The lam in His saying "li-yudhhiba" is the lam of the preposition (lam al-jarr), which is added for emphasis, mostly after the two roots of will (irada) and command (amr), and the imperfect verb after it is put in the subjunctive by a hidden "an" (an) which is obligatory to hide. Among its examples is the Exalted's saying: ﴿And we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 71], and the saying of Kuthayyir:

"I wish to forget her love, yet it is as though Layla is depicted for me in every place."

It is related from al-Nahhas that some of the reciters called it "lam an." The Exalted's saying ﴿God intends to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 26] has already been discussed in Surat al-Nisa'.

His saying "ahl al-bayt" is a vocative address to the female addressees, the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, in the presence of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace. It includes everyone whom the Prophet ﷺ attached to them by declaring him to be of the People of the House, and they are: Fatimah, her two sons, her husband, and Salman; these do not exceed them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 34:

Page 18
﴿And remember what is recited in your houses of the revelations of Allah and the wisdom. Indeed, Allah is ever Subtle, Acquainted.﴾
When Allah had guaranteed them greatness, He commanded them to adorn themselves with its causes, to take pleasure in its effects, and to equip themselves with knowledge of the Shari'ah through the study of the Qur'an, so that this would combine their own guidance, increasing them in perfection and knowledge, and their guiding the community to what is good for it from the knowledge of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The verb udhkurna (remember) may be from dhikr with a dammah on the dhal, meaning tadhakkur (remembrance). This is a comprehensive expression that includes its explicit meaning, namely that they should not forget what came in the Qur'an and should not neglect acting upon it. It also includes the implicit meaning, namely that the intention is to observe acting upon what is recited in their houses, of what is revealed in them and what the Prophet (ﷺ) recites in them, and what he clarifies in them of the religion. It includes a second implicit meaning, namely remembering that great blessing, that their houses were the place where the Qur'an was recited.

It may also be from dhikr with a kasrah on the dhal, which is causing speech to pass over the tongue, i.e., convey it to the people, by reciting the Qur'an and conveying the sayings and conduct of the Prophet (ﷺ). In it is an implicit reference to acting upon it. Tilawah (recitation) is qira'ah, i.e., repeating a written or memorized speech, i.e., what the Messenger (ﷺ) recites. The phrase ﴿of the revelations of Allah and the wisdom﴾ is an explanation of what is recited, so all of that is recited, and that is the Qur'an. It has specified what is recited by two things: the revelations of Allah and the wisdom. The revelations of Allah encompass the entire Qur'an, because it is miraculous and cannot be opposed, so it is a sign that it is from Allah.

The conjunction "and the wisdom" is a specific conjunction over a general one, and it refers to what in the Qur'an is admonitions and legal rulings. He, the Exalted, said after mentioning the rulings in Surah al-Isra': ﴿That is of what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom﴾ [al-Isra': 39]. That is, what is recited in their houses at the time of its revelation, or by the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ) and their study of the Qur'an, so that what they have learned is renewed, and so that there shine for them of its lights what is hidden and whose spring never runs dry, and so that they may be participants in conveying the Qur'an and its transmission. The Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the Followers after them continued to refer to the Mothers of the Believers concerning many rulings relating to women and rulings concerning a man with his family, as in His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Mention me before your lord﴾ [Yusuf: 42], that is, convey the report of my imprisonment and my remaining in it.

Page 19
The placement of the root dhikr here is a noble placement, because it bears these meanings in a way that no other root could bear without lengthy elaboration. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Allah commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to convey what was sent down to him. So when he recited it to one person or to whoever it happened to be, the obligation was discharged from him, and it was incumbent upon those who followed him to convey it to others, and it was not required that he mention it to all the Companions.
The mention of wisdom has been repeated in the Qur'an in many places, and we explained it in Surah al-Baqarah. And earlier, shortly before, the disagreement of the readers over the kasrah or dammah on the ba' of (buyut) was discussed.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Subtle, Acquainted﴾ is a justification for the command and a conclusion for the preceding sentences. The justification is suitable for all the possible meanings of the command, because subtlety requires bestowing benefit in a manner that does not burden the one to whom it is bestowed.

What was directed to the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) of commands and prohibitions is of benefit to them and a means of bringing good through them. Likewise, in His facilitating for them the companionship of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and making them the people of his house, and in preparing them to hear and understand the Qur'an, and to witness the prophetic guidance, all of that is subtlety toward them, which is what prompts the address directed to them, so that they receive the report and convey it. Also, because the Acquainted, i.e., the All-Knowing, when He wills to remove impurity from them and purify them, His purpose is fully accomplished without defect or heedlessness.

Thus the meaning of the clause is that He, the Exalted, is described with subtlety and knowledge, as the verb (kana) indicates. So it includes the generality of His subtlety toward them and His knowledge of His subtlety toward them and of what in it is their benefit.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 35 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women, the devoutly obedient men and devoutly obedient women, the truthful men and truthful women, the patient men and patient women, the humble men and humble women, the charitable men and charitable women, the fasting men and fasting women, the men who guard their private parts and the women who guard them, and the men who remember Allah much and the women who remember Him much — Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward.﴾ This sentence may be an explanatory resumptive (isti'naf bayani), because His saying ﴿Whoever of you is devoutly obedient to Allah and His Messenger, and does righteous deeds, We shall give her reward twice﴾ [al-Ahzab: 31], after His saying ﴿You are not like any other of the women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 32],
Page 20
arouses in the souls of Muslim women the question: Are they too rewarded for the good deeds they do? Are they commanded with the same things the wives of the Prophet ﷺ were commanded with? Or are those privileges specific to the wives of the Prophet - may the prayer and peace of Allah be upon him? So in this verse there is an answer to this question, according to the Qur'anic custom whenever it mentions things commanded to a group, following it with a reminder of the condition of their likes or of their opposites.
It may also be a fresh, initiating resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) that came in connection with what was mentioned of the virtues of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ.
Ibn Jarir and al-Wahidi related from Qatada that some women entered upon the wives of the Prophet ﷺ and said: "Allah has mentioned you in the Qur'an and has not mentioned us with anything. If there were any good in us, He would have mentioned us." So Allah revealed this verse.
al-Tirmidhi and al-Tabarani related that "Umm 'Umara al-Ansariyya came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'I do not see women being mentioned with anything,' so this verse was revealed." Al-Wahidi said: Muqatil said: "It reached me that Asma' bint 'Umays, when she returned from Abyssinia with her husband Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, entered upon the wives of the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'Has anything of the Qur'an been revealed about us?' It was said: 'No.' So she came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, indeed the women are in loss and ruin.' He said: 'And why is that?' She said: 'Because they are not mentioned with goodness as men are mentioned.' So Allah revealed this verse."

The intended referents of these described qualities are women, while the mention of men is to indicate that the two categories are equal in these laws, so that they know that the Shari'a is not restricted to men — unlike most of the Torah's law, which was specific to men, except for the rulings that cannot be conceived of apart from women. The Shari'a of Islam is the opposite of that: the basic principle in its rulings is that they apply to men and women alike, except what is explicitly specified for one of the two categories. Perhaps through this verse and its like, the principle of equality was established, so that it dispensed with the need to point it out in most of the statements of the Qur'an and the Sunna. Perhaps this is the reason for
Page 21
enumerating the mentioned qualities, lest it be supposed that equality applies only to one particular quality.

The method of elaboration (itnab) was adopted in enumerating the qualities, because the context calls for greater clarification, given the differing understandings of people regarding this. Moreover, in this enumeration there is an allusion to the foundations of legislation, as we will explain at the end of the commentary on this verse.

With these reports the connection of these verses with those before them becomes clear.

And with this the reason for emphasizing this statement with the particle (inna) becomes clear, to repel the doubt of whoever doubted this ruling among the women.

By ﴿the Muslim men and Muslim women﴾ is meant whoever is characterized by this meaning, which is known in the Shari'a. Islam in the Shari'a sense is the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, the establishment of prayer, the giving of zakat, the fasting of Ramadan, and the pilgrimage to the House; and it is not considered Islam except together with faith. The mention of the believing men and believing women after it serves to alert that faith is the foundation; the discussion of it has already passed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so do not die except as Muslims﴾ [al-Baqara: 132] in al-Baqara.

﴿The devoutly obedient men and devoutly obedient women﴾: those who practice qunut, which is obedience to Allah and worship of Him; it has already passed just now: ﴿whoever of you is devoutly obedient to Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Ahzab: 31].

﴿The truthful men and truthful women﴾: those among them in whom truthfulness of speech is found, which is the opposite of lying. Truthfulness is entirely good, and lying has no good in it except out of necessity. This includes fulfilling what is bound upon one of the matters of religion, such as fulfilling a covenant and fulfilling a vow. It has already passed in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿those are the ones who have been truthful﴾ [al-Baqara: 177] in Surat al-Baqara.

By ﴿the patient men and patient women﴾: the people of patience. Patience is praiseworthy in itself because it indicates firmness of resolve, but what is intended here is bearing hardships in matters of religion and bearing adversities in defending the Islamic domain. It has been discussed fully at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O you who believe, be patient and endure﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 200], at the end of Surat Ali 'Imran.
Page 22

By ﴿the humble men and humble women﴾: the people of khushu' (humility), which is submission to Allah and fear of Him; it returns to the meaning of sincerity of the heart in what the responsible person does, and the conformity of that with what appears of its effects on its possessor. What is meant: humility before Allah with the heart and the limbs. It has already passed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and indeed it is heavy except upon the humble﴾ [al-Baqara: 45] in al-Baqara.

By ﴿the charitable men and charitable women﴾: those who give charity from their wealth to the poor. It has already passed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿except one who orders charity﴾ [al-Nisa': 114] in Surat al-Nisa'. The benefit of this for the community is great.

As for ﴿the fasting men and fasting women﴾, the evident value of fasting lies in the discipline of the self for obedience to Allah, since a person abstains from what is natural desire in order to draw near to Allah; that is, as proof that Allah's pleasure is sweeter than the strongest pleasures that accompany it.

As for guarding the private parts, it is because desire for the sexual organ is a natural desire, and it is stronger in men. Allah has praised the prophets for this, saying of Yahya: ﴿and chaste﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 39], and saying of Maryam: ﴿who guarded her private part﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12]. This guarding has limits set by the Shari'a, so what is intended is guarding the private parts from being used in what the Shari'a has forbidden, and what is not intended is guarding them from use altogether, which is monasticism (rahbana), for monasticism is rejected in Islam by widely transmitted evidence.

As for ﴿the men who remember and the women who remember﴾, it is a description suitable to be derived from dhikr with a kasra on the dhal, which is remembrance by the tongue, as in His saying ﴿so remember Me, I will remember you﴾ [al-Baqara: 152], and His saying in the hadith: "Whoever remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself"; and from dhikr with a damma, as already passed just now in His saying ﴿and remember what is recited in your homes﴾ [al-Ahzab: 34], and as in His saying ﴿they remembered Allah and asked forgiveness for their sins﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 135].

The object of ﴿the guarding women﴾ is omitted, indicated by what precedes it in His saying ﴿the men who guard their private parts﴾, and likewise the object of ﴿the remembering women﴾.

These ten qualities have included the comprehensive principles of all the chapters of the Shari'a.
Page 23

Islam encompasses the five pillars of the religion, which are obligatory actions, while faith encompasses the obligatory beliefs of the heart, and it is the condition for all the actions of Islam. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17].

Qunut encompasses all acts of obedience, both obligatory and recommended, and abandoning the forbidden acts and desisting from them by one who has committed them, which is the meaning of repentance. So qunut is the completion of obedience, and it is a good equivalent to taqwa. These are the comprehensive principles of the laws for responsible persons regarding themselves.

Truthfulness encompasses every act in which word and deed conform to reality in judgment, testimony, contracts and obligations, and in dealings through fulfilling them and abstaining from betrayal, and conformity of the outward with the inward in all levels. Among truthfulness is truthfulness of deeds.

Patience encompasses what is specific to bearing hardships in actions, such as jihad, enjoining good and forbidding evil, advising the Muslims, and bearing harm for the sake of Allah; it is a great character trait, the key to the doors of praiseworthy morals, manners, and fairness from oneself.

Khushu' is sincerity of heart and outward conduct, and it is submission and avoidance of disobedience. It enters into ihsan, which is what is explained in the hadith of Jibril: "that you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you." Under this enter all acts of nearness and voluntary worship, for they are among the effects of khushu'. It also includes repentance from the major sins that a person has committed, since khushu' is not realized without it.

Charity (tasaddaq) encompasses all kinds of charity, gifts, the giving of good, and assistance.

Fasting is a great act of worship, and for this reason it was singled out for mention, although its obligatory form is included in Islam in His saying ﴿Indeed the Muslim men and Muslim women﴾, and it covers voluntary fasting. So the explicit mention of fasting is an honoring of it. In a hadith, Allah, exalted is He, said: "Fasting is for Me, and I shall reward it."

Guarding the private parts is intended to mean guarding them from what the Shari'a has ordered them to be guarded from, and all the rulings of marriage and what branches from it and what is a means to it are included in this.

And the remembrance of Allah, as you know, has two meanings:
Page 24

The first: remembrance by the tongue, which includes reciting the Qur'an, seeking knowledge, and studying it.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "No people gather in one of the houses of Allah, reciting the Book of Allah and studying it among themselves, except that tranquility descends upon them, mercy envelops them, and Allah mentions them among those who are with Him." In His saying "and Allah mentions them" there is an allusion that the recompense is of the same kind as their deed, which indicates that they were engaged in some remembrance of Allah. And Allah has said: ﴿so remember Me, I will remember you﴾ [al-Baqara: 152], and He said, in what He related of His Messenger ﷺ: "If he mentions Me in a gathering, I mention him in a gathering better than theirs." It includes what is recited after the prayers and similar adhkar.

The second meaning: remembrance of the heart, which is remembering Allah at His command and His prohibition, as 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "Better than remembering Allah with the tongue is remembering Allah at His command and His prohibition." This is the one in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves, remember Allah and ask forgiveness for their sins﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 135]. Repentance enters it, and restraint from all wrongs enters it: from killing, seizing people's wealth, highway robbery, and harming people in dealings. What makes clear that it covers all the laws is restricting it with ﴿much﴾ (kathiran), because when a person remembers Allah much, his remembrance has encompassed, in both senses, all that Allah is remembered at.

It is required in attaining these qualities that they proceed according to what the Shari'a has defined in their details.

Forgiveness (maghfira) is non-imposition of blame for the sins one has committed. It has already passed in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'raf: 23] in Surat al-A'raf. Know that conjoining qualities with the conjunction waw, which conveys mere sharing in the ruling without the ordering particles fa and thumma, means that the ruling mentioned with it is established for each one who is characterized by one of the qualities derived from which his description is formed, because the original function of waw in coordination is to indicate the difference of the coordinated items in essence. So when you say: "I found among them the generous, the brave, and the poet," the meaning is that you found among them three people, each of whom is described by one of the things mentioned. And in the hadith, "among them are the sick, the weak, and the one with need," meaning the possessors of sickness, weakness, and need. This is unlike conjoining with fa, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿By those lined up in rows, then those who drive away with reproof, then those who recite the reminder﴾ [al-Saffat: 1–3], where the qualities mentioned in that verse are established

for one and the same subject. Therefore the clause ﴿Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward﴾ should be, in meaning, a predicate reported about each of the conjoined items, as if it were said: "Indeed the Muslim men, for them Allah has prepared forgiveness and a great reward; indeed the Muslim women, for them Allah has prepared forgiveness and a great reward," and so on. The verb occurring in the predicate clause, namely (a'adda, "prepared"), is transitive and takes an object and a complement conjoined to that object. So the validity of predicating it of each of the described and conjoined groups, with respect to the conjoined object, is clear, because a great reward can be given to each individual and admits of degrees, so each of the possessors of these attributes receives his reward for being characterised by it, and the reward of some of them will be greater than the reward of others.
