As for the validity of predicating the verb (a'adda) of each of the conjoined groups with respect to the direct object (maghfiratan, "forgiveness"), what prevents it is the evidence of the Book and the Sunnah indicating that major sins that have been committed are not guaranteed forgiveness for the sinners except on condition of repentance from the sinner, as a promise from Allah in His saying: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy: whoever of you does evil in ignorance and then repents after it and makes amends, indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-An'am: 54].

The Sunnah has also added to the causes of forgiveness the accepted pilgrimage (al-hajj al-mabrur) and jihad in the way of Allah, and other things.

In my view, the proper way of interpreting this is that each of these attributes be understood as implying the absence of whatever contradicts it and entails accountability, that is, its possessor being free from involvement in major sins. This is an interpretation in which I take into account the practice of the Qur'an's manner in contexts of praise and commendation of Muslims, considering the state of the perfection of Islam, as in His saying: ﴿Those are the true believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 4]. For we do not find distinctions among the states of Muslims except in contexts of warning against sins.

The reference point for this interpretation is clarifying the general by combining the evidences of the Sharia. Most exegetes have refrained from undertaking to explain the implication of this promise and did not touch upon it, as far as I have seen, except the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari), who made the meaning of His saying ﴿Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward﴾: that those who combine these acts of obedience, for them Allah has prepared forgiveness and a great reward. He made the conjunctive waw carry the sense of accompaniment (ma'iyyah), and made the conjunction based on considering difference among the conjoined items in attributes, not difference in essences. This is an artificial contrivance (takalluf wa sun' bil-yad), and al-Baydawi and many others followed him. What weakens it is that the combination of these attributes does not necessitate forgiveness, because major sins do not remove their possessor from them except through repentance, unless one adds to his statement an addition, namely taking the male and female remembrers of Allah to mean those characterised by verbal and heartfelt remembrance, so that heartfelt remembrance includes repentance, as in His exalted saying: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins﴾ [Al 'Imran: 135]. Thus those who combined these ten qualities would have attained repentance. However, this excuse of al-Zamakhshari does not extend beyond this verse, for the Qur'an contains many verses like it to which the scope of this excuse cannot stretch. Among them is His saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan: 63] up to His saying: ﴿Those will be rewarded with the high chamber for what they patiently endured﴾ [al-Furqan: 75], the verse in Surat al-Furqan.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 36:

﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decreed a matter, that they should have any choice in their affair. And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger has certainly strayed into clear error.﴾

Most of the narrations hold that this verse was revealed concerning the proposal of Zaynab bint Jahsh to Zayd ibn Harithah. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out proposing on behalf of his freedman Zayd ibn Harithah to Zaynab bint Jahsh, and she shrank from it and refused, and her brother 'Abdullah ibn Jahsh also refused. So Allah the Exalted revealed ﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman﴾ — the verse — and she then complied and was content." This is because the marriage of Zaynab to Zayd ibn Harithah took place before the Hijrah, so this verse would have been revealed in Makkah, and its placement in this surah, which is Madani, is by way of attaching it to it, for the appropriateness that it should precede the mention of the marriage of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to Zaynab, which appears to have occurred after the Battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab). Allah had known that from before, and so He ordained for it the circumstances that came about afterward.

The presence of the conjunctive wa at the beginning of the sentence requires that it be coordinated with a statement revealed before it from another surah, whose specific identity we have not determined, nor the surah in which the verse was located. This is the coordination of one sentence with another for a connection between them.

It has been narrated from Jabir ibn Zayd that the occasion of revelation of this verse was that Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, who was the first of the women to emigrate, offered herself to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he married her to Zayd ibn Harithah, after Zayd had divorced Zaynab bint Jahsh, as will come shortly. She and her brother disliked that, and she said: "I only wanted the Messenger of Allah, and he married me to his slave." Then she and her brother were content after the revelation of the verse.

The connection is that it follows the praise of people of qualities which are part of obedience to Allah, by the obligation of obeying Allah and the Messenger (ﷺ). When this was followed by what concerns the attributes that are from the command of Allah, which earn for them His promised forgiveness and reward, and He equated in this men and women, He followed it with the explanation that obedience to the Messenger (ﷺ) in what he commands and resolves upon is an obligatory obedience and is joined to obedience to Allah, and that the two categories of people, men and women, are equal in this just as they were equal in the previous rulings.

The insertion of (kana) in the negation is the strongest indication of the negation of the ruling, because the verb kana, by its indication of existence (kawn), namely being, requires that its negation entails the negation of the particular state in its entirety, as has been explained more than once before.

The verbal noun derived from ﴿an takuna lahumu al-khiyarah﴾ is in the position of the nominative noun of the negated kana, and this kana is the complete (tamma) kana.

The decreeing of a matter (qada' al-amr) means clarifying it and informing of it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We decreed to him that matter: that the last remnant of these would be cut off by morning﴾ [al-Hijr: 66].

The meaning of ﴿when Allah and His Messenger have decreed﴾ is: when His command has been resolved upon and He has not given the one commanded any option in carrying it out. This is the command that the believers must carry out, as a safeguard against things like his saying to those who were grafting their palm trees: "If you had left them, they would have been good." Then they said: "We left them and they were not good." He said: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your worldly life." And like what preceded at the beginning of the surah of his intention to make a settlement with the confederates for half the produce of Madinah, then his retraction of that when he consulted the two Sa'ds; and like his command on the day of Badr to descend at the nearest water of Badr, whereupon al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir said to him: "Is this a position that Allah has caused you to descend, which it is not for us to advance beyond or fall back from, or is it opinion, war and stratagem?" He said: "Rather it is opinion, war and stratagem." He said: "Then this is not a position; rise with the people until we come to the nearest water of the enemy and occupy it, then we fill up the wells beyond it, then we build a basin over it and fill it with water, so we drink and they do not drink." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You have indeed given the right opinion," and he rose with the people. And in the hadith: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was on a journey and he was fasting, and when the sun set he said to Bilal: 'Get down and prepare the sawiq for us.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if only you would wait until evening.' Then he said: 'Get down and prepare it for us.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if only you would wait until evening; there is still daylight.' Then he said: 'Get down and prepare it,' so he got down and prepared it for him the third time, and he drank." So Bilal's reconsideration of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was because he knew that the command was not a firm resolve.

The mention of the name of Allah here is to allude to the fact that obedience to the Messenger (upon him be prayers and peace) is obedience to Allah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [an-Nisa': 80]. So the intended meaning is: when the Messenger of Allah decrees a matter, as preceded in His saying ﴿Then indeed for Allah is one-fifth of it and for the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 41] in surah al-Anfal, since the intended meaning is: indeed for the Messenger is one-fifth of it.

Al-khiyarah is the verbal noun of takhayyara, like al-tiyarah being the verbal noun of tatayyara. It is said that no other word of this pattern has been heard besides these two, and it was mentioned in His saying ﴿What they had no choice in﴾ [al-Qasas: 68] in surah al-Qasas.

The (min) in ﴿min amrihim﴾ is partitive (tab'idiyyah). Amrihim means their affair/condition, and it is a generic noun, i.e., their affairs. The meaning: the choosing of some of their affairs is not a possession that they own; rather it is obligatory for them to follow what Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) have decreed, so there is no choice for them.

Since (mu'minin wa mu'minatin) fall within the scope of negation, they encompass all believing men and believing women; therefore their pronoun came as a plural pronoun, because the meaning is: it is not for their collectivity, nor for each one of them, to have choice, as is the nature of generality.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿an takuna﴾ with a feminine (tā' fawqiyyah) prefix, because its subject is feminine in form. 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, Hisham, and Ibn 'Amir read it with a masculine (tahtiyyah) prefix, because a feminine non-real subject may take masculine agreement in its verb, especially when there is a separation between the verb and its subject.

His saying ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger has certainly strayed into clear error﴾ is a generalizing concluding statement (tadhyil ta'mim) warning against opposing the Messenger (upon him be prayers and peace), whether in matters where there is a choice or whether it is deliberate opposition out of desire.

[p. 29]

﴿And when you said to him upon whom Allah had bestowed favour, and you had bestowed favour: "Keep your wife to yourself and fear Allah," and you concealed within yourself what Allah was to disclose, and you feared the people, while Allah has more right that you should fear Him.﴾

(Idh) is a noun of time in the accusative, governed by a verb omitted in the sense of "remember." It has many similar instances. It derives from the root dh-k-r with a dammah on the dhal, meaning remembrance (tadhakkur). Allah did not command him to tell this to the people, since there would be no benefit in that. Rather, He reminded His Messenger (ﷺ) so that his saying, ﴿and you concealed within yourself what Allah was to disclose﴾, would follow from it. The purpose of this reminder is to show Allah's ordaining of causes for their effects, in order to realise His will, glorified is He. For this reason He said after it:

﴿So when Zayd had no further need of her, We married her to you﴾ up to His saying ﴿and the command of Allah is ever executed﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37–38], and His saying ﴿and the command of Allah is a decree decreed﴾ [al-Ahzab: 38].

This is the beginning of the aim of the transition to the ruling that abolishes adoption (tabanni) and refutes what the hypocrites had built upon its false foundation. This is because of the disbelief of the hypocrites, who made insinuations about the marriage of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to Zaynab bint Jahsh after Zayd ibn Harithah had divorced her. They said: "He married the wife of his son, and he had forbidden marriage to the wives of sons." For this reason this story and what follows it are concluded with praise of the believers in His saying ﴿He it is who sends blessings upon you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 43], and with turning away from the polytheists and the hypocrites and from their harm.

Zayd is the one meant by His saying, ﴿to him upon whom Allah had bestowed favour, and you had bestowed favour﴾. Allah bestowed favour upon him by faith and by deliverance from the hands of the polytheists, when He facilitated his entry into the possession of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, bestowed favour upon him by manumission, adoption and affection. His proper name is explicitly mentioned right after this verse, in His saying ﴿So when Zayd had no further need of her﴾. He is Zayd ibn Harithah ibn Sharahil al-Kalbi, of the Kalb ibn Wabarah, and the Banu Kalb are of Taghlib. Horsemen from the Banu al-Qayn ibn Jasr raided tents of the Banu Ma'n, who were with him from Tayy. Zayd's mother, Su'da bint Tha'labah of the Banu Ma'n, had gone out with him to visit her people, and the raiding horsemen overtook them. They sold him in the market of Hubasha, with the letter ḥ vowelled with a dammah, in the vicinity of Makkah. Hakim ibn Hizam bought him for his aunt Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, wife of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) married her, Khadijah gave him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Zayd was then eight years old, and this was before the prophethood. Some people of Kalb performed the pilgrimage and saw Zayd in Makkah, and they recognised him, and he recognised them. They informed his father and described his location and with whom he was. His father Harithah and his uncle Ka'b went out to ransom him. They entered Makkah and spoke with the Prophet (ﷺ) about his ransom. The Prophet (ﷺ) brought him to them, and they recognised him. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to him: "Choose me or choose them." Zayd said: "I am not one who would choose anyone over you." His father and uncle departed, and their hearts were content with his remaining.

[p. 30]

When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw this from him, he brought him out to al-Hijr and said: "O you who are present, bear witness that Zayd is my son; he will inherit from me and I will inherit from him." He thus became a son of the Prophet (ﷺ) under the rule of adoption as practised in the Jahiliyyah, and he was called Zayd ibn Muhammad.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had married him to Umm Ayman, his freed woman, and she bore him Usamah ibn Zayd, and then he divorced her. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) married him to Zaynab bint Jahsh al-Asadi, ally of the Al 'Abd Shams. She was the daughter of his paternal aunt Umaymah bint 'Abd al-Muttalib, and this was in Makkah at that time. Then after the Hijrah, the Prophet (ﷺ) established brotherhood between him and Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib. When the ruling of adoption was abolished by His saying ﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4], he came to be called "the beloved of the Messenger of Allah." In the fifth year before the Hijrah, after the Battle of the Trench, Zayd ibn Harithah divorced Zaynab bint Jahsh, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) married him to Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, whose mother was al-Bayda' bint 'Abd al-Muttalib. She bore him Zayd ibn Zayd and Ruqayyah, then he divorced her. He also married Durrah bint Abi Lahab, then he divorced her, and he married Hind bint al-'Awwam, sister of al-Zubayr.

Zayd witnessed Badr and all the campaigns. He was killed at the Battle of Mu'tah in the eighth year, while he was commander of the army, at the age of fifty-five.

The wife of Zayd mentioned in the verse is Zaynab bint Jahsh al-Asadiyyah, whose name had been Barrah. When the Prophet (ﷺ) married her, he named her Zaynab. Her father Jahsh was of the Banu Asad ibn Khuzaymah, and her father was an ally of the Al 'Abd Shams in Makkah. Her mother was Umaymah bint 'Abd al-Muttalib, paternal aunt of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Zayd ibn Harithah had married her in the Jahiliyyah, and then divorced her in Madinah. The Prophet (ﷺ) married her in the fifth year. She died in the twentieth year of the Hijrah at the age of fifty-three, so she was born in the thirty-third year before the Hijrah, that is, the twentieth year before the prophethood.

The use of the verb of saying in the present tense is to evoke the image of the saying and its repetition, like His saying ﴿He disputes with us concerning the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 74], and His saying ﴿and he was constructing the ark﴾ [Hud: 38]. In this there is a depiction of the Prophet (ﷺ) urging Zayd to keep his wife and not to divorce her, and of his returning to this matter repeatedly.

The expression of Zayd ibn Harithah here by a relative pronoun, rather than by his proper name which comes in His saying ﴿So when Zayd had no further need﴾, is because of what the conjoined clause implies: ﴿and you had bestowed favour upon him﴾. It indicates the Prophet's (ﷺ) freedom from making use of his patronage (wala') to compel him to divorce his wife. The intended meaning is the second relative clause, ﴿and you had bestowed favour upon him﴾, because its purpose is that Zayd was the person closest to him, that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was most eager for his well-being, and that he advised him to keep his wife for her own good through him. As for the clause ﴿to him upon whom Allah had bestowed favour﴾, it is a preparation for the second.

Know that the authentic transmitted report about this incident is that Zaynab remained with Zayd for years without bearing him children. Whenever a dispute arose between them, as happens between spouses, she would at times take pride in her nobility and belittle him for his patronage. When this recurred, he resolved to divorce her and came to inform the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of his resolve, because the Messenger had arranged her marriage to him.

It is reported from 'Ali Zayn al-'Abidin that Allah revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) that He would marry him to Zaynab bint Jahsh. It is reported from al-Zuhri that Gabriel descended upon the Prophet (ﷺ) informing him that Allah had married her to him, and that this is what he concealed within himself. Al-Qurtubi mentioned that this is the view preferred by Bakr ibn al-'Ala' al-Qushayri and Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi.

My own view is that this occurred in a dream, as he was shown in a dream that he said to 'Aishah: "The angel brought you to me in a dream wrapped in a piece of silk, saying to me: 'This is your wife.' Uncover her, and behold, it was you. I said: If this is from Allah, He will carry it out."

So the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to Zayd, ﴿Keep your wife to yourself﴾, was a fulfilment of the obligation of sincere counsel. It is a command of advice and an indication of good, not a command of legislation, because the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, in this situation was acting by the right of patronage and companionship, not in his capacity as legislator and Messenger. The discharge of this trust does not necessarily mean that he knew that Zaynab would become his wife. This is because knowledge of the Prophet about what will happen does not require his implementing, guiding or legislating it, unlike his knowledge or supposition. For the Prophet (ﷺ) knew that Abu Jahl, for example, would not believe, yet this did not prevent him from conveying the message to him and repeatedly calling him to faith. Also, his desire to obtain something does not require that he implement his will in accordance with his desire, if his desire contradicts what he obliges people to do. For example, he wished that someone would kill 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh before hearing his declaration of repentance from apostasy, when 'Uthman ibn 'Affan brought him repentant on the Day of the Conquest.

For all of this, Zayd's determination to divorce Zaynab is not considered disobedience to the Prophet (ﷺ), because his command in this matter was in the manner of reconciling between him and his wife. And it is not binding upon anyone to follow the advice of one who advises, as is implied by the hadith of Barirah with her husband Mughith, when he said to her: "If only you would return to him?" She said: "O Messenger of Allah, are you commanding me?" He said: "No, I am only interceding." She said: "I have no need of him."

His saying (Keep your wife to yourself) indicates that it was a reply to a statement made by Zayd, in that Zayd came seeking counsel about separating from his wife, or informing him of his resolve to separate from her.

(Keep to yourself) means: remain in her companionship. Holding back (imsak) is used figuratively for continuing the companionship, comparing the companion to a thing held in the hand.

The addition of (upon yourself) serves the function of (ʿalā) indicating constancy and firmness, like His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. Or it is because (amsik) includes the meaning of (ihbis), that is, keep your wife in your house. His command to fear Allah follows from the indication to keep her, that is, fear Allah regarding her companionship as He commanded, and do not deviate from the obligation of good treatment. That is, fear Allah by observing His saying ﴿then either keep her in an acceptable manner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229].

The clause ﴿and you concealed within yourself what Allah was to disclose﴾ is conjoined to the clause (you say). The use of the present verb in (and you conceal) indicates the repetition of this concealing and its not being mentioned. What was within him was his knowledge that he would marry Zaynab and that Zayd would divorce her. That was a secret between him and his Lord, not something he was obliged to convey, nor something from which the people would benefit by knowing, so that they should convey it. Do you not see that he did not inform 'Aishah or her father about the vision of the angel bringing her to him in a piece of silk, except after he had married her?

Thus the referent of (what was within yourself) is the marriage to Zaynab, which is what Allah was to disclose,

[p. 31]

because Allah disclosed it in the marriage of the Prophet (ﷺ) to her. No one knew that he would marry her, and Allah disclosed nothing other than that. Therefore it follows that what he concealed within himself was a matter suitable for manifestation in external existence, that is, it would be among the perceptible forms.

The clause ﴿and you conceal within yourself﴾ is not a circumstantial clause (hal) of the pronoun in (you say), as al-Zamakhshari (in al-Kashshaf) made it. This is because that is based on the assumption that the speech is directed as a rebuke, so that he would say words contrary to what he concealed within himself, which yields no sound meaning. For it would lead to the conclusion that what was appropriate for him was to say something other than that, and this contradicts the requirement of consultation. It would also lead to a criticism of Zaynab's suitability to remain under the marriage of Zayd. Al-Zamakhshari sensed this and said: "If you say: What did Allah want from him when Zayd said to him: 'I want to separate from her'? It would have been improper for him to say: 'Do it, for I want to marry her.' I say: What He wanted from him, mighty and majestic is He, was that he remain silent at that point, or say: 'You know best your own affair,' so that his secret in this matter would not contradict his public statement." End of quotation. But that is built on the premise that it was a rebuke, and in it there is weakness.

The clause ﴿and you fear the people﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿and you conceal within yourself﴾, that is, you conceal what Allah will disclose, and you fear the people because of its disclosure.

The fear (khashyah) here is aversion to what the hypocrites would spread as rumour. Aversion is one of the kinds of fear, since fear is a generic concept applied to its individual instances by gradation. So it is not fear of dread, since the Prophet (ﷺ) did not fear anyone regarding the public knowledge of his marriage to Zaynab, and the hypocrites' rumours had not yet appeared. Rather, the Prophet (ﷺ) was perceiving from their wickedness and evil dispositions what they had done in the matter of the slander. It was not a fear that reached the point of diverting him from what he desired, as evidenced by the fact that he did not hesitate to marry Zaynab after Zayd divorced her. Rather, it was an inner apprehension and an anticipation of what the hypocrites would spread.

The definite article in (the people) is for specific reference, that is, you fear the hypocrites, meaning they would harm you with their words.

The verse's clause ﴿Allah has more right that you fear Him﴾ is a parenthetical insertion, prompted by the mention of fearing people. The waw is parenthetical (i'tiraḍiyya), not the waw of circumstance (waw al-ḥāl). So the meaning of the verse is the same as His words ﴿So do not fear the people, but fear Me﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 44]. Taking it as a circumstantial clause is what led many exegetes (mufassirūn) to treat the speech as a reproach to the Prophet ﷺ.

[Page 34]

"Aḥaqq" is an elative form (ism al-tafḍīl) stripped of its comparative sense, so it means "worthy" (ḥaqīq). This is because the preceding speech does not indicate that people were being preferred over Allah in fear, nor that there was a conflict between the two fears that would require giving preference to fearing Allah over fearing people. The meaning is: Allah is worthy that you fear Him.

This construction does not indicate that he placed fear of people above fear of Allah, because Allah had not charged him with anything which he then acted against.

From this you know that the Prophet ﷺ did only what pleases Allah. He acted as a sincere companion (ṣāḥib nāṣiḥ) when he told Zayd to keep his wife, and he held sound knowledge when he feared that the hypocrites would fabricate slander if he married Zaynab in secret, and that their talk would become a trial (fitna) for those weak in faith. This is like his saying to the two men who saw him at night with Zaynab, and who quickened their pace: "Take it easy, it is only Zaynab." This displeased them, and they said: "Glory be to Allah, O Messenger of Allah!" He said: "Satan flows through the son of Adam as the blood flows. I feared he would cast something into your hearts."

Thus the Prophet's ﷺ position among the Ummah is like that of a sincere physician in a bimaristan (hospital) containing various kinds of patients. When he sees food brought in that is unsuitable for some of his patients, he forbids its entry out of fear that some patient for whom it is not suitable would eat it, thereby worsening his illness or leading to a relapse.

There is no reproach or blame in His words ﴿and you feared the people﴾. It is rather a reminder of what happened to him in guarding against the speech of the hypocrites. Many exegetes took it as reproach, but there is nothing in the context that requires this. I consider them mistaken in this, but it is a form of encouragement for him, a belittling of the enemies of the religion, and an instruction to him to proceed on his way and to enjoy what Allah has permitted to him and to His messengers of the lawful things they desire and love, provided nothing turns them away from obedience to their Lord. As He said: ﴿There is no fault upon the Prophet concerning what Allah has ordained for him. That was the practice of Allah with those who passed before, and the command of Allah is a decree decreed﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 38]. ﴿Those who convey the messages of Allah and fear Him, and fear none but Allah﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 39].

[Page 35]

He must turn away from the words of the hypocrites, in the manner of His words ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not believe﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 3]. This is the core of what the verse points to, and there is nothing in it indicating anything else.

Various mixed reports (akhbār makhlūṭa) have been related about this story. Beware lest any error creep into your mind from them. Do not give your attention to what the storytellers (ahl al-qiṣaṣ) have attached to this verse of belittling the state of the Prophet ﷺ when he told Zayd to keep his wife. That is among the fabrications of the storytellers (qaṣṣāṣīn). Either it is variation by the storytellers to embellish the narrative, or all or part of it is from the hypocrites' rumours and slander, which the storyteller picked up. This is what we are certain of.

Evidence for this is that you will not find, among what is transmitted from the early generations (al-salaf) in the tafsīr of this verse, any report with an isnad traced to the Prophet ﷺ, or to Zayd, or to Zaynab, or to any of the Companions, men or women. Rather, they are stories, reports, and "it was said" and "he said."

Because of the misunderstanding of this verse, its matter became grave for some Muslims, and it provoked many of the heretics (malāḥida) and enemies of Islam from the People of the Book. Abū Bakr ibn al-'Arabī addressed the weakness of its chains in Aḥkām al-Qur'ān, and likewise 'Iyāḍ in al-Shifā'.

Now we want to shift the course of discussion to accepting that what has been reported of the very weak reports has occurred, so that we do not leave in this verse a pitfall for anyone. The gist of the story from these reports is that the Prophet ﷺ came to Zayd's house asking for him, and he saw Zaynab. It was said: the wind lifted the curtain of the house, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) saw Zaynab suddenly, unintentionally, and her beauty pleased him, and he glorified Allah. Zaynab knew that he had been impressed by her, and Zayd knew this, and he wished to divorce her so that he could give preference to his master (mawlā), the Prophet ﷺ. When he informed the Prophet ﷺ of that, the Prophet said to him: ﴿Keep your wife for yourself﴾, while in his heart he wished for her divorce, knowing that she would become his wife.

Although the chains vary in weakness, the story was spread among people, so its fat and lean parts were passed on, and its light and weighty elements were borne. Each took from it what his understanding and religion could hold. Even if all of it had actually happened, it would not have been a flaw in the station of prophethood.

[Page 36]

As for his seeing Zaynab in Zayd's house: if it was intentional, then he had asked permission to enter Zayd's house, since seeking permission is obligatory, so there is no doubt he saw her face and was pleased by it. I do not think that was because women did not cover their faces. He said: ﴿and not reveal their adornment except what appears of it﴾ [al-Nūr: 31], meaning the face and the two hands. Zayd was among the people most closely connected with the Prophet, and Zaynab was the daughter of his paternal aunt and the wife of his mawlā and adopted son. She was thus mixing with his household, and it was he who married her to Zayd. So it is not correct that he saw her except when he came to Zayd's house. And if the wind lifted the curtain and he saw of her beauty and adornment what he had not seen before, then there is also no wonder in this, because a sudden glance is not blameworthy, and the arising of admiration immediately after a look that is not forbidden is a compelling matter that a person cannot turn away from himself. Is admiration of a woman's person anything other than admiration of gardens, gardens of paradise, flowers, horses, and the like, which Allah has called adornment, when the onlooker does not follow the glance with another?

As for what came to the Prophet's ﷺ mind of desire to marry her: if it occurred, it is not a grave matter, because it is a passing thought that a person cannot prevent from himself. You know that His words ﴿and you feared the people﴾ are not blame, and His words ﴿Allah has more right that you fear Him﴾ contain no reproach or rebuke for not fearing Allah, but rather an affirmation of not caring about fear of people.

The stations of souls become manifest in the arenas of nobility (futuwwa) in proportion to their steadfastness in perfection while resisting what arises from those appearances of weakness in souls and frailty of resolve. And let it suffice you as evidence of the firmness of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in this station, and he is the most excellent of those whose foot is firm in such matters, that he kept urging Zayd to keep his wife, advising him with what was good for him, while Zayd saw this as counsel and sincere advice, not as a command or a legal ruling.

If it were correct that Zayd knew of the Prophet's ﷺ desire to marry Zaynab and divorced her for that reason, without a command from the Prophet (peace be upon him) or a request from him, it would not be strange, for they used to prefer the Prophet ﷺ over themselves. Dahya al-Kalbī relinquished Ṣafiyya bint Ḥuyayy to him after she had fallen to him in his share of the spoils of Khaybar. And Sa'd ibn al-Rabī' offered 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn 'Awf that he would relinquish one of his two wives, whomever he chose, for the brotherhood which the Prophet ﷺ established

[Page 37]

between them.

As for the Prophet's ﷺ (peace be upon him) indication to Zayd to keep his wife, while knowing that she would become his wife, this is the fulfilment of the trust of sincere counsel and consultation. A person may indicate something he knows to be beneficial while being certain that his indication will not be obeyed. Confusing the two situations is a confusion between conduct based on what the apparent circumstances require and what is in Allah's knowledge within. The most similar station to this is the station of Mūsā with al-Khiḍr in the three incidents. This is not "the treachery of the eyes" (khā'innat al-a'yun), as one who lacks understanding imagines, because the blameworthy treachery of the eyes is only that which stems from betrayal and deceit.

Nor is it a lie, because the words of the Prophet (peace be upon him) to Zayd ﴿Keep your wife for yourself and fear Allah﴾ do not contradict his desire to marry her. It would contradict it only if he had said: "I love that you keep your wife." For it is not hidden that consultation is seeking consideration of what is good for the one consulting, not what is good for the one consulted. It is the right of the consulted to inform the one consulting of what is good for him in the view of the advisor, even if the advisor's own good lies in the opposite, in addition to the fact that what is in this story is only a divergence between counsel and what the advisor knows, that his counsel will have no effect.

If you say: what is the meaning of what is related in the Ṣaḥīḥ from 'Ā'isha that she said: "If the Messenger of Allah had concealed anything of the revelation, he would have concealed this verse: ﴿And when you said to the one on whom Allah had bestowed favour and you had bestowed favour: Keep your wife for yourself﴾" and so on?

I say: she meant that the Prophet's ﷺ desire to marry Zaynab, or Allah's informing him of it, was a secret in his soul which no one had been informed of, since he had not been commanded to convey it to anyone. Upon that secret was built what proceeded from him to Zayd in his words ﴿Keep your wife for yourself﴾. When Zayd divorced her and he intended to marry her, he knew that the hypocrites would spread evil talk. When Allah commanded him to mention that to the Ummah and convey its news, he conveyed it and did not conceal it, though there was in its concealment neither suspension of a law nor loss of a benefit. So had he been a concealer, he would have concealed this verse, which is a narration of a secret in his soul between him and his Lord, the Exalted. But since it was a revelation, he conveyed it, because he is commanded to convey everything that has been sent down to him.

Know that truths have their proper measure, and actions have their barriers and causes. People may be seized by customs, which come between them and perceiving benefits. When conditions spread among their habits, they approve of them even if they are evil. When praiseworthy things are rare, they repel them whenever they try to enter their minds and make their way in. All of this comes from distorting the innate nature (fiṭra) from its proper state, and from separating truths from their law.

When Islam came, it began to raid those armies to uproot them from their far corners and bring them down from their fortresses. So what is good is what the innate nature testifies to its goodness, and what is ugly and forbidden is that which the Sharī'a has caused to die and commanded to be buried.

* * *

﴿So when Zayd had accomplished from her what he needed, We gave her to you in marriage, that there should be no difficulty for the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons when they have accomplished from them what they needed; and the command of Allah is always executed﴾. This is a consequence (tafrī') of the sentence ﴿And when you said to the one on whom Allah had bestowed favour and you had bestowed favour﴾ and so on. A statement has been omitted which the context indicates, and its estimate is: So he did not accept from you what you indicated to him, and he did not keep her.

The meaning of "qaḍā" is: he fulfilled and completed. The name "Zayd" is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, because the apparent expectation would be to say: "So when he had accomplished from her what he needed," meaning: when the one on whom Allah had bestowed favour and you had bestowed favour accomplished it. So it departs from the expected pronoun in order to honour Zayd's position. Al-Qurṭubī said, citing al-Suhaylī: He used to be called Zayd ibn Muḥammad. When this nobility was removed from him, when it was revealed ﴿Call them by their fathers' names﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 5], and Allah knew his distress over that, He honoured him with a distinction that He did not give to any other of Muḥammad's Companions: He named him in the Qur'an. Whoever Allah mentions by name in the Wise Reminder is elevated to the highest elevation. End of quotation.

"Waṭar" is an important need and an urgent desire. Al-Nābigha said:

"Whoever has achieved a need of his from a friend, then I have achieved my needs from you."

The meaning: when Zayd had completed the period of living with Zaynab and divorced her, that is, when he had no more need of her.

[Page 39]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 37 (part 3 of 3):

The meaning of "We married her to you" (zawwajnākahā) is: a permission for you to marry her. Zaynab was a divorcee (ayyim), and the Messenger (ﷺ) married her with her consent. The historians (ahl al-siyar) mention that her brother Abū Aḥmad ibn al-Ḍarīr, whose name was ʿAbd ibn Jaḥsh, gave her in marriage to him. When God commanded him to marry her, he said to Zayd ibn Ḥārithah: "I find no one in myself more trustworthy than you, so propose to Zaynab on my behalf." Zayd said: "I went to her and turned my back to her out of reverence for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and I said: 'O Zaynab, the Messenger of God sends to mention you.' She said: 'I will not do anything until I consult my Lord,' and she stood at her place of worship and performed the prayer of istikhārah (seeking guidance), and she was content. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came, entered, and consummated the marriage with her." Zaynab used to boast over the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) and say: "Your guardians married you off, but my Lord married me off."

This implies that, if her brother Abū Aḥmad did not arrange her marriage, then this is a particularity (khuṣūṣiyyah) of the Prophet (ﷺ) according to those who require a guardian (walī) in marriage, such as the Mālikīs, as opposed to the view of the Ḥanafīs. It is not mentioned in the narrations that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave her a dower (ṣadāq), and some historians counted this among his particularities (ﷺ), so there were two prophetic particularities in her marriage.

He indicated the wisdom of this marriage in establishing the Sharia, which is the removal of the embarrassment (ḥaraj) that the people of the Jāhiliyyah felt about a man marrying the wife of his adopted son (daʿiyy). When God nullified this by word, saying "Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons" (Q. 33:4), He confirmed its nullification by deed, so that not even the slightest trace of embarrassment would remain, such that someone might say: "Even though that has become lawful, it is proper for people of perfection to abstain from it." So, to ensure the absence of this, the marriage to the wife of the adopted son was carried out by one of the best of people, who is the Prophet (ﷺ).

The combination of "la-" (in order that) and "kay" (so that) is an emphasis on the causal purpose, as if he were saying: the reason is nothing other than this. The verse also indicates that the principle in legislative rulings is that they are equal between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the community (ummah), unless a proof establishes a particularity.

The clause "And the command of God is always accomplished" (wa-kāna amru llāhi mafʿūlan) is a concluding remark (tadhyīl) for the clause "We married her to you." The "command of God" may refer to the legislative command, namely the permission to marry the former wives of adopted sons, and this is the meaning of the legislative command in it. The meaning of "accomplished" (mafʿūlan) is that it is followed and obeyed, so no one is exempt from it, as God says: "Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?" (Q. 7:32).

It may also refer to the creative (takwīnī) command, which is what He knows will occur and what He has decreed as the causes of its occurrence, so the meaning of "accomplished" is that it takes place. The "command" here is by way of attributing the cause to its effect, and "accomplished" is the effect.

The Prophet's (ﷺ) marriage to Zaynab was by God's command in both senses.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verses 38–39:

﴿There is no restriction upon the Prophet in what Allah has ordained for him. That has been the way of Allah with those who passed on before, and the command of Allah is a decree determined.﴾ ﴿Those who convey the messages of Allah and fear Him, and fear none but Allah. And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner.﴾

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) to further clarify the equality of the Prophet ﷺ with the Ummah in the permissibility of marrying the divorced wife of his adopted son, and to clarify that this does not diminish the quality of prophethood. This is because partaking of permissible things is part of the practice (sunnah) of the prophets. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 51]. And when the Prophet desires to benefit from something permissible due to the inclination of his soul towards it, it is fitting for him to partake of it, so that he does not strive against his soul in matters in which he was not commanded to strive against the soul; for what is most fitting for him is that he preserve his resolve and his striving for repelling what he was commanded to avoid.

In this resumptive statement there is also a beginning of refuting the sayings of the hypocrites: that the Prophet ﷺ married the wife of his son.

The meaning of ﴿Allah ordained for him﴾ is that He decreed it, since He permitted him to do it. The construction of the verb (fara·a) with the preposition lam indicates this meaning, unlike its transitivity with the preposition (ʿala), as in His saying ﴿We have certainly known what We have ordained for them concerning their wives﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50].

And the sunnah (sunnah): the course of conduct, of action or character, which its doer keeps to constantly. The discussion of whether sunnah is a fixed noun or a verbal noun has passed at His saying ﴿Indeed there have passed before you examples (sunan)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 137] in Surat Al 'Imran. According to the first view, the accusative of "sunnata Allah" here is because it is a noun placed in the position of a verbal noun, as it indicates the meaning of a verb and a verbal noun. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: like their saying "turban and jandal," meaning in supplication, i.e., "may he be in dust (tariba turaban)." Its original form is: "turbun lahu wa jandalun lahu." Following the original form is the saying of al-Ma'arri:

They desired Quwayq while the highland lay between them,
Dust for them from camels and herds.

He placed it in the manner of wonder mixed with anger.

According to the second view, the accusative of "sunnata" is as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). In both cases the verb is implied, indicated by the verbal noun or its substitute. The estimate is: Allah prescribed His sunnah concerning those who passed before.

The meaning: Muhammad ﷺ follows the sunnah of the prophets who preceded him, in compliance with what Allah ordained for him just as He ordained for them, i.e., permitted.

The intended referents of "those who passed on" are the prophets, by the context of the word "Prophet," i.e., those who passed on before prophethood. His saying ﴿Those who convey the messages of Allah and fear Him﴾ has added clarification, for the prophets were married, and many of them had multiple wives, and some of their wives were more beloved to them than others.

If we stop at what came in this verse and what authentic reports clarified, then the lesson is drawn from the conditions of all the prophets.

And if we accept, with some leniency, some of the weak reports that have been attached to the story of Zaynab's marriage, then David (peace be upon him) is an example in particular: he had many wives, and he loved to marry the wife of Uriah (Uriyya), the one for whom Allah set forth the parable of the two litigants who scaled the sanctuary and disputed before him. This will come in Surat Sad, and the story is mentioned in the Book of Kings. The point of the comparison with David lies in the origin of his desire turning towards a woman who had not been lawful to him, so she became lawful to him; the point of comparison is not what surrounded David's story of Allah's rebuke of him for that, as He said ﴿And David thought that We had only tested him, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness﴾ [Sad: 24] and so on, because that does not apply to the story of Zaynab's marriage.

The clause ﴿and the command of Allah is a decree determined﴾ is parenthetical between the qualified and the qualifier if the clause ﴿Those who convey﴾ is a qualifier of ﴿those who passed on before﴾, or a concluding statement like the clause ﴿and the command of Allah is ever a thing done﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37] if the clause ﴿Those who convey﴾ is a resumptive statement, as will come; and the discussion concerning it is like its counterpart mentioned just above.

The word qadar (with a fatha on the dal): the bringing into existence of things in a intended form, and it is derived from qadr (with a sukun on the dal), which is a specified and precisely controlled quantity. It was discussed at His saying ﴿so the valleys flowed according to their measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17] in Surat al-Ra'd, and His saying ﴿And We do not send it down except in a known measure﴾ [al-Hijr: 21] in Surat al-Hijr. Since it is necessary to this meaning that it be precise and firm, the use of qadar as a metonymy for perfection and for proceeding from knowledge became frequent. From this is the hadith: "Everything is by decree (qadar) and destiny (qada')," meaning from Allah.

The scholars of kalam have agreed that qadar is the name for the eternal will related to things as they are, and they apply it to the thing to which qadar is related, which is the decreed (maqdur), as in this verse. So the meaning is: "the command of Allah was decreed according to a wisdom which Allah intended from that command." So when Allah commanded His Messenger, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, to marry Zaynab, whom Zayd had divorced, He knew that this was fitting for His Messenger, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, just as He had decreed it for his predecessors among the prophets.

In His saying ﴿Those who convey﴾ the relative pronoun was used rather than a demonstrative or pronoun, because of what this relative clause implies of the removal of restriction from the prophets in partaking of the permissible: Allah intended from them the conveying of the message and the fear of Allah by avoiding what He forbade, and He did not burden them with straining their souls by abandoning the good things they desire, nor with blinding their conscience from perceiving things as they truly are, of the goodness of good and the ugliness of ugly, nor from the turning of desire towards what is good in their sight when that is within the limits of permissibility, nor did He burden them with observing the inclinations of people, their conventions and customs which lead to deviating from matters from their proper paths. For in their pursuit of their permissible desires there is help for them to be energetic in conveying the messages of Allah. For this reason He followed it with His saying ﴿and fear none but Allah﴾, i.e., they do not fear anyone with a fear that requires doing or abandoning something.

Then, the clause ﴿Those who convey﴾ to its end may be in the position of a qualifier of ﴿those who passed on before﴾, i.e., the prophets. Since it is known that the Prophet ﷺ follows what Allah permitted him to follow of the sunnah of the prophets before him, it is known that he is characterized by the content of the clause ﴿Those who convey the messages of Allah and fear Him and fear none but Allah﴾ by the rule of analogy of equality. So it is known that the fear mentioned in His saying ﴿and you feared the people﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37] is not the fear of dread that necessitates abandoning what people dislike or doing what they desire, such that people would be taking account of the Prophet ﷺ; rather it is an anticipation that the people, namely the hypocrites, might do what the Prophet ﷺ dislikes. This is indicated by His saying ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner﴾, i.e., Allah alone is the Reckoner of the prophets, and no other.

This is the proper way of explaining these verses. So do not take a path in the meaning of the verse that leads you to suppose that the Prophet ﷺ experienced fear of people, and that Allah alluded to him with His saying ﴿and fear none but Allah﴾ explicitly after having alluded to him implicitly in His saying ﴿and you feared the people﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. Rather, the Prophet ﷺ did not concern himself with them and proceeded to marry Zaynab; all of that was before the revelation of these verses, which were only revealed after the marriage to Zaynab, as is clear from His saying "We married her to you," and it was not delayed until the revelation of this verse.

The mention of the divine name Allah in the place of a pronoun in His saying ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner﴾, where its mention had already preceded, is for the purpose that this sentence should function as a proverb and a maxim.

And since this is the description of the prophets, there is no room in the verse for the objection based on the question of taqiyya in His saying (except when you fear from them a fear) [Al 'Imran: 28].

Since it is known that the Prophet ﷺ follows what Allah permitted him to follow of the sunnah of the prophets before him, it is known that he is characterized by the content of the clause ﴿Those who convey the messages of Allah and fear Him and fear none but Allah﴾ by the rule of analogy of equality. So it is known that the fear mentioned in His saying ﴿and you feared the people﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37] is not the fear of dread that necessitates abandoning what people dislike or doing what they desire, such that people would be taking account of the Prophet ﷺ; rather it is an anticipation that the people, namely the hypocrites, might do what the Prophet ﷺ dislikes. This is indicated by His saying ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner﴾, i.e., Allah alone is the Reckoner of the prophets, and no other.

This is the proper way of explaining these verses. So do not take a path in the meaning of the verse that leads you to suppose that the Prophet ﷺ experienced fear of people, and that Allah alluded to him with His saying ﴿and fear none but Allah﴾ explicitly after having alluded to him implicitly in His saying ﴿and you feared the people﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. Rather, the Prophet ﷺ did not concern himself with them and proceeded to marry Zaynab; all of that was before the revelation of these verses, which were only revealed after the marriage to Zaynab, as is clear from His saying "We married her to you," and it was not delayed until the revelation of this verse.

The mention of the divine name Allah in the place of a pronoun in His saying ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner﴾, where its mention had already preceded, is for the purpose that this sentence should function as a proverb and a maxim.

And since this is the description of the prophets, there is no room in the verse for the objection based on the question of taqiyya in His saying (except when you fear from them a fear) [Al 'Imran: 28].

[The passage begins mid-commentary; the first sentence is Ibn 'Ashur's comment on the verse.]

﴿Muhammad is not the father of any man among you, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets, and Allah is ever Knowing of all things.﴾

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) to state explicitly the refutation of the claims of the hypocrites, of those in whose hearts is a disease, and of the doubts that the Jews cast into their souls.

It refers to His saying, ﴿nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4]. The purpose of this generality is to cut off the suspicion that the Prophet (ﷺ) might have a male child whose rulings of prophethood would apply to him, so that rumour and fabrication would not reach those among the Muslims who might marry his wives after him, such as Umm Salamah and Hafsah.

The phrase "among you" (min rijalikum) is a qualifier of "any man" (ahad), and it is a precaution, because the Prophet (ﷺ) had daughters. The intended meaning is the negation of his being the father of any man at the time of the revelation of this verse. For he had had children, or two children, by Khadijah in Mecca, namely al-Tayyib and al-Tahir (or they were two names for one person), and al-Qasim, and Ibrahim was born to him in Medina by Mariyah the Copt. All of them died as infants, and none of them was alive at the time of the revelation of this verse.

What is negated is the attribute of direct fatherhood, because it is the purpose for which the statement was made, and it is the point about which whoever erred did err. Therefore, no attention should be paid to his being a grandfather to al-Hasan, al-Husayn and Muhsin, the sons of his daughter Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, since that is not the intended meaning. Nor does it occur to anyone to negate his fatherhood of them in the higher sense (of spiritual fatherhood), or the intended meaning is fatherhood of the loins, to the exclusion of fatherhood of kinship.

The idafah (construction) of "men" (rijal) to the pronoun of the addressees, and the departure from defining it with the article (al-), is intended to direct the address to those who were engaged in the matter of Zaynab's marriage, so that the speech takes the form of rebuke and severe admonition.

As for the interpretation that it is like a precaution against his grandchildren, and that he said "among your men" while his grandchildren are among his men, this is an insipid interpretation. It would imply in the speech a suggestion that Muhammad (ﷺ) is free of the addressees, namely the hypocrites, and that there is no bond between him and them resembling the bond of fatherhood, established by way of the implication of the address in His saying, ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6], as has been explained earlier.

The istidrak (corrective conjunction) of His saying, ﴿but the Messenger of Allah﴾, serves to remove what might be suspected from the negation of his fatherhood, namely the severing of the bond of mercy and kindness between him and the Ummah. So they are reminded that he is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and so he is like a father to all his Ummah in his compassion and mercy toward them, and in their kindness to him and their reverence for him, as is the case of every prophet with his people.

The waw that enters upon "but" (lakin) is additional, and "lakin" is coordinating. "Lakin" has not occurred in the speech of the Arabs as a coordinating particle except when accompanied by waw, as al-Muradi stated explicitly in his commentary on al-Tashil. The particle "lakin" conveys istidrak.

The coordination of the description "Seal of the Prophets" to the description "Messenger of Allah" is a completion and an addition in exalting his station (ﷺ), and an allusion that in the negation of his fatherhood of any man there is a wisdom which Allah Most High has decreed, namely the intention that he should be only like the Messengers or better than them in all his distinctive qualities.

Since the Messengers have had the line of their sons never free of a prophet, his being the Seal of the Prophets required that he should have no sons after his death. For if they had been alive after his death and had not been invested with the mantle of prophethood, because the seal of prophethood was with him, that would have been a reproach against him in comparison with the other Messengers, and that is not what Allah intends for him. Do you not see that when Allah intended to end prophethood among the Children of Israel after 'Isa (peace be upon him), He turned 'Isa away from marriage?

So do not make His saying, ﴿and the Seal of the Prophets﴾, fall within the scope of the istidrak, for you know that it is a completion and a digression occasioned by the attaching of the description of messengerhood to him. And by explaining the wisdom, the excellence of the placement of the concluding clause ﴿and Allah is ever Knowing of all things﴾ becomes apparent, since it manifests what His wisdom requires in what He has decreed of the destinies, as in His saying, ﴿Allah made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of standing for mankind﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 97], up to His saying, ﴿that you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth, and that Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 97].

The verse is a clear text that Muhammad (ﷺ) is the Seal of the Prophets, and that there is no prophet after him among mankind, because "the Prophets" is a general term, so "Seal of the Prophets" means their seal in the attribute of prophethood. The fact that the generality's indication of individuals is speculative (zanni) does not undermine the definitiveness of the verse, because that is due to the possibility of the existence of a specifier. We have verified the absence of a specifier through inductive survey.

The Companions have agreed (ijma') that Muhammad (ﷺ) is the Seal of the Messengers and the Prophets, and this was known and widely transmitted among them and in the generations after them. For this reason they did not hesitate to declare Musaylimah and al-Aswad al-'Ansi to be apostates. It became known as a matter of religion by necessity (ma'lum min al-din bil-darurah), so whoever denies it is a disbeliever who has left Islam, even if he acknowledges that Muhammad (ﷺ) is the Messenger of Allah to all mankind.

This category is outside the disagreement of some scholars over the authority of ijma', since what is disputed as to its authority is the ijma' that rests on reasoning and interpretive evidence, unlike the widely transmitted matter known necessarily. This contradicts al-Ghazali's statement at the end of his book al-Iqtisad fi al-I'tiqad, despite its lack of precise exposition. Ibn 'Atiyyah attacked him with an unjust attack and imposed on him a gross implication from which his knowledge and religion are exempt. May Allah have mercy on both of them.

For this reason, no Muslim hesitates to declare disbelief in anyone who affirms prophethood for anyone after Muhammad (ﷺ), and to expel him from the fold of Islam. No group of Muslims is known to have undertaken this except the Babis and the Baha'is, and the second of these two sects is derived from the first. The emergence of the first sect was in the land of Persia around the year 1200 [AH, i.e., the 1780s–1840s CE: the Bab's claims date to 1260 AH, so the sentence is as in the source], and it spread to Iraq. Its leader was a man from Shiraz whose followers called him "al-Sayyid 'Ali Muhammad" (this is the name by which he became known). At the beginning of his affair he was among the extremist Imami Shi'ah. He took from a man of the Sufis named Shaykh Ahmad Zayn al-Din al-Ahsa'i, who professed Sufism by the esoteric path (al-tariqah al-batiniyyah), which is the path received from al-Hallaj. His path was known as the Shaykhiyyah. When this 'Ali Muhammad made his sect public, he titled himself "Bab al-'Ilm" (Gate of Knowledge), and so the name "al-Bab" (the Gate) came to dominate him. His sect became known as the Babiyyah, and he claimed prophethood for himself, and he asserted that a book named "al-Bayan" had been revealed to him, and that the Qur'an had alluded to him in His saying, ﴿He created man, taught him eloquence﴾ [al-Rahman: 3].

The Book of al-Bayan is composed in weak Arabic and mixed with Persian. He was sentenced to death in the year 1266 [AH] in Tabriz.

As for the Baha'iyyah, they are a branch of the Babiyyah, attributed to its founder, who was titled Baha' Allah, and whose name was Mirza Husayn 'Ali, from the people of Tehran. He became a pupil of the Bab by correspondence. The government of the Shah of Persia expelled him to Baghdad after the killing of the Bab. Then the Ottoman state transferred him from Baghdad to Edirne, then to Acre, and there his sect appeared. They believe in the prophethood of the Bab, and the followers of the Babi sect gathered around him and made him the successor (khalifah) of the Bab. So the name Baha'iyyah took the place of the name Babiyyah, and thus the Baha'is are the Babis. Baha' had built a structure on Mount Carmel to make it a burial place for the remains of the Bab. His affair ended with the Ottoman Sultanate imprisoning him in the prison of Acre, where he remained for seven years. He was not released from prison until the Turkish constitution was proclaimed, and he was among the political prisoners who were released on that day. He then travelled, moving through Europe and America for two years, then returned to Haifa and settled there until he died in the year 1340 [AH]. After his death, a dispute arose among his sons and brothers, they split over leadership, and his sect dwindled.

So whoever among the Muslims follows the Baha'iyyah or the Babiyyah has left Islam and apostatized from his religion, and the rulings of the apostate apply to him. He does not inherit from a Muslim, and the community of Muslims inherits from him. Their saying, "We are Muslims," and their pronouncing of the testimony of faith (shahadah), do not benefit them, because they affirm the messengerhood of Muhammad (ﷺ), but they assert the coming of a messenger after him. We have declared the Ghurabiyyah among the Shi'ah to be disbelievers, because of their saying that Gabriel was sent to 'Ali, but he was mistaken, so that Muhammad was confused with 'Ali, since one of them resembled the other as one crow resembles another (and they lied). Then he delivered the message to Muhammad (ﷺ). So they affirmed the messengerhood of Muhammad (ﷺ), but they claimed that it was an unspecified person sent by Allah.

The rituals of the Baha'iyyah resemble the rituals of Freemasonry, except that the Baha'iyyah claim to receive from divine revelation, and by this they differ from Freemasonry, and so they are counted among the religions and creeds, and are not counted among the political parties.

The phrase "Messenger of Allah" (rasul Allah) is in the accusative as a coordination with "any man among your men" (ahadin min rijalikum), by coordination with the waw that accompanies "lakin", to convey the lifting of the negation that entered upon the governing element of the coordinated term.

The majority of readers recite "wa-khatima al-nabiyyin" with a kasrah on the ta' of "khatim", as an active participle from "khatama". 'Asim recited it with a fathah on the ta', by likening it to the seal (khatam) with which a written document is sealed, in that its appearance was a closing of prophethood.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 33, verses 41–42:**

﴿O you who have believed, remember Allah with much remembrance﴾ ﴿And exalt Him morning and evening.﴾ This is an address to the believers, directing them to occupy their tongues with the remembrance of Allah and His glorification. That is, they should refrain from disputing with the hypocrites, or from reviling them, concerning what they spread as rumour about the matter of Zaynab's marriage. So He commanded the believers to take, in exchange for that, the remembrance of Allah and His glorification, which is better for them. This is like His saying, ﴿So when you have completed your rites, remember Allah as you remember your fathers or with a more intense remembrance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200], that is, better than boasting about the remembrance of your fathers and your lineages. That is more beneficial for them and further from a turmoil of sedition arising in Madinah between the Muslims and the hypocrites. This is of the same kind as His saying to His Prophet, ﴿And leave off their harm﴾ [al-Ahzab: 48], and of the same kind as His saying, ﴿And do not revile those they invoke other than Allah, lest they revile Allah in enmity without knowledge﴾ [al-An'am: 108]. So they were commanded to employ their tongues and their times in what returns to their benefit, and to avoid whatever might lead to harm.

In this verse there is also a record against the hypocrites, that their immersion in that matter after this verse is a sign of hypocrisy, because the believers do not oppose the command of their Lord.

The sentence is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) connected to what precedes it, for the reason we have indicated.

Page 48

The remembrance (al-dhikr) here is remembrance by the tongue, which is the one suited to the position of the verse with respect to what comes before and after it.

Glorification (al-tasbih) may be intended to mean the voluntary prayers (nawafil). In that case, the conjunction of ﴿and exalt Him﴾ with ﴿remember Allah﴾ is not a conjunction of the particular over the general (ʿatf al-khass ʿala al-ʿamm, the specific being joined to the general).

It is also possible that what is commanded of glorification is the saying "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to Allah). In that case the conjunction of ﴿and exalt Him﴾ with ﴿remember Allah﴾ is a conjunction of the particular over the general, for the sake of giving attention to the particular. The meaning of tasbih is declaring Allah free from whatever is not befitting for Him of deficiencies. It is therefore among the most complete forms of remembrance, because it comprises the comprehensive forms of praise and glorification. Moreover, in glorification there is an allusion to disavowing what the hypocrites say concerning the Prophet ﷺ. It thus carries the sense of His saying, ﴿Why, when you heard it, did you not say, "It is not for us to speak of this. Glory be to You! This is a great slander"?﴾ [al-Nur: 16]. The phrase "Subhan Allah" is frequently said in a context of disavowing the attribution of something unfitting to anyone, such as the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, "Glory be to Allah! The believer does not become impure." And such as the saying of Hind bint 'Utbah when the Prophet ﷺ took the pledge from the women (that they would not commit fornication): "Glory be to Allah! Does a free woman commit fornication?"

Al-Bukrah means the beginning of the day, and al-Asil means the evening, the time after 'Asr. Both are in the accusative of time (zarfiyyah), which both verbs govern: ﴿remember Allah﴾ and ﴿exalt Him﴾.

The purpose of mentioning the morning and evening is to fill the parts of the day with remembrance and glorification to the extent of one's capacity. Mentioning the two extremes of a thing is a metonymy (kinayah) for encompassing the whole of it, as in the verse of Tarafah:

*Like the stretched rope and its twisted strands in the hand*

From this is the common saying "the East and the West," as a metonymy for the whole earth, and "the head and the heel" as a metonymy for the whole body, and "the back and the belly" likewise.

He placed al-Bukrah before al-Asil because the morning is necessarily earlier than the evening. The evening does not deserve to be placed first in mention, as the word ﴿you enter the evening﴾ (tumsun) was placed first in His saying in Surah al-Rum: ﴿So glory be to Allah when you reach the evening and when you reach the morning﴾ [al-Rum: 17]. This is because the word al-masa' includes the beginning of the night, so the word (tumsun) was placed first there, out of regard for the night being earlier in the reckoning of the days of the month among the Arabs and in Islam. The word al-Asil does not have this feature.

صفحة ٤٩
﴿He it is who sends blessings upon you, and His angels, that He may bring you out of darkness into light. And He is ever merciful to the believers.﴾

This is a justification (ta'līl) for the command to remember Allah and glorify Him: that such remembrance is a means for the believers to benefit from Allah's recompense for it, with something better of its own kind, namely His blessing (ṣalāh) upon them and the blessing of His angels. The meaning is: He blesses you, and His angels bless you, when you remember Him with remembrance morning and evening.

The placing of the subject (hu) before the predicate verb in His words ﴿He it is who sends blessings upon you﴾ serves to affirm and confirm the ruling. The aim is to establish what is connected to the verb yuṣallī (sends blessings) in the statement that follows, "that He may bring you out of darkness into light."

Ṣalāh (blessing, ṣalāh) means supplication and mention of someone with goodness, and when it comes from Allah it means praise. He commanded him to direct His mercy in this world and the Hereafter; that is, "Remember Him, so that He may remember you," in accordance with His words, "So remember Me, and I will remember you," and His words in the sacred hadith: "If he remembers Me within himself, I remember him within Myself; and if he remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than theirs."

The blessing of the angels is their supplication for the believers, so their supplication is answered by Allah, and it increases those who remember Him beyond what He has given them through His own blessing upon them. The verb (yuṣallī) is attributed both to Allah and to His angels, because the conjunction particle indicates the sharing of the conjoined and the conjoined-to in the governing element. It is thus a single governing element with two objects, and it is used for the common meaning that suits both the blessing of Allah the Exalted and the blessing of the angels, which applies to each in a manner fitting to it, according to the necessary implications of the meaning of blessing, which takes on the form appropriate to the one to whom it is attributed.

There is no need to claim the use of a homonym (mushtarak) in both its meanings, since there is no barrier to this according to the more correct view, nor to claim the generality of the metaphor. The use of (yuṣallī) in the present tense indicates the recurrence and renewal of the blessing whenever remembrance and glorification are renewed, or indicates its renewal according to other causes from the deeds of the believers and in consideration of their faith.

The introduction of the relative pronoun (alladhī) indicates that He, the Exalted, is known to them by the content of the relative clause according to common usage: either because Muslims know in general terms that no good reaches them except from Allah the Exalted, so every detail of that generality falls within their knowledge, and among it that He blesses them and commands His angels to do so; or because knowledge of this in detail had preceded for them earlier. Some verses of the Qur'an, such as His words, "The angels glorify their Lord with His praise and ask forgiveness for those on earth" (Ash-Shura: 5), indicate that the angels' seeking forgiveness for the believers is by a command from Allah the Exalted, based on His words, "There is no intercessor except after His permission," and supplication for someone is among the forms of intercession for him. Moreover, among the content of the relative clause is that His angels bless the believers. This is known from many verses. It may also be that this was conveyed by the Prophet (ﷺ) to the believers before the revelation of this verse, and the meaning is supported by His words after it, "And He is ever merciful to the believers," as will come shortly.

The lām in His words "that He may bring you out of darkness" is connected to (yuṣallī). Thus it is known that this blessing is an immediate reward, occurring at the time of their remembrance and glorification.

By "darkness" is meant misguidance, and by "light" guidance. By bringing them out of darkness is meant the continuation of that and seeking increase of it, because when they were believers they had already come out of darkness into light (and Allah increases those who are guided in guidance).

The clause "And He is ever merciful to the believers" is a concluding statement (tadhyīl).

By informing of His mercy toward the believers, using the verb (kāna) and its predicate inserted, there is indicated what the verb kāna requires of the establishment of that predicate for Him, the Exalted, and its confirmation, and that this is one of His attributes known through it in many verses.

His mercy toward the believers is more general than His blessing upon them, because it includes conferring benefit upon them and bringing good to them through words, deeds and kindnesses.

Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be "Peace," and He has prepared for them a generous reward.

This sentence follows the immediate reward that the verse "It is He who sends blessings upon you, and His angels" pointed to, by mentioning a deferred reward: the manifestation of the effect of the deeds they performed in this world, and the effect of the recompense He hastened for them, through His honour for them on the Day they meet their Lord.

So the sentence completes what came before it, to convey that Allah's blessings and those of His angels take place both in the present life and in the Hereafter.

And the tahiyyah (greeting) is the speech addressed at the beginning of an encounter, expressing joy at the meeting, consisting of a supplication or the like. This term is originally a verbal noun of "hayyahu," when one says to him, "Ahyaka Allah," meaning, "May Allah prolong your life." Thus the speech expressing the seeking of good for the one met, or praise of him, was called by this name, because it was customary to say "Ahyaka Allah" at the beginning of an encounter, so its name was applied to every supplication and praise said at a meeting. The greeting of Islam is "Salamun 'alayka" or "As-salamu 'alaykum," a supplication for safety and security, that is, from what is disliked, because safety is the best thing sought in life. So when Allah grants a person life but does not grant him safety, life becomes pain and evil. For this reason, the greeting of the believers on the Day of Resurrection is "Salam," as good tidings of safety from the awesome terrors that people witness awaiting them. Likewise, the greeting of the people of Paradise among themselves is a delight in naming what they are in of safety from the terrors of the people of the Fire. This was already discussed in His saying "and their greeting therein will be 'Peace'" in Surah Yunus.

The attribution of the greeting to the pronoun of the believers is an idafah of a verbal noun to its object, meaning a greeting with which they are greeted.

And the meeting with Allah is the presence from the sphere of His holiness for reckoning at the gathering place. This was discussed in detail at His saying, Exalted is He, "and know that you will meet Him," in Surah al-Baqarah. This meeting is common to all people, as Exalted is He said, "So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him." Allah distinguishes the believers that day by the greeting, as an honour for them.

The clause "and He has prepared for them a generous reward" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the Majesty, meaning: He greets them on the Day they meet Him, while having prepared for them a generous reward. The meaning: among His mercy toward them is that He began them with what contains good tidings of safety, and He has prepared for them a generous reward, completing His mercy toward them.

Al-ajr is the reward. Al-karim is the precious of its kind, and it was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He, "Indeed, there has been delivered to me a noble letter," in Surah al-Naml. The generous reward is the bliss of Paradise.

﴿O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good news, and a warner﴾ ﴿and as one who calls to Allah by His permission, and as a illuminating lamp﴾.

This is the third address to the Prophet (ﷺ). When Allah had conveyed to him, in the first address, what concerns his own person, and in the second, what concerns his wives and the duties and reminders that lie between them, He addressed him with attributes that He placed in him to honour his station, to raise his rank, and to set out for him the pillars of his mission. Allah the Exalted said, confirming what is before it of the Book and as a guardian over it. In the hadith of the Gathering: "He will ask every messenger, 'Did you convey?' He will say, 'Yes.'
