[Page 53]

The bringer of good news (mubashshir) is one who informs of glad tidings (bushra and bishara). These are an event that gladdens the one informed of it, and a promise of a gift. The Prophet (ﷺ) brings good news to the people of faith and to the obedient of the degrees of their success. This attribute also includes what the Law contains of calling to good through commands. This is the category of compliance (imtithal) from the two categories of piety (taqwa), for piety is compliance with what is commanded and avoidance of what is forbidden. What is commanded contains benefits, so it entails the good news for its doers of a good condition in this world and in the next.

The good news is mentioned before the warning because the Prophet (ﷺ) was predominantly characterised by giving good news, since he is a mercy to the worlds, and because of the great number of believers in his community.

The warner (nadhir) is derived from warning (inzar), which is informing of the arrival of an event that is harmful or of its imminent arrival. The Prophet (peace be upon him) is a warner to those who oppose his religion, from among disbelievers and from among the people of disobedience, according to the varying degrees of their accountability for their deeds.

(Shahidan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the kaf of address, and it is a prospective circumstance (hal muqaddarah). That is: We have sent you, intending that you be a witness over the messengers and the nations in this world and in the Hereafter. Sibawayh gave as an example of the prospective circumstance his saying: "I passed by a man with a falcon, hunting with it."

In the case of warning, the pattern fa'il is used rather than the active participle (ism al-fa'il), to indicate the noun-status, for nadhir in their speech is a name for one who informs of the enemy's arrival at the dwellings of a people. From the proverbs: "I am the naked warner," that is, the one who brings news of the enemy's arrival at the dwellings of the people. "Naked" means that he strips off his shirt to signal from a high place, so that whoever cannot hear his call sees him. So the attribute "warner" is an image of the condition of the warner of a people, as He said: ﴿He is only a warner to you before a severe punishment﴾ [Saba: 46], to suggest the confirmation of what he warned them of, until it is as if it has already befallen them, and as if the one reporting it is reporting an event that has already occurred. This is not conveyed except by the name nadhir, and therefore the attribute "nadhir" occurs often in the Qur'an, while the attribute "mundhir" occurs rarely.

(a word by which one calls for help). They gathered to him, and he said: "Tell me, if I informed you that horsemen would come out from the foot of this mountain, would you believe me?" They said, "Yes." He said: "Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment." This points to the image of the situation which he drew out in his saying "Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment." And in "before a severe punishment" is the sense of nearness.

The name "warner" encompasses the comprehensive prohibitions and penalties in the Law, and this is the category of avoidance from the two categories of piety, for prohibited things contain corruptions, so they entail the frightening of those who proceed to do them of a bad condition in this world and the next.

The original meaning of da'a-hu ila fulan is that he invited him to come into his presence. One says: "Call so-and-so to me." Since it is known that Allah the Exalted is exempt from a direction where people can be present with Him, it is established that the meaning of calling to Him is calling to abandon acknowledging other than Him, just as they say: "Abu Muslim al-Khurasani calls to the satisfaction of the Family of the House," [meaning calling for allegiance to them]. So this attribute includes the foundations of belief in the Law of Islam that relate to the attributes of Allah, because calling to Allah is calling to knowing Him, and what relates to the attributes of those who call to Him, namely the prophets, the messengers, and the revealed books.

The addition of "by His permission" (bi-idhnihi) is to convey that Allah sent him as one who calls to Him, and facilitated for him the calling to Him, despite the heaviness of this call and the greatness of its gravity. This is what the Prophet (ﷺ) had sensed at the beginning of revelation of apprehension, until there was revealed to him ﴿O you who are wrapped up, arise and warn﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1]. That is: We have sent you as a lamp that is bright in the clear guidance, in which there is no confusion, and which leaves no doubt for falsehood without exposing it and making people stand on its hidden secrets, just as a blazing lamp lights the darkness of a place. This attribute includes what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought of clarification and clarifying reasoning, and the dispersing of what came before him of religions, of paths of alteration and distortion. It encompasses what is in the Law of the foundations of deduction (istinbat) and of understanding (tafaqquh) in religion and knowledge, for knowledge is likened to light, so the illuminating lamp fits it. This attribute is comprehensive of all the attributes that were described before, so it is like a summary (fadhlaka) and like a concluding appendix (tadhyil).

[Page 54]

The lamp was described as "illuminating" (munir), although illumination is a necessary property of a lamp. This is like describing a thing with an attribute derived from its own word, as in the expression "a poet's poetry" (shi'r sha'ir) and "a very dark night" (layl alyal), to give the emphasis of the meaning of the noun in the particular thing described by it, for the guidance of the Prophet (ﷺ) is the clearest guidance, and his guidance is the most eloquent guidance.

Al-Bukhari related in the Book of Tafsir of his Sahih, in the commentary on Surat al-Fath, from Ata ibn Yasar, that Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As said: "This verse in the Qur'an, ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good news, and a warner﴾, is mentioned in the Torah: 'O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good news and a warner, and a guardian for the unlettered. You are My servant and My messenger; I have named you the one who relies (al-mutawakkil). He is not harsh, nor coarse, nor loud in the markets, and he does not repel evil with evil, but rather he pardons and overlooks (or forgives), and Allah will not take him until through him He sets right the crooked religion, by their saying: There is no god but Allah, and He opens (or he opens) through him blind eyes, deaf ears, and veiled hearts.'" End of quotation.

Abdullah ibn Amr's saying "in the Torah," by "the Torah" he means: the books of the Torah and what goes with it of the books of the prophets, since such a thing is not found in what I have seen of the five original books of the Torah. In Chapter 42 of it: "Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen one in whom my soul delights; I have put my spirit upon him, and he will bring forth justice to the nations. He will not cry out, nor lift up, nor will his voice be heard in the street. A bruised reed he will not break, and a dimly burning wick he will not quench; he will bring forth justice to truth. He will not fail nor be discouraged until he has set justice in the earth, and the coastlands will wait for his law. I am the LORD; I have called you in righteousness, and I will hold your hand and keep you, and make you a covenant for the people and a light for the nations, to open the eyes of the blind, to bring out the prisoners from the prison, those who sit in darkness. I am the LORD; this is my name, and my glory I will not give to another."

"You are My servant and My messenger": ﴿Praise be to Allah, who revealed the Book to His servant﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], Surat al-Kahf. "I have named you the one who relies": ﴿And rely upon Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 48], Surat al-Ahzab. "He is not harsh, nor coarse": ﴿And if you had been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159], Surat Al 'Imran. "But rather he pardons and overlooks": ﴿So pardon them and overlook﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 13], Surat al-'Uqud [the Ma'idah]. Let us mention here what is in the book of Isaiah, and insert in it an explanation of the comparison of its words with the words that came in the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr.

A bruised reed he shall not break, (nor repel evil with evil), and smoking flax he shall not quench (he pardons and forgives). He will faithfully bring forth judgment (and a protection). I am the LORD; I have called you in righteousness, and I will hold your hand (I named you "the one who relies" (al-Mutawakkil)) and keep you (and God will not take him), and I will give you as a covenant to the people (we sent you as a witness) (and a light to the nations) (a bringer of good news) to open the eyes of the blind (and through him we open blind eyes), to bring the prisoners out of the prison, and those who sit in darkness out of the house of confinement (and deaf ears) (and hearts uncircumcised). I am the LORD; that is my name, and my glory I will not give to another (that they should say, "There is no god but God").

﴿And give good tidings to the believers that they will have from Allah a great bounty.﴾ It is coordinated with the clause "Indeed, We have sent you," conjoining an imperative clause (*'atf al-insha' 'ala al-khabar*, the coordination of a performative/imperative clause onto a declarative one) to a declarative clause, without doubt. It is the clearest evidence for the soundness of coordinating an imperative clause onto a declarative one, since no interpretation of the kind that the opponents of this coordination (*al-mani'un*) gave can be applied to it. These opponents are the majority of scholars (*al-Jumhur*), al-Zamakhshari, and al-Taftazani, and I will mention their view, God willing, when discussing the verse ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Saff: 11] up to His saying ﴿and give good tidings to the believers﴾ [al-Saff: 13] in Surat al-Saff. Thus the clause that is coordinated onto is a report about the Prophet (ﷺ) that Allah sent him possessing these five qualities. This is a command to him to act in the capacity of one who gives good tidings. Because the contents of the two clauses differ, this one is coordinated onto the first.

Al-fadl (bounty) is the gift which the giver increases beyond the gift itself. Thus *al-fadl* is also a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the gift, since it is not a bounty unless it exceeds the gift. The meaning is that they will have the reward of their deeds, which has been promised to them, and an increase from their Lord. Allah the Exalted says:

﴿For those who have done good is the best [reward] and an increase.﴾ [Yunus: 26]

The description "great" (*kathiran*) is used metaphorically for what surpasses others of its kind. Ibn 'Atiyya said: My father (may Allah be pleased with him) said to me: "This is the verse I hope for most in the Book of Allah, because Allah has commanded His Prophet to give good tidings to the believers that they will have with Him a great bounty." Allah the Exalted has explained what this great bounty is in His saying: (﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds will be in the gardens of paradise; they will have whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the great bounty.﴾ [al-Shura: 22]). So the verse in this surah is a report, and the verse in (Ha Mim 'Ayn Sin Qaf) is an explanation of it. End of quotation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 48:

[p. 58]
﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and disregard their harm, and rely upon Allah. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾

It comes in contrast to His saying "and give good tidings to the believers," by His saying "and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites," as a warning to him against agreeing with them in what they ask of him, and as a confirmation of his action toward them when the hypocrites asked his permission to withdraw from the confederates (al-Ahzab), and he did not grant them permission. So he was forbidden from giving ear to what they desire, lest he abandon what was made lawful for him of marriage, or lest he give the disbelieving confederates a portion of the dates of the palm-trees as a settlement, or the like. The prohibition is used to express the sense of perpetual abstention (al-dawam ʿala al-intiha').

It is known from the contrast of the command to give good tidings to the believers with the prohibition against obeying the disbelievers and the hypocrites that the disbelievers and the hypocrites are the object of the warning in His saying "and a warner" (nadhiran), because the description "a bearer of good tidings" (bashiran) has already taken its object, so this has come to correspond to His saying "and a warner."

His saying "and disregard their harm" (wa da' adhahum) may be understood in two ways. It may be that the verb "da'" (disregard/leave) is intended to mean that he should not punish them, so that "da'" is used in its literal sense, and the idafa of "adhahum" is an idafa of the verbal noun to its object, i.e., leave your harming of them. It may also be that "da'" is used figuratively to mean not caring about and not being distressed by what they say that is hurtful, and the idafa of "adhahum" is an idafa of the verbal noun to its agent, i.e., do not concern yourself with the harm that proceeds from them toward you, for you are too exalted for preoccupation with that. This is the use of a word in both its literal and figurative senses. Most of the exegetes restricted themselves to this last possibility. The correct view is to take both meanings together, so that the command to leave their harm covers both turning away from the hurtful speech with which they harm the Prophet ﷺ and refraining from retaliating against them. That is, the Prophet ﷺ should rise above calling them to account for what proceeds from them concerning him. This is a turning away from a particular harm, with no general scope, and it is thus like the definite article of prior mention (al-ʿahd); therefore the verses on fighting do not abrogate it (naskh).

This implies that he leaves off harming them and leaves them to a deferred punishment, and this is part of the meaning of His saying "as a witness" (shahidan), since he bears witness against them by this, like His saying "so turn away from them for a while and watch them."

Al-tawakkul: reliance and entrusting the management of affairs to Allah. It has already been discussed at His saying, exalted is He, "So when you have resolved, then rely upon Allah" [Al 'Imran: 159] in Surat Al 'Imran, and His saying "And upon Allah rely, if you are believers" [al-Ma'idah: 23]

[p. 59]
in Surat al-'Uqud, that is: rely upon Allah in conveying the message and in His sufficiency for you against the evil of your enemy. This corresponds to His saying "and as one who calls to Allah" [al-Ahzab: 46]. His saying "and sufficient is Allah as Disposer" is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) for the clause "and rely upon Allah."
The meaning: indeed Allah is the Disposer who suffices in agency, that is, the one who grants to whoever relies upon Him what he has entrusted to Him. The "ba'" is for emphasis. His saying "and sufficient is Allah as Disposer" has been discussed in Surat al-Nisa' [81]. The implied sense is: "Allah suffices." "Wakilan" is a specifier (tamyiz).

Thus these imperative clauses come in correspondence with and as counterparts to the declarative clauses from His saying "Indeed We have sent you as a witness" through "and as a light-giving lamp." So His saying "and give good tidings to the believers" corresponds to His saying "and a bearer of good tidings."

His saying "and do not obey the disbelievers" corresponds to His saying "and a warner," because it came in contrast to the good tidings for the believers, as has preceded.

His saying "and disregard their harm" corresponds to His saying "as a witness," as you have known. His saying "and rely upon Allah" corresponds to His saying "and as one who calls to Allah" [al-Ahzab: 46]. As for His saying "and as a light-giving lamp" [al-Ahzab: 46], no counterpart is mentioned for it among these demands, except that since it is like a concluding phrase for the attributes, as has preceded, it is fitting that it be matched by what serves as a concluding phrase for the demands, namely His saying "and sufficient is Allah as Disposer." This is closer than some of what is in al-Kashshaf of the aspects of correspondence, and than some of what is in al-Alusi. So look into both and judge.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 49:

﴿O you who have believed, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, you have no right to count [any] waiting period for them that you should compute. So provide for them and release them with a fair release.﴾

This verse came as legislation on the ruling for divorced women before consummation, that they are not obligated to observe a waiting period ('idda), on the occasion of the divorce of Zayd ibn Harithah from his wife Zaynab bint Jahsh, so that the verse would specify (mukhassisa) the verses of the waiting period in Surat al-Baqarah, since al-Ahzab was revealed after al-Baqarah. It also specifies the verse of the waiting period in Surat al-Talaq, which was revealed after it, lest someone suppose that the waiting period is among the effects of the contract on the woman, whether or not the husband had consummated it. Ibn al-'Arabi said: The scholars of the Community have unanimously agreed that there is no waiting period for a woman whose husband has not consummated the marriage with her, on account of this verse.

Al-nikah (marriage) is: the contract between a man and a woman making her a spouse through her guardian (wali). It is literally (haqiqa) used for the contract, because the original meaning of nikah in its literal sense is joining and attaching. The contract of marriage was likened to attachment and joining, given that it involves considering the union of the man and the woman, so that they become like two connected things. This is just as both are called spouses (zawj). It is not known in the speech of the Arabs that nikah is applied to anything other than the meaning of the contract, not the meaning of intercourse (wat'). Hence they say: "The woman married (nakahat) so-and-so," meaning she married him, just as they say: "So-and-so married (nakaha) a woman." Many compilers of lexicography claimed that nikah is literally the insertion of one thing into another, and from this they took that it is literally used for intercourse. Al-Azhari, al-Jawhari and al-Zamakhshari followed this, but it is far-fetched. Based on what they built, al-Mutanabbi erred in his usage when he said:

"I married the hard stones of its gravel to the hooves of a swift she-camel, which bore me forcibly to you across the plain and the mountain."

There is no proof in his words. For this reason Abu al-'Ala al-Ma'arri interpreted it in his commentary on Mu'jiz Ahmad as meaning: I joined the deaf stones and the soft hooves of the swift she-camel.

The ruling on the waiting period is linked to "believing women" in accordance with what is usual, because the wives of the believers at that time were not all believers, and there were no People of the Book among them. This ruling extends to the women of the People of the Book, just as the ruling of 'idda is included for them when intercourse has occurred, by means of analogy (qiyas).

Al-massu and al-masis: a metaphor (kinaya) for intercourse, just as touching (mulamasa) is called so in His words: "or you have touched women" [al-Nisa': 43]. Al-'idda, with a kasra on the 'ayn, is originally the noun of the form (ism hay'a) from al-'add, with a fatha on the 'ayn, meaning counting. The term 'idda was then applied to the counted thing, as one says: "a number (idda) of men came," and God the Exalted said: "then a number (fa-'idda) of other days" [al-Baqarah: 184]. In the language of the Shari'a, this term came to be used predominantly for the specified period during which a woman waits before a second marriage, because her waiting is a period of countable durations, either by specification or by what occurs in it of a purity or the delivery of a child. It thus became a generic noun (ism jins), and therefore the particle min (from), which enters upon an indefinite negated noun to express generality, entered upon it, meaning: "you have no right to any kind of waiting period for them."

The address in "lakum" (you have) is to the husbands who married the believing women. The 'idda was made for them, that is, for their benefit, because its purpose returns to the benefit of the husbands by preserving their lineage, and because they have the right to take back their wives as long as they are within the 'idda period, as indicated by His words, "You do not know, perhaps God will bring about after that a matter" [al-Talaq: 1], and His words: "And their husbands have more right to take them back in that [period], if they desire reconciliation" [al-Baqarah: 228]. Nevertheless, it is a right that the Shari'a has imposed, so if the husband wished to drop the 'idda from the divorced woman, he would not have that right, because what the 'idda includes of preserving lineage is a purpose from the fundamental purposes of legislation, and so it does not drop by the husband's waiving it.

The meaning of "ta'taddunaha" is "you count them against them," that is, you count their days against them, as one says: "the woman observed her 'idda" (i'tadda) when she completed the days of her 'idda.

The form of al-iftial is not for the sense of being affected (mutawa'a), but is in the sense of the verb itself, like "idturra ila kadha" (he was compelled to such-and-such). Attempting to take the form of mutawa'a in its well-known meaning is forced.

This is similar to one who takes back a woman in her waiting period and then divorces her before touching her, for the taking back resembles marriage but is not its essence, since it does not require offer and acceptance. The jurists differed on her 'idda from that divorce. Malik, al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions, and the majority of jurists said: she begins a new 'idda from the day of the divorce and does not build upon the 'idda she was in, because the husband nullified that 'idda by taking her back. Perhaps Malik considered that intercourse after taking back may be concealed, unlike consummation in an existing marriage, so he perhaps required the 'idda to be resumed on account of this suspicion, as a precaution for lineages. Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan, Abu Qilaba, Qatada and al-Zuhri said: she builds upon her first 'idda in which he took her back, because his divorce after taking her back without touching her is like the sequence of a second divorce upon a woman while she is in her 'idda, since a sequential divorce has no separate 'idda of its own. Al-Qurtubi attributed to Dawud al-Zahiri that he said: a woman with a revocable divorce whose husband takes her back before her 'idda ends and then separates from her before touching her, she is not obligated to complete her 'idda nor to observe a new 'idda, because she is divorced before consummation. End.

This is strange, and Ibn Hazm's statement in al-Muhalla is explicit that she begins the 'idda anew, so perhaps it is from Ibn Hazm's view and not the school of Dawud. And how is it if he took her back a day or two after divorcing her; by what would one know the innocence of her womb?

The particle of consequence (fa') in "fa-matti'uhunna" is because the ruling on providing a consolation gift is established in Surat al-Baqarah in His words: "And provide for them, the wealthy according to his means and the poor according to his means" [al-Baqarah: 236], etc. Mut'a (consolation gift) is a gift that the husband gives to the woman when he divorces her. His words, the Exalted, have already been mentioned: "There is no blame upon you if you divorce women as long as you have not touched them or specified for them an obligation. But give them [a gift]: for the wealthy according to his capacity and for the straitened according to his capacity - a provision according to what is reasonable, a duty upon the doers of good" [al-Baqarah: 236]. Therefore the command to provide consolation is joined by fa' to the divorce before touching.

God has made the consolation gift a mending of the heart of the woman broken by divorce. It was mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah that the consolation gift is a right of the divorced woman whether or not a dowry was named for her, by the ruling of this verse in Surat al-Ahzab, because God commanded providing consolation for a divorced woman before consummation absolutely, so its generality in conditions is like its generality in persons. The verse of al-Baqarah does not contradict this verse, for it contains no restriction by a condition that would require limiting the consolation gift to the one for whom no dowry was named, since it was revealed to lift blame from divorce before consummation and before naming a dowry; then it commanded consolation for those two divorced women. So combining the two verses is possible.

Al-sarah al-jamil (the fair release) is: free from harm, injury and withholding of rights.

[Page 63]

This is the fourth address in which the Prophet ﷺ was addressed, concerning a matter specific to him. It explains what was made lawful for him of wives and concubines, what goes beyond that, and what does not. Some of it confirms a ruling that already existed, and some of it is a new ruling for the future. Some of it applies equally to the Prophet ﷺ and the community, and some of it is specific to him. Allah honoured him with this particular privilege, which is a broadening for him, or which takes into account the elevation of his rank.

Perhaps the occasion for its placement after the verses preceding it is that when the hypocrites criticised the Prophet's ﷺ marriage to Zaynab bint Jahsh and said, "He has married the one who was the wife of his adopted son," Allah wished to gather in this verse those women whom the Prophet may lawfully marry, so that people would not fall into doubt and the spreaders of rumours would not mislead them. Perhaps what occurred of the disapproval of some women, that a woman would offer herself to a man, was among the reasons for the inclusion of His words ﴿and a believing woman, if she gives herself to the Prophet﴾, and so the verse combined the confirmation of what was already legislated with the legislation of what had not been legislated, in order to cover all circumstances. That is more comprehensive and more decisive in removing doubt and ambiguity.

As for the confirmation of what was already legislated, it is in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful for you your wives whom you have given their bridal payments﴾ up to His words ﴿and the daughters of your maternal aunts﴾. As for the legislation of what had not been legislated, it is in His words ﴿who emigrated with you﴾ up to His words ﴿nor to exchange them for other wives﴾ [al-Ahzab: 52].

His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful for you your wives﴾ are a declarative statement intended to convey legislation. The entry of the particle (inna) upon it does not contradict the intention of legislation, since the function of (inna) here is merely to express emphasis, and emphasis suits both the purpose of informing and the purpose of creating a ruling. For this reason, a series of coordinated items were joined to the object of (ahlalna), and these were qualified by descriptions whose legal status had not been known before. This applies to His words ﴿and the daughters of your paternal uncles﴾ and what is conjoined to it, insofar as they are qualified by the description ﴿who emigrated with you﴾, and to His words ﴿and a believing woman, if she gives herself﴾, insofar as she is qualified by the description of faith and by the condition ﴿if she gives herself to the Prophet, if the Prophet wishes to marry her﴾. This is the interpretation of the verse according to what the exegetes have followed, with slight differences among their opinions.

In my view, the verse is an expression of favour and a reminder of His blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ. From the expression of favour, permission is derived. From the apparent meaning of His words ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this﴾ [al-Ahzab: 52], it is derived that the permission is restricted to those who were in his marriage at the time the verse was revealed. The purpose of this verse is to pave the way for His words ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this﴾ [al-Ahzab: 52], etc.

[Page 64]

What we have to say about the meaning of His words ﴿after this﴾ and about the position of His words ﴿if the Prophet wishes to marry her﴾ will come later.

The meaning of ﴿We have made lawful for you﴾ is permission granted to him. For this reason, after the enumeration of what was made lawful for him, it is contrasted with His words ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this﴾ [al-Ahzab: 52].

The attribution of "wives" to the pronoun of the Prophet ﷺ indicates that they are the wives who are in his marriage. Thus the statement is informative, confirming an earlier legislation, and is presented in the manner of an expression of favour. Then it is a preparation for the legislation specific to the Prophet ﷺ that follows, from His words ﴿who emigrated with you﴾ up to His words ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this, nor to exchange them for other wives﴾ [al-Ahzab: 52]. This is the view I hold in interpreting this verse.

Ibn al-Faras reported from al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd that the meaning of His words ﴿your wives whom you have given their bridal payments﴾ is that Allah made lawful for him to marry every woman whose dower he pays, so He permitted him all women. This is far from the implication of the attribution of "wives" to his pronoun, and from the expression ﴿you have given their bridal payments﴾ in the past tense. The people of interpretation differed about how this view can be reconciled with His words, exalted is He, at the end of the verse ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this﴾ [al-Ahzab: 52].

﴿Whom you have given their bridal payments﴾ is a qualifying clause for ﴿your wives﴾, meaning: and they are the women whom you married according to the rule of marriage that applies to the community. Thus the past tense in His words ﴿you have given their bridal payments﴾ is used in its literal sense. Among them are those who were of his kin, namely the Qurashi women: Aishah, Hafsah, Sawdah, Umm Salamah and Umm Habibah. Among them are others who were not of this kind: Juwayriyah from Banu al-Mustaliq, Maymunah bint al-Harith from Banu Hilal, Zaynab Umm al-Masakin from Banu Hilal, who had died at that time, and Safiyyah bint Huyayy, the Israelite.

Joined to these are other women, of three categories. The first category is those whom his right hand possessed of what Allah granted him as fay' (spoils obtained without combat), that is, what Allah gave him of fay', which is what the Muslims obtain from the enemy without fighting, but which the enemy left behind. Or it is what was given to the Prophet ﷺ, such as Mariyah the Copt, mother of his son Ibrahim. Allah granted her to him as fay', since al-Muqawqis, the ruler of Egypt, gave her to him as a gift, and he gave her as a gift only because of his prophethood. She was therefore in the position of fay', because what was considered in her case was only the aim of peace from the side of the neighbourhood, since he had no prior companionship or acquaintance with the Messenger ﷺ. It is known that the Prophet ﷺ did not take any concubine other than Mariyah the Copt. It has also been said that he took another slave-girl whom his wife Zaynab bint Jahsh gave him, but this is not established. It has also been said that he took Rayhanah from the captives of Banu Qurayzah, whom he chose for himself, and this verse does not include her because she was not from fay' but from the spoils of war (maghnam), unless by ﴿what Allah granted you as fay'﴾ is meant the more general meaning of fay', which includes ghanimah (war booty). This ruling is shared by many of the community, from everyone to whom his commander gave something of fay', as Allah, exalted is He, said ﴿What Allah has granted to His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah and to the Messenger and to the near relatives and orphans and the needy and the traveller﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. Therefore, whoever is given a slave-girl from fay' by the commander from these categories, she becomes lawful for him.

His words ﴿what Allah granted you as fay'﴾ are a descriptive qualifier for ﴿what your right hand possesses﴾, and it is here a descriptive qualifier that reveals, because what is meant by it is Mariyah al-Qutbiyyah, or she and Rayhanah, if it is established that he took her as a concubine.

The second category is women from the close kin of the Prophet ﷺ, on either his father's or his mother's side, who are believers and emigrants. His words ﴿who emigrated with you﴾ dispensed with the description of faith, because emigration is not possible except after faith. Allah therefore permitted the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, to marry whomever he wished from this category by the known marriage contract. It is therefore not lawful for him to marry in the future a woman from outside this category, which is restricted by the condition of kinship through paternal or maternal relation and the condition of emigration. In my view, the two descriptions of "the daughters of his paternal uncles and paternal aunts, and the daughters of his maternal uncles and maternal aunts," and of their having emigrated with him, are not intended to exclude those who are not so described. Rather, it is a revealing description, given to honour their status.

He singled out these women from the general prohibition to honour the status of kinship and of emigration, which is considered equivalent to kinship, according to His words, exalted is He, ﴿As for those who believed but did not emigrate, you have no obligation of guardianship toward them until they emigrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72]. The ruling on emigration ended with the conquest of Makkah. This ruling is pulled in two directions, between the specificity to the Messenger ﷺ and its generality to his community. Thus a woman who fulfils this description is lawful for the Messenger, upon him be prayer and peace, and for those members of his community who have a kinship with the woman similar to this kinship, to marry women like her. A woman who does not fulfil this description is not lawful for the Messenger, upon him be prayer and peace, to marry. This is what the majority has followed, and it is supported by a report transmitted from Umm Hani' bint Abi Talib. Abu Yusuf said: it is lawful for the men of his community to marry women like them. Since the wives of the Messenger ﷺ were not restricted by a number, this permission is specific to him and not to his community, since it is not lawful for anyone else to marry more than four.

The daughters of the paternal uncles of the Prophet ﷺ are the daughters of the brothers of his father, such as the daughters of al-Abbas, the daughters of Abu Talib, and the daughters of Abu Lahab. As for the daughters of Hamzah, they are daughters of a brother by fosterage, and they are not lawful to him. The daughters of his paternal aunts are the daughters of Abd al-Muttalib, such as Zaynab bint Jahsh, who is the daughter of Umaymah bint Abd al-Muttalib.

The daughters of his maternal uncles are the daughters of Abd Manaf ibn Zuhrah, and they are the maternal uncles of the Prophet ﷺ: Abd Yaghuth ibn Wahb, brother of Aminah. They did not mention that he had daughters. Likewise, I have not found mention of a maternal aunt of the Messenger of Allah in what I have seen of the books of genealogy and biography. Furay'ah bint Wahb has been mentioned in al-Isabah, and they mentioned Halah bint Wahb al-Zuhriyyah. However, because she was the wife of Abd al-Muttalib and her daughter was Safiyyah, the aunt of the Messenger of Allah, she has already been included earlier among the daughters of his paternal uncles.

The word (ʿamm, paternal uncle) is used in the singular and (ʿammāt, paternal aunts) in the plural because in the usage of Arabic, ʿamm is applied to the brother of the father, and also to the brother of the grandfather and the brother of the great-grandfather, and so on. Thus they say: these are sons of a paternal uncle or daughters of a paternal uncle, when they are of one paternal uncle or of several paternal uncles, and the intended meaning is understood from the context. The rajiz (rhyming verse) recited by al-Akhfash says:

"They are not free of suspicion and blame in our war, except the daughters of the paternal uncle."

Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj said:

"The daughters of the paternal uncle said: O Salma, even if he is poor and destitute, she said, even if."

As for the word ʿammah (paternal aunt), it is not used generically in their speech. So when they say: these are sons of a paternal aunt, they mean that they are sons of a specific paternal aunt. Thus in the verse ﴿paternal aunts﴾ is used in the plural, and in ﴿the daughters of your maternal aunts﴾ the plural of khālah (maternal aunt) is used.

[Page 67]

Some people said: what is meant by the daughters of the paternal uncles and the daughters of the paternal aunts is the women of Quraysh, and what is meant by the daughters of the maternal uncles is the Zuhri women. This is a purely theoretical disagreement on which no practical ruling depends, because the wives of the Prophet are known.

His words ﴿who emigrated with you﴾ are a descriptive qualifier referring back to ﴿the daughters of your paternal uncles, the daughters of your paternal aunts, the daughters of your maternal uncles, and the daughters of your maternal aunts﴾, in the same manner as a qualifier that follows a series of nouns. It is a condition of legislation that had not been conditioned before.

The sense of being "with" in His words ﴿who emigrated with you﴾ is the "with" of accompaniment in the description contained in the verb "emigrated," so it does not follow that they had left with him on his route to emigration.

The third category: a woman who gives herself to the Prophet ﷺ, that is, makes herself a gift to him without a dower. Thus it was the custom of women before Islam to do this with the great men of the Arabs. Allah therefore permitted the Prophet to take her as a wife without a dower, if the Prophet ﷺ wished that. This is the literal meaning of the word "gave" (wahabat). The meaning of gift here is marrying herself without consideration, that is, without a dower. This is not the gift used in marriage formulas when it is accompanied by the mention of a bridal payment, because that word is a metaphor for marriage, by the indicator of the mention of the dower. Our school and the Hanafis hold that the marriage may be contracted by it, in contrast to al-Shafi'i.

So His words ﴿and a woman﴾ are a conjunction upon ﴿your wives﴾. The implied sense is: and We have made lawful for you a believing woman.

[Page 68]

The indefinite form in *imra'atan* (a woman) indicates a category. The meaning is: "We inform you that We have made lawful to you a woman who is a believer, on condition that she gives herself to you and that you wish to marry her." His saying "to the Prophet" in both places is an explicit noun used in place of a pronoun (*izhar fi maqam al-idmar*). The meaning is: if she gives herself to you and you wish to marry her. This is a specification of the generality of His saying, "and the daughters of your paternal uncles and the daughters of your paternal aunts and the daughters of your maternal uncles and the daughters of your maternal aunts, who have emigrated with you" [Al-Ahzab: 50]. So if a woman gives herself to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he wishes to marry her, it is permissible for him without those two conditions. For this reason, *imra'atan* is described as *mu'minatan* (a believer), so that it is known that anything beyond faith is not a condition. Zaynab bint Khuzayma al-Hilaliyya, who was called in the Jahiliyya "Umm al-Masakin" (Mother of the Needy), is counted among those women who gave themselves (to the Prophet). But Zaynab did not remain with him except briefly, and then she died. Her marriage to him was in the third year after the Hijra, so she is not among those covered by the verse. It is not established that the Prophet (ﷺ) married any other of those who gave themselves to him, and they are: Umm Sharik bint Jabir al-Dawsiyya, whose name was 'Izziyya; and Khawla bint Hakim, who offered herself to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and 'A'isha said: "Is a woman not ashamed to give herself to a man?" And another woman offered herself to the Prophet (ﷺ). Thabit al-Bunani narrated from Anas, who said: "A woman came to the Messenger of Allah and offered herself to him, saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, do you have any need of me?' Anas's daughter, who was listening to her father's narration, said: 'How little modesty she has! Shame on her, shame on her!' Anas said: 'She is better than you; she desired the Prophet and so offered herself to him.'" And from Sahl ibn Sa'd: "A woman offered herself to the Prophet (ﷺ), but he did not respond to her. A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, marry her to me,' until he said to him: 'We have given her to you in ownership (*mallakna-kaha*) in exchange for what you have of the Qur'an.'" So this category's ruling is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), because it is a marriage contrary to the sunna of marriage, as it is without a dowry (*mahr*) and without a guardian (*wali*).

It has been reported that the women who gave themselves to the Prophet (ﷺ) were four: Maymuna bint al-Harith; Zaynab bint Khuzayma al-Ansariyya, known as Umm al-Masakin; Umm Sharik bint Jabir al-Asadiyya or al-'Amiriyya; and Khawla bint Hakim bint al-Awqas al-Sulamiyya. As for the first two, the Prophet (ﷺ) married them, and they were among the Mothers of the Believers.

The meaning of *"wahabat nafsaha lil-Nabiyy"* (she gave herself to the Prophet) is that she made herself his possession in a manner similar to the ownership of the right hand (*milk al-yamin*). For this reason it is joined by conjunction to *"ma malakat yaminuka"* (what your right hand possesses) [Al-Ahzab: 52], and it is followed by His saying, *"khalisatan laka min dun al-mu'minin"* (exclusively for you, apart from the believers), meaning: exclusively for you, that you may take her as a wife by that gift, that is, without a dowry, and this is not for the rest of the believers. For this reason, when it occurred in the aforementioned hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd that "a woman gave herself to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the man present knew that the Prophet (peace be upon him) had no need of her, he asked the Prophet (peace be upon him) to marry her to him, knowing that this gift had no dowry with it. The man did not have anything to give her as a dowry. The Prophet (ﷺ) knew this about him and said to him: 'What do you have?' He said: 'I have nothing.' He said: 'Go and seek, even an iron ring.' So he went and came back and said: 'No, by Allah, not even an iron ring, but this is my waist-wrap (*izar*), and half of it is hers.' Sahl said: 'He did not have a cloak.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'What will you do with your waist-wrap? If you wear it, nothing of it will be on her, and if she wears it, nothing of it will be on you.' Then he said to him: 'What do you have of the Qur'an?' He said: 'I have such-and-such surah and such-and-such surah,' enumerating surahs. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'We have given her to you in ownership in exchange for what you have of the Qur'an.'"

In His saying, *"in wahabat nafsaha lil-Nabiyy"* (if she gives herself to the Prophet), there is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, because the expected form would be "if she gives herself to you." The purpose of this explicit noun is the praise contained in the word "Prophet," by which her act of giving herself is characterized as motivated by desire for the honor of prophethood.

His saying, *"in arada al-Nabiyyu an yastankihaha"* (if the Prophet wishes to marry her), is a parenthetical clause (*jumla mu'taridha*) placed between "if she gives herself" and "khalisatan" (exclusively). It is not intended as a restriction, since there is no need to mention the wish to marry her, for this is understood from the meaning of permissibility. It was introduced by this condition only to prevent the supposition that his acceptance of her gift of herself would be obligatory upon him, as was the custom of the people of the Jahiliyya. Its response (*jawab*) is omitted and indicated by what precedes it. The estimated sense is: if he wishes to marry her, then she is lawful to him. Thus this is an independent condition and not a condition attached to the preceding condition.

The shift from the pronoun in His saying, *"in arada al-Nabiyyu"* (if the Prophet wishes), to saying "in arada an yastankihaha" (if he wishes to marry her) with the explicit noun is for the sake of the exaltation and honoring that the word "Prophet" carries.

The benefit of this second condition is the nullification of the custom of the Arabs in the Jahiliyya, namely that when a woman gave herself to a man, marrying her became binding on him, and it was not permissible for him to reject her. So Allah nullified this obligation by giving the Prophet (peace be upon him) the choice of accepting or not accepting a woman's gift of herself to him, and to remove the reproach against the woman who gives herself, by making clear that refusal is permitted.

The *sin* and *ta'* in *yastankihu* (he marries her) are not for requesting (*li-al-talab*) but are for emphasizing the verb (*li-ta'kid al-fi'l*), like the saying of al-Nabigha:

*"They killed the Ta'i man by the stone, by force,*
*Abu Jabir; so they took Umm Jabir (in marriage)."*

That is, the Banu Hunn killed Abu Jabir al-Ta'i, so Umm Jabir, who had been married to Abu Jabir, became the wife of the Banu Hunn, that is, the wife of a man among them. This is like the *sin* and *ta'* in His saying, *"fastajaba lahum rabbuhum"* (so their Lord responded to them) [Al Imran: 195].

Thus it becomes clear, from treating the clause *"in arada al-Nabiyyu an yastankihaha"* as a parenthetical clause, that this verse is not valid as an example for the issue of a condition interposed on a condition (*i'tiraḍ al-shart 'ala al-shart*), as occurred in the treatise of Shaykh Taqi al-Din al-Subki, which was composed on the interposition of a condition upon a condition. Al-Suyuti followed him in the seventh chapter of his book *al-Ashbah wa al-Naza'ir al-Nahwiyya* (Analogues and Parallels in Grammar). It appears from the words of the author of *al-Kashshaf* that he sensed the verse was not suitable for considering a condition within a condition, so he undertook to contrive an explanation of that.

*Khalisatan* (exclusively) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) from *imra'atan* (a woman); that is, that woman is exclusively for you, meaning this category of women. Exclusivity here means the absence of sharing, that is, the sharing of the rest of the community in this ruling, since the root *kh-l-ş* (exclusivity) gathers the meanings of being free from mixing. Thus His saying, *"min dun al-mu'minin"* (apart from the believers), explains a circumstantial state from the pronoun of address in His saying *"laka"* (for you), in the ambiguity of the attribution of exclusivity. The description of *imra'atan* as *mu'minatan* (a believer) indicates that a woman who is not a believer is not lawful to the Prophet (peace be upon him) by her giving herself. And by the implication of the discourse (*dalalat lahn al-khitab*) it indicates that it is not lawful for the Prophet (ﷺ) to marry Kitabiyyat (women of the People of the Book), let alone polytheists. Imam al-Haramayn (al-Juwayni) reported a disagreement on this. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The correct view in my opinion is its prohibition for him." By this he is distinguished above us, for what pertains to virtues and honor is more abundant in his favor, and if it is not lawful for him to marry one who did not emigrate, because of her lack of the virtue of emigration, then it is all the more so that a free Kitabiyya is not lawful for him.

* * *

*"Qad 'alimna ma faradna 'alayhim fi azwajihim wa ma malakat aymanuhum"* (We know what We have imposed upon them regarding their wives and what their right hands possess) [Al-Ahzab: 50].

This is a parenthetical clause placed between the clause "apart from the believers" and His saying *"li-kay la yakuna 'alayka haraj"* (so that there will be no difficulty upon you). Or it is a causal circumstantial state (*hal sababi*) from "the believers," meaning: while they are the ones for whom We know what We impose.

The meaning is: the believers continue under what was legislated for them before in the rulings of marriage and what their right hands possess, so the specific rulings prescribed for you, mentioned earlier, do not include them. That is, We know that what We have imposed upon them in this matter is what is fitting for the condition of the community as a whole, not what We have imposed on you specifically.

*Ma faradna 'alayhim* is a relative pronoun with its relative clause. The transitive use of *faradna* with the preposition *'ala*, which implies obligation and imposition, indicates that among the legislation for their wives and what their right hands possess are things they would wish to be lightened for them, such as the number of wives and the obligation of dowries and maintenance. When they heard what the Prophet (ﷺ) was specifically granted of ease in those rulings, they wished to be included with him in that. So Allah recorded against them that they remain upon what was previously legislated for them in that matter. The announcement that Allah knows this is an allusion to the continuation of those rulings, because its meaning is: We have not been unmindful of that, that is, We have not abrogated it; rather, with knowledge We specified Our Prophet with what We specified him with in that matter, so it does not include the rest of the believers in what We have made lawful for him.

The adverbial sense of *fi* (in) here is figurative, because what is contained (*al-maẓrufu*) is the legal rulings, not the persons of the wives and what the right hands possess.

* * *

*"Li-kay la yakuna 'alayka haraj wa kana Allahu ghafuran rahiman"* (So that there will be no difficulty upon you; and Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful) [Al-Ahzab: 50].

This is a reason (*ta'lil*) for what Allah legislated for His Prophet (ﷺ) in the preceding verses of ease, by increasing the number of wives and marrying women who give themselves without dowry, and by making the acceptance of their gift dependent on his wish, and by what He left him of equality with his community in what is beyond that of permissibility, so He did not constrict him. This is a teaching and a favor.

*Haraj* means constriction. What is meant here is the least degree of difficulty, which is the part of difficulty inherent in obligations that no obligations are free of. As for severe difficulty, it is negated for him and for his community. The degrees of difficulty vary, and the criterion for what is negated from the community and what is not negated, and the estimations of the states in which some of it is negated because of necessity, is the measure of the legal obligation. Allah knows best its degrees and knows best the measure of His servants' scrupulousness. That is explained in the issues of *'azima* (the strict ruling) and *rukhsa* (the concession) in the science of the principles of jurisprudence (*'ilm al-usul*). Shihab al-Din al-Qarafi has set out its criterion in the fourteenth *Farq* (distinction) of his book *Anwa' al-Buruq* (The Lightning of Lights). We have elaborated on the verification of this in our book entitled *Maqasid al-Shari'a al-Islamiyya* (The Objectives of Islamic Law).

Know that the Prophet (ﷺ), in taking up these expansions by which Allah elevated his rank, followed the path of perfection among His servants, and he is the most perfect of them. So he did not benefit himself from any of them, and he was a grateful servant, as he said in the hadith about his seeking forgiveness from his Lord, "many times a day."

The conclusion with the clause *"wa kana Allahu ghafuran rahiman"* is a conclusion (*tadhyil*) for the rulings that He legislated for the Prophet (ﷺ), not for the parenthetical clause. That is, what We intended by removing difficulty from you is among the objects of the two attributes of forgiveness and mercy, which are among the objects of the two attributes of will and knowledge, so they arise from the essential attributes. Therefore the attribution of these two to Allah is made a firmly established matter by the verb *kana* (was), which indicates precedence and permanence, as you know from many places.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 51 (part 1 of 2):

﴿You may postpone whom you will of them, and take to you whom you will. And whomever you desire of those you have set aside, there is no blame upon you.﴾

This is a clarifying resumption (istinaf bayani) arising from His words ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful to you your wives﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50] up to His words ﴿so that there will be no difficulty for you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50], for it stirs in the soul a desire to know the extent of this permission. The sentence is a declarative statement used to create the permission of postponing and sheltering for whomever the Prophet (ﷺ) wills.

The basic meaning of al-irja' (postponement) is delay until a future time. It is said: arja'tu al-amr and arjaytuhu, with and without hamza, meaning "I delayed the matter" when one defers it.

Its verb refers to conditions, not to persons. When its verb is transitive to the name of a person, its meaning is specified as referring to some suitable attribute that is intended by it. So when you say: arja'tu gharimi ("I postponed my creditor"), the meaning is: you delayed the payment of his debt to a coming time.

Al-iwa' (sheltering) basically means making a thing a place of return, i.e., returning to its place. It is said: awa, when one returns to where one departed. Here it is a metaphor for general settling, whether after distancing or without it, and whether after a prior settling in the place or not.

The contrast between al-irja' and al-iwa' requires that al-irja' is meant as the opposite of al-iwa', or that al-iwa' is the opposite of al-irja', both in their literal and figurative senses.

The pronoun in (minhunna) refers to the women mentioned, from among those who are in his marriage and those whom God permitted him to marry besides them, such as the daughters of his paternal uncles and aunts and his maternal uncles and aunts, and the women who gave themselves to him. These are four categories:

The first category: those who are in the marriage of the Prophet (peace be upon him). They are connected to him, so the postponement of this category refers to delaying intimacy until a future time he wishes, and sheltering is its opposite. It is therefore necessary that the postponement refers to the division (qasm) of time. God thus gave his Prophet (ﷺ) latitude by permitting him to waive the right of some of his wives regarding spending the night with them, so the right of the night became a right for him, not for them, unlike the rest of the Muslims. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah, and Abu Razin, as reported by al-Tabari.

One of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), Sawda bint Zam'a, had waived her right to spend the night with him and gave her day to 'A'isha, so the Prophet (ﷺ) would divide [his time] for 'A'isha with her day and the day of Sawda. This was before the revelation of this verse. When this verse was revealed, the Prophet (peace be upon him) became free to choose in the division among his wives. This is the view of the majority. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: this is what should be relied upon. This is an option given to the Prophet (ﷺ), but he did not take it for himself, out of generosity towards his wives. Al-Zuhri said: "We do not know that the Messenger of God postponed any of his wives; rather he sheltered all of them." Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: this is the intended meaning. Abu Razin al-'Uqayli said: he postponed Maymuna, Sawda, Juwayriya, Umm Habiba and Safiyya, so he would divide for them as he wished, i.e., without equality with the rest of his wives. Ibn al-'Arabi declared this weak.

Al-irja' has been interpreted as meaning divorce, and al-iwa' as keeping in marriage, so that it would be a permission for him to divorce whomever he wishes. But applying al-irja' to divorce is strange.

They have mentioned other opinions and reports concerning the occasion of revelation, whose chains are not authentic, so they are opinions not to be relied upon.

Al-irja' includes the second category: those whom his right hand possesses. This is an original ruling, since equality in companionship and in spending the night is not obligatory for slave-women.

Al-irja' includes the third category: the daughters of his paternal uncles, the daughters of his paternal aunts, the daughters of his maternal uncles, and the daughters of his maternal aunts. Thus al-irja' is the delay of marrying those of them who are lawful, and al-iwa' is contracting marriage with one of them. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not marry any of them after the revelation of this verse. That is the postponement of acting upon the permission regarding them to no specified term.

Likewise is the postponement of the fourth category: those women who gave themselves [to him], whether that occurred after the revelation of the verse or some of it occurred after its revelation. Their postponement is his not accepting the marriage of the woman who gave herself; he expressed it as postponement to preserve her hope that he might accept her in the future. Their sheltering is his accepting their gift.

Nafi', Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, and Khalaf read (turji) with a yā' at its end, the light form of (turji'), the hamzated verb. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, and Ya'qub read (turji'u) with hamza at its end. Al-Zajjaj said: the hamza is better and more common. The meaning is one.

The transmitters agree that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not employ with his wives what was permitted to him, taking from it the best of morals; he would be just in the division among his wives, except that Sawda gave her day to 'A'isha, seeking to please the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

As for His words ﴿And whomever you desire of those you have set aside, there is no blame upon you﴾, this is to clarify that this option does not require the continuation of what was undertaken by either of the two parties between whom one is given the choice; i.e., his setting aside (of a wife) is not binding to continue permanently, like zihar and ila', rather God permitted him to return to whomever he had set aside. Here He explicitly states that postponement includes setting aside.

In the speech there is an implied clause indicated by His words ﴿desire﴾, for it implies that he desired to cancel her setting aside. So the object of (desire) is omitted, indicated by His words ﴿You may take to you whom you will﴾, as is required by the contrast with His words ﴿You may postpone whom you will﴾, since setting aside and postponement have one and the same function.

The meaning: if you set aside one of them by postponement, the setting aside is not obligatory to continue; rather you may return her if you desire to return to her. That is, this is not like a man giving his wife the choice so that she chooses herself, which implies she is separated from him. The complement of "no blame" is omitted, indicated by His words "desire", i.e., if you desire her sheltering, there is no blame upon you for her sheltering.

(Man) may be conditional, with the clause ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾ as the answer of the condition. It may also be relative, a subject, since the relative pronoun is treated like the conditional in their speech frequently when a general sense is intended. Therefore the predicate of a general relative often takes fa' (then), as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203]. Accordingly the clause ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾ is the predicate of the subject, joined with fa' because the relative is treated like the conditional. The object of (you set aside) is omitted, referring back to (man), i.e., those whom you desire of those you have set aside, and this is the omission of a accusative returning pronoun.

* * *

﴿That is nearer that their eyes may be cooled, and they will not grieve, and they will all be content with what you give them. And God knows what is in your hearts, and God is ever Knowing and Forbearing.﴾

The demonstrative refers to something of what preceded, and it is the nearest of it. It may refer to the sense of delegation derived from His words ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them, and take to you whom you will﴾. It may also refer to the seeking implied by the verb (you desire), i.e., there is no blame upon you in seeking them after setting them aside; that is nearer that their eyes may be cooled. Seeking (ibtigha') is desire and request, and what is meant here is seeking companionship with those he has set aside.

On the first interpretation, the meaning is that in this delegation the Prophet (ﷺ) was given the right to choose one of the two matters, and he left no right for them. So when he assigns one of them one of the two states, she is content with it; because it places the decision of God, by the ruling of His words ﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when God and His Messenger have decided a matter, that they should have any choice in their affair﴾ [al-Ahzab: 36], so the eyes of all of them are cooled by what he assigns to each one. For whoever knows he has no right to something is content with what is given to him from it, while whoever knows he has a right thinks what is given to him is less than his right and insists on getting it in full. This interpretation is related from Qatadah, and az-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-'Arabi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya followed it. This fits His words "and they will be content", but does not fit His words "that their eyes may be cooled", because the coolness of the eye comes only from a beloved matter, and His words "and they will not grieve", because grief from a troubling matter is not within one's choice, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "So do not blame me for what I do not control."

On the second interpretation, the meaning is: that seeking after the setting aside is nearer that the eyes of those whom you had set aside may be cooled. In this interpretation there is encouragement to the Prophet (ﷺ) to choose not to set them aside from the division, which is appropriate to His words "that their eyes may be cooled and they will not grieve", as you have learned just above, and to His words "and they will be content", and to the abundant good in what is mentioned, which the Prophet (ﷺ) certainly desires to attain: bringing joy to a Muslim and achieving contentment among the Muslims, which strengthens the Islamic brotherhood that is encouraged. Something close to this meaning is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, and Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i chose it, and it is the more probable, because the coolness of the eye is not obtained through distress, and because diminishing a right causes turmoil. It is supported by the fact that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not act except in this way, and it is not preserved from him that he favored one of his wives with a night other than the night of Sawda which she gave to 'A'isha; this continued until his death (ﷺ). It is related in the Sahih that during his illness in which he died, he was carried each day around the houses of his wives, and the start of his sickness was in the house of Maymuna, until the turn of the night of 'A'isha came, and his wives permitted him to be nursed in her house, out of gentleness towards him.

It is also reported from him (ﷺ) that when he divided among them he said: "O God, this is my division in what I control, so do not blame me for what I do not control." Perhaps that was before the grant of this delegation to him by this verse.

In His words "and they will all be content with what you give them" there is an indication that the intended contentment is that in which they are equal; otherwise the emphasis by "all of them" would have no added purpose. So the combination of their pronoun in His words "all of them" points to an equal contentment among them.

The two pronouns in "their eyes" and "they will not grieve" refer back to (man) in His words "those you have set aside". The mention of "they will not grieve" after "that their eyes may be cooled", along with what the coolness of the eye implies of the negation of grief, is an allusion encouraging the Prophet (ﷺ) to seek the continuation of all his wives in his companionship, because setting aside some of them causes grief to those set aside, and he is "gentle and merciful to the believers," and does not wish to grieve anyone.

"All of them" is an emphasis for the pronoun of "they will be content", or the pronouns all together are in apposition.

Al-iita' means giving, and it has come to be used for giving good when its second object is not mentioned, or is mentioned but not specified, as in His words ﴿So take what I have given you and be among the grateful﴾ [al-A'raf: 144]. When its second object is mentioned, it is generally not something bad. I have not seen it used for giving evil; you do not say atahu sijnan ("he gave him prison") or atahu darban ("he gave him a beating"), except in a context of sarcasm or of verbal correspondence (mushakala). So what is here is of the first kind, and therefore it is far-fetched to interpret it as meaning that they will be content with what God permitted to His Messenger of setting them aside and postponing them. Its explanation in al-Kashshaf is strained.

The concluding statement, ﴿And God knows what is in your hearts, and God is ever Knowing and Forbearing﴾, is a comprehensive saying that combines the sense of encouragement and warning. It contains encouragement to the Prophet (ﷺ) to show kindness to his wives, his maidservants, and those who are seeking to marry him, and a warning to them against concealing dissatisfaction with what they receive from the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

In the placing of the two attributes ʿAlīman (All-Knowing) and Ḥakīman (All-Wise) after the name of Allah, there is an indication of this. So the fitting connection of the attribute of knowledge with His saying, ﴿And Allah knows what is in your hearts﴾, is clear. As for the fitting connection of the attribute of forbearing (ḥalīm), it is in view of the fact that the purpose is to encourage the Messenger ﷺ toward the condition most befitting the attribute of forbearing, because his ﷺ concern was to take on the character of Allah the Exalted. Allah has also bestowed upon him ﷺ attributes from among His own attributes, such as Raʾūf (Kind) and Raḥīm (Merciful). ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was never given a choice between two matters without choosing the easier of them, so long as it was not a sin." For this reason, the Messenger of Allah did not apply this option in the case of the wives who were with him in his household, but he did apply it in the case of the women who offered themselves to him, while treating them kindly both in word and in giving, for Allah has prescribed excellence (iḥsān) in everything. He also applied it in refraining from marrying the daughters of his paternal uncles, his paternal aunts, his maternal uncles and his maternal aunts, because there is no blame upon them in that.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 33, verse 52:**

﴿It is not lawful for you to take women after this, nor to exchange them for other wives, even if their beauty pleases you, except those whom your right hand possesses. And Allah is ever watchful over all things.﴾

The placement of this verse in the Qur'an, directly after the preceding one, indicates that it was revealed in this same sequence, that the discourse is connected part to part, and that it is arranged in this wondrous order. Moreover, the deletion of the noun to which (ba'du, "after") is attached indicates that it is an understood deletion, the meaning of which is indicated by the preceding discourse. Its late revelation relative to the verses before it, and its being connected to them as a completion, is something that should not be doubted. Accordingly, the omitted genitive noun may be supplied in one of two ways. Either it is taken from the mention of the categories before it, meaning "after the categories mentioned in His saying ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful for you your wives﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50], etc." Or it is what the discourse implies as to time, meaning "after this time." The first is the preferred view.

Ba'du may also mean "other than," as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Then who can guide him after Allah?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23]. This is a common usage in the language. On this understanding, this verse is neither abrogated by any other Qur'anic verse nor abrogating of anything else. What supports this meaning is the use of the word "wives" in His saying ﴿nor to exchange them for other wives﴾, i.e., other than them. Ibn 'Abbas understood the verse in this sense. al-Tirmidhi narrated from him that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was forbidden from [marrying] categories of women except those who were believing emigrants, and so He said: ﴿It is not lawful for you to take women after this, nor to exchange them for other wives, even if their beauty pleases you, except those whom your right hand possesses﴾, and Allah made lawful believing slave women, and ﴿a believing woman if she gives herself to the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50]." Similar is narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, 'Ikrimah, and al-Dahhak.

Ba'du may also be understood to mean "that which comes later than something else," which is the literal meaning of the notion of "afterness." In that case, one must posit a word indicating something prior.

Constructing ba'du with a dammah implies that a genitive noun has been omitted, which is indicated by the preceding discourse, according to the view adopted by Ibn Malik in al-Khulasa (a summary of grammar in verse) and verified by Ibn Hisham in his commentary on Qatr al-Nada. Thus the supplied phrase could be: "after those mentioned," in either of the two senses of afterness. In the sense of "other than," one supplies "other than those mentioned," or in the sense of "after those mentioned," one supplies "after those mentioned." This gives rise to the possibilities that what is meant is the categories of those mentioned, or the numbers of those mentioned (and they were nine), or those whom you have chosen.

It is also possible to supply the genitive noun as a time: "after the day," or "after the hour," i.e., the time at which the verse was revealed. In that case it would be an abrogation of His saying ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful for you your wives﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50] up to His saying ﴿exclusively for you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50].

As for what al-Tirmidhi narrated from 'A'ishah, that she said: "The Messenger of Allah did not die until Allah had made women lawful for him," and he said it is a good hadith (and it implies that this verse is abrogated), it indicates that its abrogating text is from the Sunnah, not from the Qur'an. This is because her saying "did not die" indicates that this was the last period of his life. Therefore, this verse, which was revealed with its surah five years before his death (ﷺ), cannot be abrogating of the permission to which 'A'ishah referred. Rather, the permission is a permission of honour for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). al-Tahawi narrated a report similar to the hadith of 'A'ishah from Umm Salamah.

The word "women" (al-nisa'), when used without qualification in such a context, is predominantly understood to mean wives, i.e., free women, not slave women, as al-Nabighah said:

"Lest they take my leadership and my women, until they die free."

That is, "wives other than those mentioned are not lawful for you after them."

His saying ﴿nor to exchange them for other wives﴾ originally was tatabaddalu with two tas, one of which was deleted for lightness. It is said: baddala and tabaddala. The root of "exchange" (al-badal) requires two things: one is given as a substitute for taking the other. So tabdil is transitive to the object taken directly, and to the object given by means of the preposition bi or min. This was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith has certainly strayed from the sound way﴾ [al-Baqarah: 108] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The meaning is: whoever among the categories mentioned has come into your marital bond, it is not lawful for you to divorce her. Thus "exchange" is used as a metaphor for divorce, because in common usage it is its usual concomitant, since a man does not divorce except that he substitutes another woman for the divorced one. This metaphor is specifically required here, because if the literal meaning of exchange were intended, the end of the verse would contradict its beginning and what precedes it. For the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was permitted to add to the women he had, provided the additional ones were from the three categories previously mentioned, and everything else was forbidden to him. So if the one exchanged for were one of the women from the three categories, it would not be coherent to forbid him to exchange any one of them specifically, because forbidding that would contradict the permission of the categories, and no one holds that the two verses abrogate one another. And if the one exchanged for were from outside the three categories, her prohibition would be general in all circumstances, and so there would be no benefit in forbidding her specifically in the case of exchanging for her. Therefore it became clear that the exchange is a metaphor for divorce, with the intention of exchanging being taken into account.

So the meaning is: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was permitted to add to the women who had come, or would come, into his marital bond from the three categories, but he was not permitted to replace an old wife with a new one.

Thus the meaning is: nor to replace a woman who has come into your bond, or who will come, with another woman.

Therefore the preposition bi denotes separation.

The word min is superfluous, attached to the second object of tabaddala, for the purpose of conveying generality. The implied sense is: nor to exchange them for other wives. Thus this ruling is specific to wives from the three categories, and the concubines remain outside it by His saying ﴿except those whom your right hand possesses﴾. As for the woman who gives herself, if the Prophet (ﷺ) wished to marry her, she is included in the bond of marriage and thus falls under the ruling concerning them. If he did not wish to marry her, she remains a foreigner who does not enter those categories.

Al-Jumhur read lā yaḥillu with a yā' (third person masculine), taking the verb as masculine because its subject is a broken plural, which permits considering the original form. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a tā' (feminine), treating the plural as a group. These are two permissible readings for a non-sound plural.

The clause ﴿even if their beauty pleases you﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥal), and the wāw is its wāw. It is a ḥal from the pronoun in tabaddala. (Law) is a conditional particle whose negation is certain, used for supposition and assumption. It is called wasliyya (the "conjunctive" law), so it indicates the negation of what is less than the conditioned matter, as has been mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿even if he were to offer it as ransom﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 91] in Surah Al 'Imran.

The meaning is: it is not lawful for you to take women after this, whether by adding to your wives or by replacing one of them with a new one, in every circumstance, even in the circumstance in which their beauty pleases you.

In this is an indication that when Allah permitted His Messenger the three categories, He intended to be gentle to him and not to frustrate his desire when a woman pleased him. Yet He specified for him definite categories, and in them is sufficiency.

'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, expressed this meaning in an elegant phrase, when she said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I see that your Lord is only hastening to fulfil your desire." This exaggeration is emphasized by the concluding clause ﴿And Allah is ever watchful over all things﴾, i.e., knowing the course of everything, whether in conformity with what He has determined or contrary to it, so He recompenses according to that. This is a promise to the Prophet (ﷺ) of a great reward for what was determined for him of this ruling.

The exception in His saying ﴿except those whom your right hand possesses﴾ is disconnected (munqati'). The meaning is: "but those whom your right hand possesses are lawful in every circumstance." The purpose of this disconnected exception is to prevent the supposition that the word "women" in His saying ﴿It is not lawful for you to take women﴾ means merely females in general, rather than its customary usage meaning wives, as has been mentioned earlier.

[Page 81]

Ya ayyuha alladhina amanu la tadkhulu buyuta al-Nabiyyi illa an yu'dhana lakum ila ta'amin ghayra nathirina inahu, wa lakin idha du'itum fadkhulu fa-idha ta'amtum fantashiru wa la mustanisina li-hadithin. Inna dhalikum kana yu'dhi al-Nabiyya fa-yastahyi minkum wallahu la yastahyi min al-haqq.

(O you who believe, do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless you are given permission for a meal, without waiting for its preparation. But when you are invited, enter, and when you have eaten, disperse, and do not linger for conversation. Indeed, that would trouble the Prophet, and he would be shy of you, but Allah is not shy of the truth.)

When Allah had explained in the preceding verses the etiquette of the Prophet ﷺ with his wives, He instructed him in this verse about the etiquette of the community (ummah) toward them, and He introduced it by alluding to the incident that was the occasion of its revelation. It is what is in Sahih al-Bukhari (the authentic collection of al-Bukhari) and elsewhere, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ married Zaynab bint Jahsh, he prepared food with bread and meat and invited the people, and they ate, then they sat conversing. He appeared as though he were preparing to stand, but they did not stand. When he saw that, he stood up, and when he stood, those who stood up stood, and three men remained seated. The Prophet came to enter, and behold, the people were still sitting. So the Prophet ﷺ went out and returned, and he went to the room of Aishah.
