Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 58:

﴿And those who harm believing men and believing women without their having earned it have certainly borne a slander and a clear sin.﴾ The sanctity of the believers has been attached to the sanctity of the Messenger (ﷺ), to honor their standing, and they are mentioned separately to indicate that their rank is lower than the rank of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. This is a digression (istitrad) interposed between the rulings on the sanctity of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the etiquette of his wives and his believing daughters.

The conjunction of "believing women" (al-mu'minat) with "believing men" (al-mu'minin) serves to make explicit the equality of the ruling, even though this is already known from the Sharia, in order to deter those who would harm women, because they are a weak party, unlike men, whom the fear of their anger and of their retaliation on their own behalf may restrain.

The intended meaning of "harm" (al-adha) is harm by speech, as indicated by His saying ﴿they have certainly borne a slander﴾, since slander (buhtan) is one of the kinds of speech. This belittles their words, and He followed this belittling with the description of it as a "clear sin" (ithm mubin). The intended meaning of "clear" (mubin) is great and grave, that is, a crime of the gravest sort, and this is a warning of punishment for it.

The pronoun in "they have earned" (iktasabu) refers to the believing men and women by way of predominance (taghlib, the masculine being used to cover both genders). The prepositional phrase in the verse functions as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). This circumstantial qualifier serves to intensify the reprehensibility of that harm, by describing it as injustice and falsehood.

The purpose of the circumstantial qualifier is not to restrict the ruling, such that its implication would be that it is permissible to harm believing men and women for what they have earned, that is, to revile them for a blameworthy deed they have committed. This is because the requital for such a deed is not entrusted to people in general, but to those in authority, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And as for the two of you who commit it among you, then harm them﴾ [An-Nisa: 16]. The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade backbiting (ghiba) and said: "It is that you mention your brother with what he dislikes." It was said: "Even if it is true?" He said: "If it is not true, then that is slander (buhtan)." As for changing what is wrong (taghyir al-munkar), it is not accompanied by harm.

The relative pronoun in His saying "what they have earned" (ma iktasabu) refers to an evil deed, that is, "without their having earned any evil." The meaning of "borne" (ihtamalu) is that they have burdened themselves with a load, and this is an image of slander as a heavy load upon its bearer. A parallel to this has already occurred in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever earns a sin or an error and then attributes it to an innocent person has certainly borne a slander and a clear sin﴾ [An-Nisa: 112], in Surat an-Nisa.

"﴿O Prophet, tell your wives and your daughters and the women of the believers to draw their outer garments close around them. That is more suitable that they will be known and not be harmed. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾" The prohibition of harming believing women was followed by a command that they avoid the causes of harm, because it is part of the nature of seeking an aim that one smooth the means that lead to it, as Allah the Exalted said, ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it its due striving﴾ [al-Isra: 19]. Abu al-Aswad said:

You hope for deliverance, yet you do not take its paths; indeed, a ship does not sail upon dry land.

This returns to the principle of cooperating in establishing benefits and eliminating harms. In a hadith: "May Allah have mercy on a parent who helps his child with his righteousness." This hadith is weak in its chain, but its meaning is sound, because honouring one's parents is required, and helping toward it is helping toward the existence of goodness and virtue.

The Prophet's wives and daughters are mentioned first because they are the most perfect of women, so mentioning them is a mention of some individuals of the general category, for the sake of giving it attention.

Al-Nisa' (the women) is a collective noun for woman, with no singular form from its own root, and it was mentioned earlier at the words of the Exalted, (﴿and not their women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 55]). So the intended meaning of "al-nisa'" here is not the wives of the believers, but rather the female believers. Its annexation to "al-mu'minin" carries the sense of (min), i.e., the women from among the believers.

Al-Jalabib (outer garments) is the plural of jilbab, which is a garment smaller than a robe (ridaʾ) and larger than a head-covering (khimar) or veil (qina'). A woman places it upon her head so that both its sides hang down over her cheeks, and the rest of it falls over her shoulders and back. She wears it when going out and when travelling.

The manner of wearing jalabib varies according to the differing circumstances of women, as customs make clear. The intended meaning is what is indicated by the words of the Exalted, ﴿That is more suitable that they will be known and not be harmed.﴾

Al-idna' (drawing close) means bringing near, and it is a metaphor for wearing and placing. That is, they place their outer garments upon themselves. Bashshar said:

A night in which she wears white of the month, and another in which she draws black outer garments close (tudni jalabib sudan).

He contrasted "tudni" with "talbas" (wears), so idna' here means wearing.

Wearing the jilbab was a distinguishing mark of free women, so slave women did not wear jalabib.

Free women used to wear jalabib when going out to visits and similar occasions, and they did not wear them at night or when going out to the open areas for relieving themselves. They only went out to those places at night. So they were commanded to wear jalabib whenever they went out, so that it would be known that they were free women, and so that young libertines would not molest them, supposing them to be slave women, or so that the hypocrites would not provoke them with insulting words, which would shame them, so they would be harmed by that, and perhaps they would revile those who harmed them, so harm would result from both sides. This is among the blocking of the means (sadd al-dhara'i').

The reference with "that" (dhalika) is to the drawing close understood from "yudnina", meaning that this garment is closer to being known as free women by the distinguishing mark of free women, so men avoid harming them, and both they and the women are safe.

Umar ibn al-Khattab, during his caliphate, used to prevent slave women from veiling so that they would not be confused with free women, and he would strike any of them who veiled with the whip. Then this ended after him. This is the meaning of the words of Kuthayyir:

They are free women, not those who wear head-coverings, with dark eyes; they do not read the surahs.

The concluding phrase, ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾, is a pardon for what had preceded of harm done to free women before they were alerted to this Islamic etiquette, and a concluding phrase requires the ending of the purpose.

[Page 108]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verses 60–61:

﴿If the hypocrites, those in whose hearts is a disease, and the agitators in the city do not desist, We will surely set you against them. Then they will not remain your neighbours in it except for a little while.﴾ ﴿Cursed; wherever they are found, they will be seized and slain with a [thorough] slaying.﴾ This is a transition from rebuking a people known for harming the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believing men and women, and from threatening them with the wrath of Allah upon them in this world and the Hereafter, to threatening them with a punishment in this world that Allah will ordain for them if they do not cease from that. This is because it is known that the threat of the Hereafter will not benefit them, since they do not believe in the Resurrection. Those are the hypocrites, whom the allusion began to address from the words of the Exalted, ﴿It is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53], to His words ﹛tremendous﹜ [al-Ahzab: 53], and then from His words ﴿Indeed, those who harm Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Ahzab: 57] to His words ﴿That is more suitable that they will be known and not be abused﴾ [al-Ahzab: 59].

Here he explicitly stated what was alluded to in the preceding verses, when he expressed it by "the hypocrites." Thus it is known that those who harm Allah and His Messenger are the hypocrites and whoever is wrapped up in their manner.

As for ﴿those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 52], we have mentioned them at the beginning of the surah. They are those who harbour hypocrisy or wavering in faith.

As for "the agitators in the city," they are the hypocrites. So the three descriptions refer to one thing, as stated by Abu Razin.

The clause ﴿If he does not desist﴾ is an initial resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i). The object of "yantahi" (desist) is omitted because it is evident, i.e., they do not desist from harming the Messenger and the believers.

Al-irjaf (agitation, spreading rumours) means spreading news. It implies that the news is false or harmful to its bearers, who repeat it in gatherings so that listeners will be reassured again and again that it is true, because spreading rumour is aimed only at promoting something that has not occurred or that is not credible. It is derived from al-rajf and al-rajafan, meaning agitation and trembling.

Thus the agitators are people who receive news, then relate it in gatherings and assemblies, and inform whoever asks and whoever does not ask. The meaning of irjaf here is that they spread what harms the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslim men and women, and they speak about the expeditions of the Muslims, saying: "They have been defeated," or "killing has spread among them quickly," or something similar, in order to cast doubt into people's souls, instil fear, and cause some to think ill of others. They are from among the hypocrites, those in whose hearts is a disease, and their followers. These are the ones of whom Allah said: ﴿When there comes to them a matter of security or fear, they spread it﴾ [al-Nisa: 83] in the surah of al-Nisa. These descriptions therefore refer to categories of people. Most of the agitators were from among the Jews, and they were not from among the believers, because His words that follow, ﴿We will surely set you against them﴾, do not support that there were believers among them.

[Page 109]

The lam in ﴿la-in﴾ (if) is a preparatory lam for an oath (lam al-muwatta'ah lil-qasam), so the speech after it is an elided oath. The estimated sense is: "By Allah, if he does not desist…"

The lam in ﴿la-nughriyannaka﴾ is the lam of the response to the oath, and the response to the oath is evidence for the response to the condition.

Al-ighra' means urging and inciting to an act. Its verb is transitive with the particle ʿala (upon) and with the particle bi (with). The more common usage is that when it takes ʿala, it denotes urging to the act in itself, and when it takes bi, it denotes urging to inflict harm upon a person, because the bi indicates attachment. So the one urged upon is attached to the one in the genitive after bi, i.e., falling upon it. Therefore one does not say "aghraytuhu bihi" (I incited him with him) if one urges him to do good to that person.

The meaning, then, is: "We will surely set you against them for their punishment," i.e., by having you incite the Muslims against them, as His words indicate: ﴿Wherever they are found, they will be seized and slain with a [thorough] slaying.﴾ When that befalls them, they will leave the city, having saved themselves, their property, and their families.

The conjunction of the clause ﴿They will not remain your neighbours﴾ with thumma (then) rather than fa' (so) was chosen to indicate that the cessation of their neighbourhood is distant from the incitement against them, a distance of rank. This is because leaving one's homeland is harder on souls than the harm that reaches the bodies, as the Exalted said: ﴿Expel them from where they expelled you, for persecution is worse than killing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191], that is, the persecution of expulsion from their land is harder for them than killing.

The exception in ﴿except for a little while﴾ serves to emphasise the negation of neighbourhood and that it is not meant as hyperbole. That is, they will not stay with you in the city except for a short period, which is the time between the revelation of this verse and their being overtaken. "Qalilan" (little) is an attribute of an elided noun indicated by "yujawiruna" (they will be your neighbours), i.e., a little neighbourhood, and its littleness is considered in relation to the duration of its time. The author of al-Kashshaf made it an attribute of an elided time-noun, because the placement of their pronoun within the scope of negation requires their singularity, and the generality of individuals requires the generality of their times. So it is in the accusative as an attribute of a time-noun, and it is not an adverb of time.

"Mal'unin" (cursed) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from what the word "qalilan" contains of the meaning of neighbourhood. So "al-jiwar" (neighbourhood) is a verbal noun that bears the pronoun of its subject, because the original form of a verbal noun is to be annexed to its agent, and the estimate is: "except their neighbourhood while cursed." The author of al-Kashshaf took "mal'unin" to be excepted from circumstances, with the particle of exception entering upon the adverb and the circumstance, as in His words: ﴿unless you are given permission for a meal, not waiting for its time﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53]. But there is a great difference between this and what he compared it to, because that construction contains what can serve as a circumstantial source. The preferred reading here is what we have adopted in estimating its construction.

Al-la'n (cursing) means distancing and expelling. His words ﴿And upon you is the curse until the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Hijr: 35] have preceded in surah al-Hijr. Here it is used as a metonym for humiliation and avoidance in the city, that is, the Muslims treat them by avoiding their company, and they themselves keep away from the believers out of caution and fear. This implies that they will be hidden and concealed, fearing the assault of the believers upon them, since the Prophet (ﷺ) has incited them against these people. Thus in His words "cursed" there is a wonderful conciseness.

His words "wherever they are found" (﴿ayna ma thuqifu﴾) is an adverbial phrase of place (zarf) annexed to a clause, and it is connected to "cursed," since "cursed" is a circumstance of them after their description as being in the city, so it conveys the generality of all places in the city. "Ayna ma" is a noun of time (in use as a conditional), containing the meaning of a condition. "Al-thaqaf" means gaining the upper hand over the enemy and coming upon them unintentionally. The verb has been prepared for by His word "cursed," as already mentioned.

The meaning of "they were seized" (﴿ukhidhu﴾) is that they were held. Al-akhdh means holding and grasping, i.e., they were taken captive. The intended sense is that their property was seized, since Allah incited the Prophet (ﷺ) against them.

Al-taqtil means intensity of killing. The intensity here means abundance, because a great quantity is strong among the kinds of its type, and it is also severe in being swift, with no respite for them in it.

"Taqtilan" (a slaying) is a verbal noun emphasising its verb, i.e., they were slain with a severe and comprehensive slaying. The emphasis here confirms that the killing applies to all the individuals indicated by the pronoun in "quttilu" (they were slain), to remove the possibility of metaphor in the generality of the killing. So the meaning is: they were slain with a severe slaying from which none escapes.

By this threat, the hypocrites desisted from harming the Muslims and from agitation, so the slaying did not fall upon them, since it is not reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) killed any of them, nor that any of them left the city.

This verse guides towards giving priority to reforming the corrupt within the community over cutting off a part of it, because reforming the corrupt gains the community a righteous individual or a righteous group from whom the community benefits, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Perhaps Allah will bring forth from their loins those who worship Him." For this reason, the repentance of the apostate was legislated before killing him, for three days, during which repentance is offered to him. Likewise, calling the disbelievers whom the Muslims will raid to the religion of Islam was legislated before the raid. If they accept Islam, well; otherwise they are offered entry into the protection (dhimmah) of the Muslims, because their entering the protection benefits the Muslims through their tax (jizyah) and through strengthening them.

As for the killing of one who kills intentionally, it was legislated as a measure to remove grudges from the hearts of the victim's heirs, so that some of the community do not kill others, since there is no remedy for that ailment except retaliation (qisas). For this reason, the Law encouraged pardon and its acceptance. On this basis, Malik said regarding the verse ﴿The recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33] that the "aw" (or) in it is for classification (tanwi') and not for choice (takhyir). He said: the punishment is according to the measure of the offender's crime and the extent of his corruption. Banishment from the land was the last of the kinds of punishment, because in it there is preserving him in hope of his repentance and the improvement of his condition.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 62:

﴿The way of Allah with those who passed away before, and you will never find any change in the way of Allah.﴾ The accusative in ﴿the way of Allah﴾ is a absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) standing in place of its verb. The estimated sense is: Allah has prescribed for you, by way of urging you against them, His way toward the enemies of the prophets of old and toward the disbelieving polytheists who were killed and captured at the Battle of Badr and elsewhere.

The particle (fi) here indicates figurative containment (al-zarfiyya al-majaziyya). The way in which they were dealt with is likened to something that is in the midst of them, as a metaphor (kinaya) for its permeating them and encompassing all of them. Had the speech been without figurative usage, it would have said: "the way of Allah with those who passed away." Here, (those who passed away) means those who went before and preceded.

The more apparent view is that what is meant by them are those among the enemies of the Prophet ﷺ who came before, whom Allah had permitted to be killed, such as those among the polytheists who were killed, and such as those of the Jews of Banu Qurayza who were killed. This is the more apparent because what befell those people is more effective as admonition, since these two groups were mentioned alongside the hypocrites, some of them had witnessed others, and news of one reached the other.

It is also possible that (those who passed away) includes the earlier nations against whom Allah was angered because of their harming of their messengers, so that Allah uprooted them, such as the people of Pharaoh and their like.

Page 112

He concluded with the sentence ﴿and you will never find any change in the way of Allah﴾ to add emphasis that the punishment will surely befall the hypocrites and their followers if they do not desist from what they are engaged in, and that Allah does not contravene His way, because it is the requirement of His wisdom and knowledge; so its applications only proceed in one pattern.
The meaning: you will never find any change in the ways of Allah with those who passed away before, nor with those present, nor with those who will come. By this generality conveyed by the indefinite noun occurring in a negative context, the sentence became fit to serve as a concluding summary (tadhyil).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 63:

﴿They ask you about the Hour. Say: Its knowledge is only with Allah. And what would make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near.﴾ When the threat to the hypocrites of a worldly punishment brought to mind the discussion of the punishment of the Hereafter, namely the discourse of the deniers who mock, the discourse of the believers who fear, and the People of the Book, it followed that with this verse.

The sentence is parenthetical (mu'taridah) between the sentence ﴿Then they will not be your neighbours in it except for a little﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60] and the sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze﴾ [al-Ahzab: 64], to serve as a preparation for the sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 64].

The questioning of people about the Hour is repeated in the Qur'an, and those who ask are of several types. Among them are those who deny it, and they are the majority of the askers. Their question is mockery and an argument, drawing from its delay the conclusion that it does not exist, according to their corrupt views. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those who believe are apprehensive of it, and they know that it is the truth﴾ [al-Shura: 18].

Another type is believers who ask about it out of eagerness to know the unseen. These were forbidden from preoccupying themselves with that, as in the hadith: "A man asked the Messenger of Allah: When is the Hour? The Prophet (ﷺ) said: What have you prepared for it? The man said: By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, I have prepared for it no great amount of prayer or fasting, except that I love Allah and His Messenger. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: You will be with the one you love."

Another type asks to test the Prophet (ﷺ), hoping he will answer with something that contradicts what they know. They then make it a proof among themselves against the non-prophethood of him, and they spread it among their common folk, so as to uproot from their souls whatever might mix with them of reflection on the truth of the Muhammadan call. These are the Jews, comparable to their question about the People of the Cave and about the Spirit.

Here "the people" (al-nas) is general, encompassing all people; it is a customary generality ('umum 'urfi), meaning all the people whose habit it is to occupy themselves with asking about it, since many people ask about that. The people of these four types were present in Medina at the time this verse was revealed.

The discussion of the parallel of this verse has already preceded, in the Qur'an's words ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its appointed time?﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], in Surah al-A'raf.

The address in His words "And what would make you know" is to the Messenger (ﷺ). "Ma" here is an interrogative whose referent is a thing (shay').

"Yudrika" is from adra-hu, when it means he informed him. The meaning: what thing gives you knowledge?

The clause ﴿Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ is a new sentence, serving to express a hope (raja').

"La'alla" here suspends the verb of knowing (al-idra') from acting, that is, in regard to the second and third objects; as for the first object, it is the kaf of address.

The meaning: what makes you know whether the Hour is far or near? Perhaps it is near, and perhaps it is far. So in the speech there is ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which one term is omitted from each of two parallel elements, each being implied by the other).

The more apparent view is that "qarib" (near) is the predicate of "takun" (be), that the verb of being is incomplete (naqis), and that the predicate came without the feminine marker, although it carries a feminine pronoun in meaning, since the active participle, like the verb, takes the feminine marker when it bears a lexically feminine pronoun. It has been said that it did not take the feminine marker because the pronoun of the Hour referred back to it after it was interpreted as "the thing" or "the day." But what a group of the verifiers chose, such as Abu 'Ubayda, al-Zajjaj, and Ibn 'Atiyya, is that "qarib" in a verse like this is not a predicate of the verb of being, but is an adverb of it. They mean that the verb of being is complete (tamm), and that "qarib" is an adverb of time for its occurrence. The estimate is: it occurs in a near time. Thus the word "qarib" takes the singular and masculine form, on the intention of a time or a moment. It may be an adverb of time, as is found in its opposite, and that is a rare word in the line of verse:

"And if the daughter of al-Sahmi becomes far from us, she does not speak to us with a word."

Al-Zamakhshari (in al-Kashshaf) pointed to the permissibility of both views. These two views, though they are possible here, are not possible in a verse like His words ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾ [al-A'raf: 56].

"Qarib" and "ba'id" (far) take the feminine marker and similar secondary markers when the intention is to describe. All of these are considerations arising from their broad use of speech. The words of the Exalted ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾ [al-A'raf: 56] have already preceded in al-A'raf, so add it to what is here.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verses 64–65:**

﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein forever; they will find no protector or helper.﴾

This is the share of the disbelievers from the threat of the Hour. This curse is the curse of the Hereafter, and it is joined to the curse of this world in His saying "cursed" (*mal'unin*). For this reason He conjoined to it "and prepared for them a blaze." Thus the curse of this world is linked with seizing and killing, and the curse of the Hereafter is linked with the blaze.

The definite article in "the disbelievers" (*al-kafirin*) may be for specific reference (*al-'ahd*), meaning the disbelievers who had opposed the Messenger (ﷺ), harmed him, and spread rumours in Madinah, namely the hypocrites, those among the polytheists who supported them at the Battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), and the Jews. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 66:

﴿On the Day their faces are turned over in the Fire, they will say, "Oh, would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger!"﴾ (Yawma) is an adverbial of time (zarf) which may be linked to (la yajidun), meaning: even if they found, in the world, allies and helpers from among the Jews of Quraydhah and Khaybar on the Day of the Confederates, then on the Day their faces are turned over in the Fire, they will find neither a protector who has pity on them nor a helper who rescues them. The clause (yaqulun) would then be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (yaqulun).

It is also permissible for the adverbial of time to be linked to the verb (yaqulun), with the pronoun in (la yajidun) as its circumstantial referent.

It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative governed by a deleted verb, whose estimated form is: "Remember," following the manner of its counterparts, the many adverbials of time that occur in the Qur'an. The clause (yaqulun) would then be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (wujuhihim).

Al-taqlib (turning over) is the intense form of al-qalb (turning). Al-qalb is changing the state of a thing so that it faces a direction other than the one it was facing.

The meaning is: On the Day the angels of punishment turn their faces over in the Fire, against their will; or Allah makes that turning happen to their faces so that the Fire reaches the whole face, just as roasting meat is turned over on the grill so that it cooks evenly. If the blast of the Fire were restricted to one side of the face, the other side would have some relief.

The face is singled out for mention among the other limbs because the heat of the Fire harms the face more than the rest of the skin, since the face is the seat of the delicate senses: the eyes, the mouths, the ears and the nostrils. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is one who will shield his face from the terrible punishment on the Day of Resurrection [like one who is safe]?﴾ [al-Zumar: 24].

The particle (ya) in His saying (ya laytana) is for calling attention, aimed at making heard those whose state is to be pitied, like (ya hasratana). The wish here is a figurative expression (kinaya) for regret over what has passed; likewise (ya hasratana), meaning that regret is of no benefit.

They knew on that Day that what the Prophet ﷺ used to command them was a conveying of Allah's will concerning them, and that when they disobeyed him they had disobeyed Allah, the Exalted. So they wished on that Day that they had not disobeyed the Messenger who conveyed from Allah, the Exalted.

The alif at the end of His saying (al-Rasula) serves to maintain the rhyme-endings (fawasil) upon which the surah is built, for it is built on the rhyme-ending of the alif, which is the alif of extension (alif al-itlaq), treating the fawasil in the manner of the qawafi (rhymes) that receive the alif of extension. This was already mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you assume about Allah assumptions﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10] in this surah, and the variant readings concerning its retention or omission in continuous recitation (wasl) were previously discussed.

[p. 117]

It is coordinated with the clause "yaqūlūn" (they say), so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). It is expressed in the past tense because this speech came before their words, "Oh, would that we had obeyed God" [al-Aḥzāb: 66]. That wish arose for them at the time the punishment touched them. They offered this disavowal and supplication as an excuse when they witnessed the punishment and were gathered with their leaders into Hell. God the Exalted says: ﴿Until, when they have all overtaken one another therein, the last of them will say of the first, "Our Lord, these are the ones who led us astray, so give them a double punishment of the Fire." He will say, "For each is double, but you do not know"﴾ [al-A'rāf: 38]. This shows that the speech occurs before the punishment touches them, indeed when they are lined up and driven together, before the punishment is poured upon them and the heat of the Fire is let loose upon them.

Beginning with the call and describing Lordship (rubūbiyya) expresses humble entreaty and supplication.

"Al-sādah" is the plural of "sayyid." Abu 'Ali said: its pattern is fa'alah, like kamalah, but this is not regular, because the pattern fa'alah is regular in the plural of fā'il, not of fay'il. So the wāw was changed to alif because it is vowelled with fatḥa and the letter before it is also vowelled with fatḥa. As for "al-sādāt," it is a plural of the plural, with the addition of alif and tā' in the measure of the sound feminine plural. "Al-sādah" are the great men of the people and the tribes, like kings.

The majority read "sādatanā." Ibn 'Āmir and Ya'qūb read "sādātinā," with an alif after the dāl and with kasra on the tā', because it was pluralised with the added alif and tā' on the pattern of its singular. It is a plural of the plural which is "sādah."

"Al-kubarā'" is the plural of "kabīr," who is the great man of the clan. They are below the "sādah," for "kabīr" is applied to the head of a household, so a man says to his father, "my kabīr." For this reason their words "Oh, would that we had obeyed God and obeyed the Messenger" [al-Aḥzāb: 66] are matched with their words "we obeyed our sādah and our kubarā'."

The sentence ﴿Indeed we obeyed our sādah and our kubarā' and they led us astray from the way﴾ is a report (khabar) used for complaint and grievance, and it is a preparation for demanding redress against their sādah and kubarā'. The aim is therefore to arrive at the sentence ﴿Our Lord, give them a double punishment﴾. It is also intended by this report to make an excuse and disclaim responsibility for their misguidance, saying they were deceived and duped. This excuse is rejected against them by the truth that God caused them to utter when they said, ﴿Indeed we obeyed our sādah and our kubarā'﴾.

[p. 118]

It is therefore directed at them that it be said to them: why did you obey them so that they deceived you? This is the way of the common people, who make lords over themselves those whose dreams they admire, who are beguiled by his sweet talk, and who walk in the steps of his feet; until, when they have gathered the fruits of his blossoms and tasted the bitterness of his taste and the heat of his thirst, they turn against him with blame, while they are the most deserving of his reproach.

The emphatic particle (inna) is for mere emphasis of concern, not to refute a denial. The fronting of their words "Indeed we obeyed our sādah and our kubarā'" expresses concern with what it contains of a justification for the content of their words "and they led us astray from the way," because their kubarā' could not have caused their misguidance except through their blind obedience to them and their occupation with obeying them, away from considering and reasoning about what they called them to of corruption and evil outcome; and through their placing the sayings of their sādah and kubarā' above what the Messenger ﷺ called them to.

"Al-sabīl" is in the accusative by the omission of the preposition, because "aḍalla," with the hamza, takes only one direct object, as God the Exalted says: ﴿He had indeed led me astray from the Reminder﴾ [al-Furqān: 29]. The apparent view of al-Kashshāf is that it takes two objects, so that the unaugmented "ḍalla" takes one object. You say "ḍalaltu al-ṭarīq" (I lost the road), while "aḍalla" with the hamza takes two objects. Ibn 'Aṭiyya also said this.

The discussion of the alif in "al-sabīlā" is the same as the discussion of the alif in "al-rasūlā."

Repeating the call in their words ﴿Our Lord, give them a double punishment﴾ is an emphasis of supplication and entreaty, and a preparation for the acceptance of their request, so that when their request is accepted they hope to be freed from the punishment which they cast upon the shoulders of their kubarā'.

"Al-ḍi'f" with a kasra on the ḍād is a number equal to the counted thing, so four is the ḍi'f of two. Since punishment is a meaning among meanings and not an entity, the repetition of the number in it is a metaphor (majāz) for strength and severity.

The dual "ḍi'fayn" is used for unrestricted repetition, as a metonymy (kināya) for the intensity of the punishment, like God the Exalted's words: ﴿Then return the gaze twice; the gaze will return to you dazzled, and it will be weary﴾ [al-Mulk: 4]. For the gaze does not become dazzled by two glances. For this reason his words here ﴿give them a double punishment﴾ are equivalent to his words ﴿so give them a double punishment of the Fire﴾ [al-A'rāf: 38] in Sūrat al-A'rāf. This is an allusion [p. 119] to placing the burden of misguidance upon them, and that the punishment prepared for them will be imposed upon those who led them astray.

The curse is described as "many," just as the punishment is described as "double," indicating that the kubarā' deserved a punishment for their own disbelief and a punishment for causing the disbelief of their followers.

Thus "al-kathīr" here means the severe and strong, and it is expressed by "many" to match the sense of duality in his words "ḍi'fayn," whose meaning is multiplicity.

In al-A'rāf the reply from the Majesty was mentioned by his words ﴿For each is double﴾ [al-A'rāf: 38], meaning that the kubarā' deserved the multiplication of punishment for their misguidance and their misleading, and that their followers also deserved punishment for their own misguidance and for making their sādah lords and for their blind obedience to them.

[Page 120]

﴿O you who have believed, do not be like those who abused Moses, but Allah cleared him of what they said, and he was honorable in the sight of Allah.﴾ When the threat against those who harm the Messenger ﷺ with denial and the like, the harm arising from their disbelief, among the polytheists and hypocrites, had been concluded, from His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who abuse Allah and His Messenger, Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Ahzab: 57], He warned the believers against what harms the Messenger ﷺ by keeping them away from becoming like a people who attributed to their Messenger something that was a harm to him, while they did not care about the anger it caused him, which entails the anger of Allah, exalted is He. Since much harm may occur through the heedlessness of his companions regarding what is directed at him, so that from them there issue words that their thoughts surge with before reflecting on the possibilities surrounding them, which would dispel and negate them, and without considering what duties follow from them, and likewise there issue from them actions that bring ruin upon them before considering the outcome of their deeds, Allah alerted the believers so that they would not fall into such recklessness (ʿanjahiyya), because the faculties of the intelligent in noticing the meanings of things and their necessary implications differ in degree, and so they deserve to be awakened and warned. The benefit of the comparison (tashbih) is to render the compared state ugly, because the believers have already had firmly established in their souls the ugliness of what Moses, peace be upon him, was harmed with, as mentioned earlier in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿And when Moses said to his people: "O my people, why do you harm me, when you know that I am the Messenger of Allah to you?" So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5], and so on.

Those who harmed Moses were groups of his people, and their intention was not to harm him, but they neglected the obligation of complete courtesy and consideration toward the greatest of people among them. Allah has related this about them in summary and in detail by His saying: ﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾ [al-Saff: 5], and so on. Therefore this harm was not of the kind of denial on account of his saying: ﴿that I am the Messenger of Allah to you﴾ [al-Saff: 5]. The interrogative in His saying "why do you harm me" (lima tu'dhūnanī) is one of denial (inkārī). Thus the address to the believers of the nation of Muhammad ﷺ was directed in a way that takes into account the resemblance between the two situations in the occurrence of harm.

Those who harmed Moses once said: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are sitting here﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24], so they harmed him through disobedience and a kind of mockery. And they once said: "Do you take us in mockery?" so they attributed to him levity and ridicule, and for this reason he said to them: ﴿I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67]. In the Torah, in chapter fourteen of Exodus: "And they said to Moses: Would it not have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness?" And in chapter sixteen: "And they said to Moses and Aaron: You have brought us out into this wilderness to kill all this congregation with hunger." And in the hadith: "Moses was a modest, very private man, so a group of his people said: 'We do not see him conceal himself except because of a defect in him.' Some people said: 'He has leprosy,' and others said: 'He has a hernia,'" and the like of this. Close to this was the saying of the hypocrites: "Muhammad married the divorced wife of his son, Zayd ibn Harithah."

This verse indicates the obligation of honoring the Prophet ﷺ and avoiding what harms him, and that is the practice of the Companions and the Muslims. Yet some slips came from some of his companions who had not yet reached the full moral refinement of the Qur'an, such as the one who said to him when he judged between him and al-Zubayr concerning the water of Shiraj al-Harra: "Only because he is the son of your paternal aunt, O Messenger of Allah." And like the Tamimite Kharfusah, who said concerning the distribution of the spoils of Hunayn: "This is a distribution by which the face of Allah was not intended." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "May Allah have mercy on Moses; he was harmed with more than this and was patient."

Know that the locus of the comparison is His saying: ﴿like those who abused Moses﴾, not what is derived from it by His saying: ﴿so Allah cleared him of what they said﴾. Rather that is an embedding (idmaj) and an opportunistic use of the context, by mentioning the clearing of Moses from what they said, and it has no connection to the aspect of the comparison, because our Prophet ﷺ was not harmed in a manner that required the manifestation of his innocence from what he was harmed with.

[Page 121]

The meaning of "cleared him" (barra'ahu) is that He manifested his innocence visibly, because Moses was innocent of what they said before they harmed him with their words. So the existence of his innocence was not a consequence of their words, but Allah manifested it after their words. For Allah manifested his innocence from deceiving them, when He commanded them to enter Jericho, so He strengthened their hearts and they conquered it, and He manifested his innocence from mocking them, when He showed His miracle at the time they slaughtered the cow that He had commanded them to slaughter, so the one who killed the soul about which they disputed was made manifest. He also manifested his soundness from leprosy and hernia when he appeared to them naked after the stone that carried his garments moved away. The meaning of "cleared him of what they said" is that He cleared him of the content of their saying, not of the very act of their saying, because their saying had occurred and he was harmed by it. This is like how they named the slander a "qālah" (talk). Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and We will inherit from him what he says﴾ [Maryam: 80], meaning what his speech indicates, which is his saying: ﴿I will surely be given wealth and children﴾ [Maryam: 77], meaning We will inherit from him his wealth and his children.

The clause ﴿and he was honorable in the sight of Allah﴾ is a parenthetical statement at the end of the speech, indicating the reason for Allah's care in clearing him.

The word wajīh is an adjective, meaning one possessing wajāha, which is rank (jāh) and good acceptance among people. It is said: "the man became wajīh" (wujiha al-rajul), with the jīm vowelled with a ḍammah, wajāha, so he is wajīh. This verb is derived from the solid noun wajh, which is the face of a person. So the meaning of his being wajīh in the sight of Allah is that he is pleased with and accepted by Him, and his supplication is answered.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿honorable in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 45], has already been mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran, so add it to here. The mention of the verb "was" (kāna) indicates the firm establishment of his honor in the sight of Allah, exalted is He.

This is a rebuke to those who harmed him, in that they harmed him with what he was innocent of, and a direction toward Allah's exoneration of him, in that he deserved that clearing, because he is honorable in the sight of Allah and is not obscure.

[p. 122]

After God had forbidden the believers from what harms the Prophet (ﷺ), and had admonished them against becoming like those who harmed their Messenger, He addressed them with a call to adorn themselves with taqwa (God-consciousness) and soundness of speech. This is because the benefit of being forbidden from blameworthy deeds is to be clothed in praiseworthy qualities, and taqwa is the sum of good in action and speech. Sound speech spreads virtues.

Beginning the discourse with the call to "those who believe" serves to draw attention to it and to win the listener's attention. Addressing them with "those who believe" implies that faith requires what they are about to be commanded. This contains an indirect suggestion that those who actually do what harms the Prophet (ﷺ) intentionally are not, in their inner reality, among the believers, but are hypocrites. The mention of the command to taqwa first indicates that what they will be commanded regarding sound speech is also among the branches of taqwa, just as it is among the branches of faith.

Qawl (speech) is the utterance that comes from a person's mouth, expressing what is in his soul.

Sadid (sound) is that which conforms to sadad. Sadad is correctness and truth. From it comes tasdid al-sahm (aiming the arrow) toward the target, meaning not deviating from its mark, so that when it is released it hits its aim. Thus sound speech includes obligatory statements and good, beneficial statements, such as initiating the greeting of peace and a believer saying to a fellow believer whom he loves: "I love you."

Speech can be a great door to good, and it can likewise be a door to evil. In a hadith: "Do people get thrown into the Fire on their faces except by the harvest of their tongues?" And in another hadith:

"May God have mercy on a man who speaks a good word and profits by it, or keeps silent and is safe." And in another hadith:

"Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him say what is good or keep silent."

Sound speech includes what expresses guidance from the words of the prophets, scholars and wise men, and what conveys to others the transmitted sayings of the prophets and scholars. Thus reciting the Qur'an to people is sound speech, and narrating the hadith of the Messenger (ﷺ) is sound speech. In a hadith: "May God make radiant a man who heard my saying, memorized it, and conveyed it as he heard it." Likewise, spreading the sayings of the Companions, the wise, and the imams of jurisprudence is included. Also included in sound speech is glorifying God and praising Him, such as tasbih (saying "Glory be to God"). Among sound speech are the adhan (call to prayer) and the iqamah (second call to prayer). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ [Fatir: 10] in Surat Fatir. Thus, through sound speech, virtues and truths spread among people, and they desire to adopt them. Through bad speech, misguidance and deceptions spread, and people are deluded by them, thinking that they are doing good.

Sound speech includes commanding what is right and forbidding what is wrong.

Because taqwa and sound speech are means to righteousness, God made the reward for those who bring them about the amendment of deeds and the forgiveness of sins. This is a nashr (a rhetorical device in which the elements are mentioned in the reverse order of a previous list) in reverse order: the amendment of deeds is a reward for sound speech, because what sound speech mostly yields is guiding people to righteousness, or people imitating the one who speaks soundly.

The forgiveness of sins is a reward for taqwa, because the pillar of taqwa is avoiding major sins. God has forgiven people their minor sins by avoiding major sins, and has forgiven them major sins through repentance. Turning away from sins after intending them is a form of their forgiveness.

Furthermore, since the plural second-person pronouns refer to "those who believe," they are general to all believers across all times, whether the deeds are those of the speakers of sound speech or the deeds of other believers who hear their words. For they are never free of a group that is influenced by that speech and acts according to what it requires, with variation among those who act. In accordance with this variation, the righteousness of the deeds of those who speak sound speech, and of those who act upon it among its hearers, varies. Likewise, the deeds of one who speaks sound speech at the time of hearing another's speech. In a hadith: "For many a bearer of knowledge conveys it to one who is more learned than he." Thus it becomes clear that the amendment of deeds varies. However that may be, the righteousness of what is done is among the effects of the soundness of speech. Likewise, taqwa becomes a cause for the forgiveness of the sins of the God-conscious person and the forgiveness of the sins of others, because part of taqwa is restraining oneself from participating in the sins of sinners. Thus many of them refrain from their sins out of emulation or modesty, and some sins are thereby brought to a halt. That is a form of forgiveness. If one follows and is guided, then the matter is all the more deserving.

The mention of (lakum) ("for you") with the two verbs (yuslih) ("He will amend") and (yaghfir) ("He will forgive") serves to indicate care for the God-conscious who speak sound speech, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1].

The clause ﴿And whoever obeys God and His Messenger has certainly achieved a great achievement﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿He will amend for you your deeds and forgive you your sins﴾, meaning: and you will succeed with a great success if you obey God by carrying out His command. The clause was phrased in the form of a conditional sentence and its response in order to convey generality regarding the obedient and the types of acts of obedience. Thus the clause, with these two generalities, has the force of a tadhyil (a concluding statement that reinforces the meaning of what precedes). This is a fine weave in the composition of speech, namely conveying two purposes with a single clause.
