Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 72 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they refused to bear it and were apprehensive of it, and man bore it. Indeed, he was a wrongdoer, ignorant.﴾

It is an initial resumptive statement (isti'naf ibtida'i) which conveys information about a great sunnah (divine law/pattern) among the sunan of Allah the Exalted in the creation of the world and what is in it, and especially man, so that people may observe, in their conduct and dealings with their Lord and in their dealings with one another, the extent to which they follow this sunnah and observe its application. Their presentation of their deeds upon its standard will then indicate to them their destiny and clarify the reason for the preference of some over others and the selection of some from among others.

The placement of this verse after what precedes it and at the end of this surah requires that its content be connected to the content of what came before it, and it serves as an aid to discovering the precise meaning and removing the veils of symbolism from what is intended by it, even if only by reducing the possibilities and arriving at the ultimate outcome.

The opening with the particle of emphasis (inna) is for drawing attention to the report, or for treating it as though it were something the listener might deny, given the strangeness of its matter.

The opening of the verse with the root 'ard (offering), its formulation in the past tense, and making its object the heavens, the earth, the mountains and man, indicate that the object of this offering existed on one level, and this requires that it was an eternal offering at the origin of creation, when the divine power was directed to bringing the earthly beings into existence and depositing in them their distinguishing features which constitute their realities, their characteristics and their qualities suited to fulfilling what they were created for. This is like the saying of Him: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants﴾ [al-A'raf: 172], the verse.

The verse's closing with the cause from His saying ﴿so that Allah may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 73] to the end of the surah requires that the trust mentioned in this verse has a special relevance to a lesson concerning the conditions of the hypocrites and the polytheists among the human species, in observing the trust and in neglecting it.

Page 125

Therefore it is fitting for us to say: this offering was at the origin of the creation of the world and the human species; for when the heavens, the earth and the mountains are mentioned in it together with man, it is known that what is meant by man is his species. For if some of its individuals were meant, even at the very beginning of the creation, then there would be no connection between that individual's bearing of the trust and the punishment of the hypocrites and polytheists, and there would be no wisdom appropriate to the acts of Allah the Exalted in the bearing of the trust by some of its individuals and not others.

Thus the definite article in al-insan (man) is the definite article of the genus, that is, the species of man.

As for 'ard (offering): its reality is bringing a thing before another so that it may choose it or accept it, and from it is the offering of the water-trough to the she-camel, that is, offering it to her to drink from it, and the offering of recruits to the commander for the acceptance of those among them who are qualified. In the hadith of Ibn 'Umar: "I was presented to the Messenger of Allah when I was fourteen and he rejected me, and I was presented to him when I was fifteen and he permitted me." It has been mentioned previously at His saying ﴿They will be presented before their Lord﴾ [Hud: 18] in Surah Hud, and His saying ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows﴾ [al-Kahf: 48] in Surah al-Kahf.

So His saying (﴿'aradna﴾) here is a metaphor by way of representation (isti'arah tamthiliyyah) for placing one thing in another, because it is qualified for it to the exclusion of the rest of things, and the non-placement of it in the rest of things is due to their not being qualified for that thing. The state of withdrawing the bearing of the trust from the heavens, the earth and the mountains and placing it in man is likened to the state of one who offers a thing to people, and some of them reject it while one of them accepts it, in the manner of representation; or it is a representation of the relation of Allah the Exalted's knowledge to the unsuitability of the heavens, the earth and the mountains for having attached to them what is expressed by the trust, and the suitability of man for that. Thus the state of Allah's knowledge regarding the incapacity of the heavens, the earth and the mountains to bear the trust, in contrast to man's capacity for it, is likened to offering a thing to several things in order to ascertain the degree of suitability of one of those things for being characterized by the offered thing.

The purpose of this representation is to magnify the matter of this trust, since it has reached the point that nothing among the greatest things people see of the kinds of existents can bear it. So the specification of the heavens and the earth by mention among existents is because they are the greatest of what is known to people among existents, and the conjunction of the mountains with the earth, though they are part of it, is because the mountains are the greatest of the known parts of the visible surface of the earth, whose greatness the eyes witness, since the eyes

Page 126

do not see the terrestrial globe as a whole, as He the Exalted said: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart from fear of Allah﴾ [al-Hashr: 21].

The indicator of the metaphor is situational (hali), namely the impossibility of attributing offering and refusal to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, due to the absence of their perception; for how could they choose and reject? Likewise man, insofar as what is meant by him is his genus and quiddity, because the quiddity does not deliberate or choose, as one says: "Nature is blind," meaning it has no choice; that is, the innate nature only produces its effects by compulsion.

Therefore the verbs ('aradna, abayna, yahmilna-ha, ashfaqna minha, and hamalaha) are components of the representational compound. These components are suitable for each of them to be a single metaphor, by likening the deposit of the trust in man and its removal from others to the offering; and likening the lack of what makes the realities of the heavens, the earth and the mountains suitable for receiving the trust to refusal (aba'); and likening the deposit to commissioning and bearing (tahmil and haml); and likening the lack of compatibility among the realities of the heavens, the earth and the mountains to incapacity to accept those beings it, which is what is expressed by apprehension (ishfaq); and likening the compatibility and the factor making acceptance possible for the deposit of the attribute of trust in man to bearing a weight.

Similar metaphors are numerous in eloquent speech. The capacity of the representational compound to be dissolved into its components as a number of metaphors is one of the marks of the perfection of that representation.

This verse has been counted among the difficulties of the Qur'an, and the exegetes have wavered in its interpretation, a wavering that indicates bewilderment in determining its meaning. The source of this lies in determining the meaning of the offering to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, in knowing the meaning of the trust, and in knowing the meaning of refusal and apprehension.

As for the offering, its meanings have become clear from what you have learned of the manner of representation. As for the trust, it is what is entrusted and required to be preserved and fulfilled without waste or excess; and the exegetes have differed concerning it in twenty opinions, some of which overlap with others. Let us begin with a general outline of them and then turn to scrutinizing and clarifying them. It has been said: the trust is obedience; it has been said: prayer; it has been said: the totality of prayer, fasting and ritual washing; it has been said: all the obligations; it has been said: submission to the religion; it has been said: guarding the private parts; it has been said: the trust is monotheism, or the indications of divine unity, or the manifestations of Allah through His names

Page 127

It has been said: what is entrusted, and from it is fulfilling the covenant, and from it is the absence of deceit in action; it has been said: the trust is the intellect; it has been said: the caliphate, that is, the caliphate of Allah on earth which He deposited with man, as He the Exalted said: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successive authority (khalifah)"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], the verse.

These opinions return to categories: the category of acts of obedience and the laws (shara'i'), the category of beliefs ('aqa'id), a category opposite to betrayal, the category of intellect, and the category of the caliphate of the earth.

The category of laws should be set aside from them, because they are not necessarily inherent in human nature, since nations have long been free of obligation by laws, namely the people of the interval (ahl al-fatrah). Thus six opinions fall away, and these are what are in the first category.

The remaining categories remain, because they are firmly rooted in man's disposition and innate nature. So it is possible that the trust is the trust of faith, that is, the oneness of Allah, and it is the covenant which Allah took from the human species, which is what is in His saying: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we testify"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172], and it was mentioned previously in Surah al-A'raf. The meaning is that Allah deposited in the souls of people the indications of divine unity, so they are inseparable from human reason, and it is as if they were a covenant of Allah with them concerning it, and as if it were a trust with which He entrusted them, since He deposited it in their innate constitution, inseparable from it. This trust was not deposited in the heavens, the earth and the mountains, because this trust belongs to the category of knowledge, and knowledge is not characterized except by one in whom the attribute of life subsists, since it is what makes perception valid for the one in whom it subsists. This interpretation is suited by His saying: ﴿so that Allah may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women and the polytheist men and polytheist women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 73], for these two groups are devoid of faith in the oneness of Allah.

It is also possible that the trust is the intellect, and calling it a trust is a magnification of its status, and because psychological things are deposited with whoever keeps them.

The meaning is that wisdom required that man be the repository of the intellect among the great existents, because his creation is suited to being rational, for the intellect prompts change and movement from one state to another and from one place to another. If it were placed in a heaven among the heavens, or in the earth, or in a mountain among the mountains, or in all of them, it would have been a cause of

Page 128

the disturbance and collapse of worlds. The nearest existents that could carry the intellect are the kinds of animals other than man, and if the intellect were deposited in them, the structures of their bodies would not permit them to obey what the intellect commands them. Suppose the intellect prompted the horse not to wait for its fodder or its pasture, and to go out to a grain-merchant to buy fodder from him; it would not be able to make itself understood, nor could it hand the payment with its own hand to another horse. Likewise, if its dealing were with one of the human species.

The relevance of His saying ﴿so that Allah may punish the hypocrite men﴾ [al-Ahzab: 73], the verse, to this interpretation is like its relevance to the first interpretation.

It is also possible that the trust is what is entrusted, because man is civil by nature, mixing with his own kind, so he is never free of entrusting or being entrusted; thus man bears the attribute of trust by his innate nature, and people vary in fulfilling what they have been entrusted with, as in the hadith: "When trust is lost, then await the Hour," meaning: when trust has vanished, its vanishing is a sign of the disruption of the innate nature, and it was among the disruptions that warn of the nearness of the Hour, like the folding up of the sun, the dimming of the stars, and the crumbling of the mountains.

What clarifies this meaning is the statement of Hudhayfah: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ related to us two hadiths; I have seen one of them while I await the other. He told us that trust descended into the root of men's hearts, then they learned from the Qur'an, then they learned from the Sunnah. And he related to us about its removal, saying: a man sleeps a sleep and trust is taken from his heart, and its trace remains like the trace of a mark; then he sleeps another sleep and it is taken, and its trace remains like a blister, like an ember you roll onto your foot, so it blisters, and you see it swollen while there is nothing in it. People then rise and trade with one another, and hardly anyone fulfills the trust, so it is said: 'In such-and-such a tribe there is a trustworthy man,' and it is said of a man: 'How intelligent he is, how witty he is, how strong he is!' while there is not in his heart the weight of a mustard seed of faith" — that is, of trust, because faith is part of trust, since it is the covenant of Allah.

Page 129

The meaning of offering the trust to the heavens, the earth and the mountains falls within the meaning of interpreting the trust as the intellect, because trust in this sense is among the moral qualities which the intellect gathers and directs; and in that case its specification by mention serves to draw attention to its importance among the moral qualities of the intellect.

The discussion of the meaning of the trust (amanah) as the caliphate of God on earth is similar to the discussion of reason ('aql), because that caliphate was prepared for man only by reason, as indicated by His saying, ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am making upon the earth a successive authority (khalifah)"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], then His saying, ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31]. So the caliphate on earth is the undertaking of preserving its prosperity (i'mar), placing the existing things in it in their proper places, and using them for what their natural dispositions (ghara'iz) are prepared for.

The remaining matters by which some exegetes have explained the trust are considered, in their explanation, to be a matter of mentioning particular examples of universal meanings.

The most evident of these interpretations is that the intended meaning of the trust is its well-known reality, which is the safeguarding of what has been entrusted, tending to it, and guarding against failing in it, whether by inadvertence or negligence, which is called neglect (tafrit) and waste (idla'), or deliberately, which is called treachery (khiyanah) and betrayal (khays). This is because this interpretation is the one that fits the occurrence of this verse at the end of the surah that began by describing the treachery of the hypocrites and the Jews, their breaking of covenants, and their wavering toward the Prophet (ﷺ). God, the Exalted, says, ﴿And they had already made a covenant with God before, that they would not turn their backs﴾ [al-Ahzab: 15], and He says, ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted with God﴾ [al-Ahzab: 23]. This interpretation also includes the closest of the interpretations after it, which is that it is reason ('aql), since the acceptance of moral qualities is a branch of it.

The clause ﴿Indeed, he was wrongdoing, ignorant﴾ has a position of interjection (i'tiraD) between the clause ﴿and man carried it﴾ and what is connected to its verb, which is ﴿that God may punish the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab: 73], etc. Its meaning is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani), because the listener has heard that man bore the trust, so he awaits knowledge of how well man fulfilled what he was charged with and undertook. The clause is not causal (ta'lili), because the bearing of the trust was not by man's choice, so how can it be explained that his bearing the trust was because of his wrongdoing and ignorance?

So the meaning of ﴿he was wrongdoing, ignorant﴾ is that he fell short in fulfilling the right of what he undertook, a shortfall: part of it from deliberate intent, which is expressed by the description "wrongdoing" (zalum), and part from negligence in taking up the means of fulfillment, which is expressed by his being "ignorant" (jahul). So zalum is an intensive form of injustice, and likewise jahul is an intensive form of ignorance.

Injustice (zulm) is transgressing upon the right of another, and what is meant here is transgressing upon the right of God, to whom man committed himself by bearing the trust, which is the right of fulfilling the trust. Ignorance (jahl) is the absence of knowledge of what must be known, and what is meant here is man's lack of knowledge of the places of correctness in what he undertook. Thus the phrase ﴿Indeed, he was wrongdoing, ignorant﴾ indicates an omitted statement which it itself implies, since the implied sense is: "and man bore it, but did not fulfill it. Indeed, he was wrongdoing, ignorant." It is as if it were said: "So he was wrongdoing, ignorant," meaning wrongdoing in not fulfilling the trust, because it is an injury to the one who holds the right in the trust, whoever he may be; and ignorant in not assessing the degree of the consequence of wasting the trust, from the graded accountability that varies in its ranks. Without this assessment the speech would not cohere, because man was not charged with the trust by his own choice, but was created disposed to bear it.

It is also possible that what is meant is "wrongdoing, ignorant" in his natural disposition, that is, in the nature of injustice and ignorance, so he is exposed to them unless the restraint of religion preserves him. Thus it was from his injustice and ignorance that many people wasted the trust they had borne.

You may also make the pronoun in (innahu) refer to man, and restrict its generality to disbelieving man by specification through reason, since it is evident that the wrongdoing, ignorant one is the disbeliever.

Or you may make the pronoun in (innahu) an istikhdam, so that it refers to man while meaning by him the disbeliever. The word "man" (al-insan) has been used in many places in the Qur'an while meaning the disbeliever, as in His saying, ﴿And man says, "When I have died, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?"﴾ [Maryam: 66], and the verses, and His saying, ﴿O man, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ [al-Infitar: 6] and what follows.

In the mention of the verb (kana) there is an indication that his injustice and ignorance are attributes rooted in him, because they are the predominant ones among his individuals, which accompany them whether in abundance or in scarcity.

Thus the two intensive forms are considered with regard to abundance and intensity in most individuals of the human species, and a ruling imposed upon kinds, species and tribes takes the predominant case into account, especially in a context of warning and intimidation. This generality is explained by His saying after it, ﴿that God may punish the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab: 73], up to His saying, ﴿and that God may turn in forgiveness toward the believing men and believing women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 73]. Its detail has come by mentioning two groups: one of them neglects the trust, and the other observes it.

For this reason God praised those who fulfilled covenants and trusts. He said in this surah, ﴿And the covenant of God is ever questioned﴾ [al-Ahzab: 15], and He said in it, ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted with God﴾ [al-Ahzab: 23], and He said, ﴿And mention in the Book Ismail; indeed, he was true to his promise﴾ [Maryam: 54]. And He said of the opposite of that, ﴿And He does not cause to go astray thereby except the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26], ﴿those who break the covenant of God after its confirmation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 27], up to His saying, ﴿It is those who are the losers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 27].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 33, verse 73:

﴿So that Allah may punish the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women, and the polytheist men and the polytheist women, and that Allah may accept the repentance of the believing men and the believing women. And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ It is connected to His saying ﴿and man carried it﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72], because the hypocrites, the polytheists and the believers are all categories of mankind. This lam is the lam of metaphorical causation, called lam al-'aqibah (the lam of consequence). Its meaning was discussed more than once before, the first being His saying ﴿Indeed, We give them respite only so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 178] in Surat Ali 'Imran.

The well-known example of it is His saying ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. The grammarians (nuhat) and the scholars of rhetoric (ulama' al-bayan) customarily say that it has the sense of the fa' of consequence (fa' al-tafri'). Since this was a consequence of man's bearing the trust, and since what the lam of causation was attached to contained a generality, it is determined that this clause provides an explanation of what was stated in general terms in His saying ﴿Indeed, he was a wrongdoer, ignorant﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72], as we mentioned just above. That is, mankind became two groups: a group that is wrongdoing and ignorant, and a group that is rightly guided and knowledgeable.

The meaning is: Allah punishes the hypocrites and the polytheists for not fulfilling the trust which they had taken on in the original nature (fitrah) and according to the Law (shari'ah), and He accepts the repentance of the believers, forgiving them their sins, because they fulfilled the trust which they had taken on. This is like His saying earlier, ﴿that Allah may reward the truthful for their truthfulness and punish the hypocrites if He wills or turn to them in forgiveness﴾ [al-Ahzab: 24]. That is, just as He turned to the believers by their regretting what they had neglected of their hypocrisy, and purifying their faith, so Allah turns to them in forgiveness. This has been realised in many of them.

The manifest mention of the Name of Allah in His saying (and that Allah may accept the repentance), where the expected form would have been a pronoun, is for the sake of greater emphasis on this repentance, because of the emphasis conveyed by the explicit mention in a place where a pronoun would have been expected.

And the mention of the hypocrite women, the polytheist women and the believing women alongside the hypocrite men, the polytheist men and the believing men, though it was unnecessary, is by means of the plural form which is commonly used in Arabic speech to include women, as in their saying: "Sickness befell the sons of so-and-so," meaning and their women as well.

So the mention of women in the verse points to the fact that they had a role in the events of the Battle of the Trench (Ghazwat al-Khandaq), by assisting their men against the Muslims. The opposite was the case for the women of the Muslims.

The clause ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾ is good news for the believing men and the believing women that Allah has dealt with them by forgiveness and what the attribute of mercy requires.

* * *

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)
(Surat Saba')

This is its name by which it became well known in the books of Sunnah, in the books of tafsir (exegesis) and among the reciters. I have not come across its being named in the age of prophethood. The reason for its being named thus is that the story of the people of Saba' is mentioned in it.

It is Meccan, and the consensus of the people of tafsir on this has been reported. From Muqatil: the verse ﴿and those who have been given knowledge see﴾ [Saba': 6] up to His saying ﴿the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Saba': 6] was revealed in Medina. Perhaps this is based on their interpretation that "those who have been given knowledge" refers only to the People of the Book who embraced Islam, such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam. The truth is that those who have been given knowledge are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, or they are the community of Muhammad, as said by Qatadah; that is, because they were given much knowledge through the Qur'an. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Rather, it is clear signs in the breasts of those who have been given knowledge﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 49]. Yet there is no objection to holding that they were scholars of the People of the Book before they believed, because the aim is to argue with what is firmly established in their souls, which was indicated by the conversion of a group of them, as we will explain at His saying, ﴿and those who have been given knowledge see﴾ [Saba': 6], etc.

Ibn al-Hisar holds that Surat Saba' is Medinan, on the basis of what al-Tirmidhi narrated from Farwah ibn Musayk al-Ghutayfi al-Muradi, who said: "I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)..." up to his saying: "And there was revealed concerning Saba' what was revealed." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is Saba'?" The hadith... Ibn al-Hisar said: Farwah migrated in the ninth year after the conquest of al-Ta'if. Ibn al-Hisar also said: It is possible that his saying "was revealed" is a report of what had been revealed before Farwah's migration, meaning that a questioner asked about it when he recited it or heard it from this surah or from Surat al-Naml.

It is the fifty-eighth surah in the order of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat Luqman and before Surat al-Zumar, as is related from Jabir ibn Zayd, and al-Ja'bari relied on it, as is found in al-Itqan. It has been mentioned in Surat al-Isra' that His saying there ﴿And they said: "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth"﴾ [al-Isra': 90], up to His saying ﴿or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claim﴾ [al-Isra': 92], refers to His saying in this surah ﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them, or cause to fall upon them pieces from the sky﴾ [Saba': 9]. This implies that Surat Saba' was revealed before Surat al-Isra', which contradicts the order of Jabir ibn Zayd, who counts al-Isra' as completing the fifty.

It is not necessarily the case that their saying ﴿or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claim﴾ [al-Isra': 92] refers to this verse, since the Prophet (ﷺ) may have threatened them with that in another admonition.

The number of its verses is fifty-four according to the majority count, and fifty-five according to the count of the people of Syria.

* * *

The Aims of This Surah

Among the aims of this surah (Saba') is refuting the foundations of polytheism, the greatest of which is their associating gods with Allah, and denying the Resurrection. It begins with proof of Allah's exclusive divinity apart from their idols, and negating that the idols could be intercessors for their worshippers.

Then comes the subject of the Resurrection. From Muqatil: the reason for its revelation was that when Abu Sufyan heard His saying ﴿So that Allah may punish the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women﴾, the last verse of Surat al-Ahzab, he said to his companions: "It seems that Muhammad is threatening us with punishment after we die. By al-Lat and al-'Uzza, the Hour will never come to us!" So Allah revealed ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "The Hour will not come upon us"﴾ [Saba': 3], the verse.

Accordingly, what precedes the mentioned verse, from His saying ﴿Praise be to Allah, to Whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [Saba': 1] up to His saying ﴿And He is the Merciful, the Forgiving﴾ [Saba': 2], is a preparation for the purpose of His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "The Hour will not come upon us"﴾ [Saba': 3]. And establishing the comprehensive knowledge of Allah of whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, so whatever He informs of is certain to happen, and among that is the establishment of the Resurrection and recompense.

And establishing the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ) in what he reported, and the truthfulness of what the Qur'an brought, and that the Qur'an was attested to by the scholars of the People of the Book.

This is interspersed with various forms of warning the polytheists and admonishing them with what befell some of the polytheist nations before them. And it is hinted that their making partners with Allah is ingratitude for the blessing of the Creator. So He set forth for them the example of those who were thankful for Allah's blessing and feared Him, and so they were granted the best of this world and the Hereafter, and good things were subjected to them, like Dawud and Sulayman; and of those who disbelieved in Allah, and so afflictions were imposed upon them in this world and a punishment was prepared for them in the Hereafter, like the people of Saba'. They were warned against Satan, and reminded that what they have of the delight of the eyes brings them closer to Allah, and warned of what they will face on the Day of Recompense of disgrace, denial, regret, having no helper, and abiding in punishment, while the believers were given good news of everlasting bliss.
